additional_notes: A common colloquial phrase used to ask or demand that someone stop an action. 톤 can be anything from mild (polite) to strong (angry) depending on ending and context. Often followed by verbs like 하다, 찍다, etc. Adding polite endings (해요) makes it softer; adding rough language (씨발) makes it very strong/angry. Used to express annoyance or to tell someone they've done enough.
native_language_example: Please stop!

meaning: Stop it / Cut it out (please).
additional_notes: A common request or demand telling someone to stop doing something annoying or unwanted. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be polite with '좀' and used firmly or casually; can be more forceful without '좀'. Often used alone as an interjection (그만 좀 하다!, or colloquially 그만 좀 해!).
native_language_example: Stop it, please stop.

meaning: Stop it / Cut it out (asking someone to stop doing something).
additional_notes: A direct, commonly used phrase to tell someone to stop an action or behavior. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be annoyed, pleading, or firm. Adding names (e.g., '무라타') or polite markers changes nuance. '좀' softens the command slightly; without it, it's harsher. Not formal — avoid using with superiors without politeness.
native_language_example: Please stop it.

meaning: to stop (doing something); to quit; to finish
additional_notes: Commonly used to tell someone to stop an action or to say you will stop doing something. Can be used imperatively (그만 해!/그만 하세요!) meaning “Stop it!” or in past tense (그만했다) meaning “I quit/finished.” Often appears as two parts: 그만 (enough/stop) + 하다 (to do). Tone and politeness depend on endings and context.
target_language_example: 그만 하다 말고 이제 진짜 그만 하세요.
native_language_example: Stop saying “stop it” and really stop now.

meaning: Stop it. / Cut it out. (tell someone to stop doing something)
additional_notes: Informal or neutral command used to tell someone to stop an action or to stop bothering you. Can be softened with 제발 (please) or made stronger with repetition (그만해, 그만!). Often said abruptly; use with friends or in casual situations. Can also be used about actions (stop doing X) by adding a verb before/after (e.g., 그만해라 for stronger/formal).
native_language_example: Stop it, I really can't take it!

meaning: Stop it / Please stop (polite).
additional_notes: Polite/formal request or command to stop an action or speech. Can be used firmly or pleadingly depending on tone and added words (e.g., 제발 그만 해요 = Please stop). 이제 그만 해요 = That's enough/stop now. Common in everyday situations; not rude but not overly formal.
target_language_example: 아, 그만 해요! 더 이상 안 해요.
native_language_example: Oh, stop it! I won't do it anymore.

meaning: He/She/That person (honorific) + topic marker '는'.
additional_notes: 그분 (geubun) is an honorific way to refer to a third person (someone respected or not present). It is more polite than 그 사람 and often used when speaking respectfully about elders, teachers, or clients. The particle 는 marks the topic. Use 그분은 when introducing or talking about that person politely; for neutral reference use 그 사람은, for familiar use 그 사람/그는/그녀는 depending on context.
native_language_example: He/She is my teacher.

meaning: his/her/their (polite/formal possessive)
additional_notes: 그분 is a respectful pronoun meaning 'that person' or a polite 'he/she' (often referring to someone of higher status or deceased). Adding -의 makes it possessive (그분의 = 'that person's' or 'his/her/their' in polite contexts). Use when speaking respectfully or formally about someone; not casual. If context specifies gender or identity, it's understood from context.
native_language_example: I will follow his/her decision.

meaning: colloquial/colloquial-emphatic form of '그가' — 'he' (subject); used in casual speech
additional_notes: 그이 is a nonstandard/colloquial variant of 그(가) meaning 'he' as the subject. Appears in casual or regional speech and can add emphasis or a folksy tone. Use 가 after pronoun: 그이가 ≈ 그가. Not standard in formal writing; in polite/formal contexts use 그가 or 그분이 (for respectful 'he').
native_language_example: He says he's coming tomorrow.

meaning: as for that side/person/option; 'what about you/that one?'.
additional_notes: 그쪽 literally means 'that side' or 'that person/party' (polite neutral). When followed by 은 (topic marker) it contrasts or asks about that side/option. Used to ask someone's opinion (그쪽은 어때?), to refuse something for that side (그쪽은 안돼요!), or to contrast actions (그쪽은 나중에 하라). Tone depends on context and speech level—어떻게/어때 are casual; 어떻습니까 is formal.
native_language_example: I support option A. What about you?

meaning: that side / that person (subject/topic) — 'that one' or 'you/they' depending on context
additional_notes: 그쪽 literally means 'that direction/side' and -이 is the subject particle here, so 그쪽이 emphasizes or identifies someone/something as the subject. In conversation it often points to 'that person' or 'that option' (sometimes used like 'you' or 'they' when indicating someone). Tone and context determine whether it's a question (Is that the person?), denial (Not that one!), or correction (Not that way, this way). Politeness depends on the rest of the sentence (아냐 is informal; 아니에요 is polite).
native_language_example: Is that person my friend?

meaning: 'but you' / 'by the way, you' — a casual way to bring up or question something about the listener
additional_notes: 근데 is an informal contraction of 그런데 (meaning 'but' or 'by the way'). Placed before 너 ('you'), it introduces a follow-up question, surprise, or challenge directed at the listener. Tone is casual and can sound blunt or teasing depending on context. Use with friends or informal situations; avoid in formal settings.
target_language_example: 근데 너 오늘 약속 왜 안 왔어?
native_language_example: By the way, why didn't you come to the appointment today?

meaning: But why... / By the way, why... (used to ask for a reason, often with surprise or mild confrontation).
additional_notes: 근데 is a casual contraction of 그런데 ('but/and yet' or 'by the way'). Together with 왜 ('why') it introduces a question asking for the reason, often showing surprise, confusion, or mild annoyance depending on tone. Common in spoken, informal contexts. Use polite forms (e.g., 근데 왜 그래요?) when speaking to strangers or elders.
native_language_example: But why are you doing that?

meaning: a conversational phrase meaning 'but/so, what's this?' or 'but this…' used to express surprise, confusion, or to introduce a question about something present.
additional_notes: 근데 is an informal connector meaning 'by the way' or 'but'. 이게 literally means 'this (subject)'. Together 근데 이게 is used colloquially to point to something and ask about it, show surprise, or raise doubt. Common in spoken Korean; not formal. Followed by a question (무슨 ~?, 진짜 ~?, etc.).
native_language_example: But what's going on with this?

meaning: near; nearby (at/to the vicinity of).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity. Often follows a place or noun (근처 = vicinity); with -에 marks location (at/in/near). Common in questions and statements about where someone or something is. Can combine with verbs like 있다/살다/있다(있소) etc. Pronunciation: [geun-cheo-e].
native_language_example: There is a café near my house.

meaning: the object particle form of '글' (writing/text); marks 'writing/text' as the direct object (e.g., '글을 읽다' = to read a text).
additional_notes: 글 means 'writing', 'text', 'article', or 'post'. Adding the object particle -을 (attached as 글을) indicates that 글 is the thing being acted on. Use -을 after a noun that ends in a consonant; use -를 after a vowel. Examples: 글을 읽다 (to read a text), 글을 쓰다 (to write a post).
native_language_example: I am reading a text.

meaning: 'will come soon' (short form used in speech; 금방 = soon, 오다 = to come)
additional_notes: 금방 (soon/just now) + 오다 (to come). In these examples, 올 is the future/stem form used in casual speech before endings like - 것이다, -거야, -거지. Common in everyday conversation to reassure someone that a person will arrive shortly.
native_language_example: He will come soon.

meaning: Please wait. (polite request)
additional_notes: Polite/request form used to ask someone to wait. 기다려 is the informal imperative of 기다리다 (to wait); 주세요 makes it polite ('please give' → 'please do ...'). Common with time expressions (잠시, 삼십 분) or locations (로비에서, 밖에서). Suitable for polite everyday situations.
native_language_example: Please wait here for a moment.

meaning: 'I'm waiting' / 'are/is waiting' (progressive: waiting right now).
additional_notes: Present progressive of 기다리다 (to wait). Used in casual/informal speech. Context and subject determine English translation: e.g. '널 기다리고 있어' = 'I'm waiting for you'; '뭘 기다리고 있어?' = 'What are you waiting for?' Often shortened in speech to 기다려(요) for commands or 기다리고 있어 for ongoing action.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for you here now.

meaning: 'prayer' as an object (the act of praying) — marked with the object particle 를.
additional_notes: 기도 (noun) = 'prayer' or 'to pray' (depending on verb). When combined with 를 (object particle) it indicates the action of praying is the direct object of a verb (e.g., '기도를 하다' = 'to say/pray a prayer'). In casual speech people may shorten or trail off ('기도를?') to ask 'Pray?' or confirm 'Are you going to pray?'. Common collocation: 기도를 하다/드리다 (하다 is neutral, 드리다 is polite for offering a prayer).
native_language_example: I pray every night.

meaning: 'about how one feels' or 'the feeling (as for...)' — topic marker used when asking or talking about someone's mood/feeling.
additional_notes: 기분 (feeling, mood) + 은 (topic particle). Used to make 'feeling' the topic of the sentence, often in questions about how something feels or how someone is feeling. Common in phrases like '기분은 어때요?' (How do you feel?) or '사랑하는 사람 손을 잡은 기분은?' (How does it feel to hold the hand of someone you love?). Polite/informal form depends on the rest of the sentence (어떠니/어때요/어떻습니까).
native_language_example: How do you feel after the exam?

meaning: feeling(s), mood (used as the subject/topic marker '기분' + particle '이').
additional_notes: 기분 means 'mood' or 'feeling'. When followed by the subject particle '이' it commonly appears before verbs or adjectives to describe how someone feels (e.g., 좋다, 안 좋다, 어떻다, 보여지다). Used in questions and statements about emotional or physical state. Common collocations: 기분이 좋다 (to feel good), 기분이 안 좋다 (to feel bad), 기분이 어떠세요? (How are you feeling?).
native_language_example: I'm feeling a bit down today.

meaning: 'How do you feel?' or 'How does it feel?'.
additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase asking about someone's emotional state or asking how something feels (experience). '기분' = mood/feeling; '어때' is informal for '어때요' (polite). Use with friends; use '기분이 어떠세요?' or '기분이 어떠신가요?' for polite/formal speech.
native_language_example: How do you feel now that the exam is over?

meaning: to feel good; to be in a good mood
additional_notes: Used to describe one's emotional or physical mood/state. Often appears with a subject (e.g., 저는 기분이 좋다) and is conjugated for politeness (좋다 → 좋아요 / 좋아합니다 / 좋아). The opposite is 기분이 나쁘다 (to feel bad). Can describe a temporary feeling (after hearing good news) or a general mood.
native_language_example: I feel good right now.

meaning: '(it) feels like' / 'I'm feeling (that)...' (expresses one's feeling or impression)
additional_notes: 기분 is 'mood/feeling'. Adding -야 here is colloquial/short for '(~인) 기분이야' meaning 'it feels like...' or 'I feel...'. Used to describe one's emotional state or the impression of becoming something (e.g., 'like a child', 'like a new person'). Can appear in questions (어떤 기분이야? = 'How does it feel?'). Casual/informal speech — use with friends or family.
native_language_example: Being here makes me feel happy.

meaning: '기사' with subject marker -ga; can mean 'driver' or 'knight' or 'news/article' depending on context (here '기사가' marks the subject).
additional_notes: 기사가 is 기사의 주격형 (subject form). 기사가 can mean: 1) driver (chauffeur), 2) knight (medieval warrior), or 3) news article (less likely with 사람-like verbs). Context and verbs determine meaning: e.g. '운전하다' → driver; '용감한' → knight; '나오다' about a newspaper/TV → article/feature; counting people (몇 명) → people (drivers/knights). The -가 simply marks the subject (who/what does something).
native_language_example: The driver drove kindly.

meaning: 'an article' as the object of a verb (accusative form of 기사)
additional_notes: 기사는 '기사' (article, news story)에 목적 격조사 '를/을'이 붙은 형태입니다. English: it's the direct object — used when saying you want to write, read, or publish an article. Politeness in Korean comes from the sentence ending (e.g., -다, -습니다, -요), not from '기사를'.
native_language_example: I want to write an article.

meaning: 'don't remember' (short/informal form of 기억 안 나)
additional_notes: A short, informal way to say you don't remember. Full form is 기억 안 나 or 기억이 안 나요 (polite). Often used in casual spoken Korean; may appear clipped as 기억 안 in conversation. Use 기억이 안 나/기억 안 나요 for polite situations.
target_language_example: 그때 무슨 일이 있었는지 기억 안.
native_language_example: I don't remember what happened then.

meaning: I/you/he/she/they don't remember (colloquial).
additional_notes: Casual, contracted form of 기억이 안 나/기억이 없다. Used to say someone doesn't remember or to ask if someone remembers something (with rising intonation). Common in spoken Korean. Add a subject (나는, 너는, 걔는, 그분은) or context if unclear. To make polite, use 기억이 안 나요/기억이 나지 않아요.
target_language_example: 그 사람 이름 기억 안 나.
native_language_example: I don't remember that person's name.

meaning: I don't remember / It doesn't come to mind.
additional_notes: Polite/plain form (declarative/question) used to say you don't recall something or someone. Common in everyday conversation. Can be softened with '모르겠어요' for 'I don't know' or made more casual as '기억이 안 나' among friends. Often follows the thing you can't remember (e.g., 이름을 기억 안 나요 — I don't remember the name).
target_language_example: 그 사람 얼굴은 기억 안 나요.
native_language_example: I don't remember that person's face.

meaning: the object form of '기억하다' — 'memory' used as the direct object (e.g., 'memory' in phrases like 'lose memory' or 'remember').
additional_notes: 기억 (memory) + 을 (object particle). Appears when 'memory' is the direct object of a verb: 잃어버리다 (to lose memory), 못 하다 (cannot remember). In English you wouldn't say 'memory' with a particle, so think of it as marking what is being remembered or forgotten. Common verbs with 기억을: 잃어버리다 (lose), 못 하다/못 하다 (cannot remember), 되돌리다 (restore).
native_language_example: I lost the memory of yesterday's events.

meaning: 'memory' used as the subject/topic in expressions about remembering (literally 'memory + subject marker').
additional_notes: 기억 means 'memory' or 'recollection'. When followed by a subject/topic particle (기억이, 기억은), it's commonly used with verbs like 나다 (to come to mind), 나다 안 나다 (to remember / not remember), or 있다/없다 (to have/ not have memory). Examples: 기억이 났다 = I remembered; 기억이 안 나다 = I don't remember. Often appears in questions (기억 나세요? = Do you remember?) and casual speech uses contractions (기억이 났어).
native_language_example: I suddenly remembered that event.

meaning: I'm remembering / I remember (right now).
additional_notes: Present progressive form of 기억하다 (to remember). Used to say you currently remember something or to confirm memory. Can be casual or neutral depending on tone; often shortened in speech to 기억해 or 기억하고 있어요 for polite speech.
native_language_example: I still remember your face.

meaning: the train (object form — 'train' with the object particle 를)
additional_notes: 기차 means 'train'. Adding 를 marks it as the direct object of a verb (or the target of certain actions). In sentences like '기차를 타다' (to take/ride a train) or '기차를 놓치다' (to miss a train), 기차를 indicates what is ridden, missed, seen, etc. Spoken polite endings may vary (왔습니다/왔어요). In casual narrative past, the verb may end with -다 (봤다).
native_language_example: I took the train and went to Busan.

meaning: the (grammatical) marker indicating 'opportunity/chance' as the subject (or existence) in a sentence; literally 'a chance (exists)'.
additional_notes: 기회 (chance/opportunity) + subject particle 가. Used when talking about having/there being an opportunity to do something. Often appears with verbs like 있다/없다 (to exist/have) or in questions about whether an opportunity will occur. Not a fixed idiom — it's the noun 기회 plus the subject marker 가.
target_language_example: 다음 달에 다시 시도할 기회가 있을 거예요.
native_language_example: There will be another chance to try next month.

meaning: 'opportunity' in the object form (as in 'give/get an opportunity' or 'take an opportunity').
additional_notes: 기회 (chance/opportunity) + 를 (object particle). Used when talking about receiving, giving, taking, or seizing an opportunity. Common verbs with 기회를: 잡다 (to seize), 주다 (to give), 주지 않다 (to not give). In casual speech you may hear shortened or repeated forms, but the basic structure is 기회를 + verb.
native_language_example: Give me one more chance.

meaning: to give someone a chance/opportunity
additional_notes: Used to indicate giving someone an opportunity to try, prove themselves, or do something. Applies to work, relationships, tests, or general situations. Often follows the person receiving the opportunity (e.g., '나에게 기회를 주다' = give me a chance). Can be used politely or casually depending on ending form.
native_language_example: Please give me just one chance.

meaning: 'it's (your/my/our) chance' or 'this is the opportunity'.
additional_notes: 기회 (chance/opportunity) + 야 (informal/plain declarative ending for 있다/이다) — used in casual speech to say that now is someone's chance or an opportunity. The subject (내 기회야, 네 기회야, 우리의 기회야) is often omitted when clear from context. Informal and used in spoken Korean.
native_language_example: This is your chance, don't give up.

meaning: to/toward a road/path; by a route (indicating direction or route taken)
additional_notes: 길 means 'road' or 'path'. 길로 is the particle form using -로 to show direction ('to the road/along the road') or route ('by way of'). Used when asking which path to take, telling someone to turn onto a road, or saying you went a long/other way (e.g., 먼 길로 = by a long route). Context determines if it means 'toward', 'onto', 'via', or 'by way of.'
native_language_example: Let's go onto the left path.

meaning: the road/path (as an object, marked by the object particle -을).
additional_notes: 길 means 'road', 'way', 'path', or figuratively 'way/route' in life. 길을 is 길 + the object particle -을 (used when the verb acts on '길') and appears in many expressions: literal (making a road, blocking the way), idiomatic (길을 잃다 = lose one's way; 먼 길 = a long way; 길을 열다 = open a path/opportunity), and set phrases like 제 길을 가다 (go one's own way). Pronunciation: [gil-eul] (often reduced in speech).
native_language_example: I'll go my own way.

meaning: road; path; way (noun).
additional_notes: 길 means a physical road, path, or way. 길이 (with subject marker -이) is the noun plus particle used when the road/path is the subject of the sentence (e.g., '이 길이 ...' = 'this road is ...'). Used in questions and statements about existence or direction (e.g., '길이 없어' = 'there is no road').
native_language_example: Is this road the way to the market?

meaning: up to; as for the distance/time/point until (with topical nuance).
additional_notes: 까지 marks a limit or endpoint (up to/until). The particle 는 adds a topical contrast or emphasis, often meaning 'as for up to...' or 'as for the distance/time until...'. Common in questions about distance/time (e.g., 'from A to B') and in colloquial phrases emphasizing a limit (e.g., 'can't go up to the summit!').
native_language_example: As for from Seoul to Busan, how long does it take by train?

meaning: How to (get) to/until (a place); asking about the method or route to reach a destination.
additional_notes: 까지 means 'to' or 'until' (indicating destination or endpoint). 어떻게 means 'how'. Together, '까지 어떻게' commonly appears in questions about how to get somewhere (e.g., by what route, transport, or means). Word order: place + 까지 + 어떻게 + (가요/갑니까/간다는). Polite forms: 어떻게 가요? / 어떻게 갑니까?. Informal: 어떻게 가?.
native_language_example: How do I get to Seoul Station?

meaning: 'how far / how long until (to)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about distance or time remaining to reach a destination or event. 까지 means 'until' or 'to (a place)', and 얼마나 asks 'how much/how long/how far'. Combine to ask 'How far is it to ...?' or 'How much time remains until ...?'. Context (distance vs. time) is inferred from the verb (멀다/걸리다/가다 vs. 남다/발사 등). Informal forms: you can drop 요 in casual speech (e.g., '얼마나 멀어?').
native_language_example: How long does it take to the airport?

meaning: colloquial contraction used to indicate possession ("mine/yours") or future/intent ("will/going to") depending on context; here it's mostly the casual possessive pronoun ending and casual future marker '거야' pronounced '꺼야'.
additional_notes: 껐다/꺼야 is a colloquial pronunciation of 거야. It can appear as 네/내/내 꺼야 meaning "yours/mine" (possessive: 'it's mine/your(s)') or as a casual future/intent marker after a verb/stative stem (e.g., '올 거야' → '올 꺼야' = 'will come'). It's informal and common in spoken Korean; avoid in formal writing. Tone and meaning depend on whether it's attached to a noun (possession) or a verb (future).
native_language_example: This is mine.

meaning: kid; little one (vocative — used to call or address a child, sometimes playful or slightly teasing).
additional_notes: 꼬마 means 'small child' or 'little one'. Adding -야 makes it vocative/informal (used when directly addressing someone). Sounds casual and may be affectionate, playful, or mildly condescending depending on tone and relationship. Avoid using with adults you don't know. Common in speech, often followed by a name question or greeting.
native_language_example: Hi, kid.

meaning: appearance/state (usually of someone), often used to comment on how someone looks or acts (often negative or surprised).
additional_notes: 꼴이 comes from 꼴 (appearance/shape) plus the subject particle -이; it's used in colloquial Korean to ask or remark about someone's appearance, condition, or behavior. Common in expressions like '너 꼴이 왜 그래?' (What's wrong with you?/Why do you look like that?). Can sound informal, blunt, or rude depending on tone and context. Often used with 어때서?, 왜 이래?, etc.
target_language_example: 너 꼴이 왜 그래? 무슨 일 있어?
native_language_example: What's wrong with you? Is something going on?

meaning: Don't move! / Freeze!
additional_notes: Very strong command used to tell someone to stay exactly where they are, often used by police, guards, or in urgent situations. Informal and abrupt — not polite. Often followed by instructions (e.g., '거기 서!' '총 버려!').
native_language_example: Police! Don't move!

meaning: object marker with '꽃' (flower) — indicates 'flower' as the direct object (e.g., 'a flower', 'flowers').
additional_notes: 꽃 = flower. The particle 을 marks the noun as the direct object of the verb (used after a noun ending in a consonant). In English you don't need a particle; here it shows what is being liked, bought, seen, etc. If the noun ends in a vowel, use 를 instead (e.g., '사과를').
native_language_example: I bought flowers.

meaning: 'flower' (with the subject particle -이); marks 'flower' as the subject of the sentence
additional_notes: 꽃 means 'flower'. Adding the particle -이 (used after a noun ending in a consonant) marks that noun as the subject or topic depending on context. In English you don't translate the particle separately; it tells you the noun is the subject (who/what does or is something). Examples above show questions and comments using 꽃이 as the subject: asking if someone misses flowers, asking permission to look closely at a pretty flower, asking which flower is good, or questioning whether flowers are important now.
native_language_example: That flower is really pretty.

meaning: to hold tightly; to grip firmly
additional_notes: 꽉 is an adverb meaning 'tightly' or 'firmly'. 잡다 means 'to hold' or 'to grab'. Used for physically holding something strongly (hand, handle, rope) or figuratively (seize an opportunity, hold on tight). Common in commands: '꽉 잡아!' ('Hold on tight!').
native_language_example: to hold the handle tightly.

meaning: 'Hold tight' or 'grip tightly' (imperative, informal)
additional_notes: Used as a command telling someone to hold something firmly (a handrail, someone's arm, an object) or to hold on during a fast/rough ride. 꽉 = tightly/firmly; 잡아 is the informal imperative form of 잡다 (to hold/grab). Common in urgent or casual speech. For polite situations, use 꽉 잡으세요.
native_language_example: Hold the handrail tightly!

meaning: 'Don't dawdle' / 'Don't hesitate' / 'Stop dilly-dallying and (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used as an imperative telling someone to stop lingering, delaying, or hesitating and to do the next action quickly. Common in spoken Korean and can be followed by another verb (e.g., 가, 들어가, 잡아). Tone can be firm or impatient depending on context. Informal; typically used with friends, family, or when scolding.
native_language_example: Don't dawdle — come quickly!

meaning: 'dream' as the direct object marker (꿈 + 을).
additional_notes: 꿈 means 'dream'. When followed by 을 (object particle for consonant-final nouns), it marks 꿈 as the direct object of the verb (e.g., 꿈을 꾸다 = to have/experience a dream; 꿈을 믿다 = to believe a dream). In spoken Korean, you'll often see 꿈을 shortened in pronunciation, but written form remains 꿈을. Useful with verbs like 꾸다 (to dream), 믿다 (to believe), 잊다 (to forget).
native_language_example: I had a good dream last night.

meaning: 'dream' (as the subject/topic marker + particle '이').
additional_notes: 꿈 means 'dream' and when followed by the subject particle '이' it marks 'dream' as the subject/topic of the sentence. It can refer to (1) a goal/aspiration (나는 꿈이 있어 — I have a dream/goal), (2) a dream experienced while sleeping, or (3) a metaphorical idea (e.g., 'life might be a dream'). Context determines which meaning is intended. The particle '이' is the subject marker used after a noun ending in a consonant. For learners, remember 꿈이 = 'dream' + subject particle '이'.
native_language_example: I have one dream.

meaning: 'to the end', 'until the end', or 'throughout' (doing something all the way until it's finished).
additional_notes: Used adverbially to say that an action continues until the very end or is carried out fully/persistently. Can refer to physical movement to the end, emotional commitment, or finishing a task (e.g., read until the end). Tone varies with context — can be determined, pleading, or casual. Common with verbs like 가다 (go), 하다 (do), 버리다 (leave), 읽다 (read), 들어 (listen).
native_language_example: You promised, so I'll stay with you until the end.

meaning: 'It's over' / 'That's the end' (used to declare something finished or to warn that something will be the end/consequence).
additional_notes: Casual/plain form of 끝이다; can be used to state that something has finished ('That's it, we're done') or as a threat/warning ('that's the end for you'). Tone depends on context and intonation. Common in spoken Korean; can sound blunt or dramatic. Use polite form (끝이에요/끝입니다) in formal situations.
native_language_example: Once this task is finished, it's over.

meaning: 'the thing that has ended' / 'it's over' (referring to something finished)
additional_notes: 끝난 is the past participle/adjective form of 끝나다 (to end, to be finished). 거 is short for 것 meaning 'thing' or an abstract situation. Together, 끝난 거 often refers to a finished event, situation, or matter — e.g. 'it's over' or 'the thing that's finished.' In casual speech the meaning can be 'that's over/that's finished.' You may hear it alone as a short response (끝난 거야 — it's over).
native_language_example: This matter is already finished / It's already over.

meaning: 'you're finished' / 'it's over' (used to say someone/something is doomed or ruined)
additional_notes: Informal, strong expression. Often used to warn or threaten someone (you're finished) or to say a situation is hopeless/ruined (it's over). Tone can be angry, joking among friends, or dramatic. Common in spoken Korean. Not literal; '끝' means 'end' + ending ~이야 (copula).
native_language_example: If you keep doing that, you're finished.

meaning: Do ... (as a suggestion/imperative meaning 'just do X' or 'at least do X')
additional_notes: The particle 나 after a verb or noun here gives a sense of 'at least' or 'just' and is often used in imperatives or suggestions to tell someone to do something (sometimes impatient or dismissive). It can soften a command into a suggestion ("just do X") or express resignation/limited expectation ("at least do X"). Common in spoken Korean. Position: verb stem + 나 + 하다 (or noun + 나 하다).
native_language_example: Just study. / At least study.

meaning: someone/something like me; 'someone like me' (used to refer to oneself as an example).
additional_notes: 나 = 'I/me'. 같은 = 'like/similar'. Used before a noun to mean 'a [noun] like me' or 'people/things like me'. Often carries self-reference and can sound humble, self-deprecating, proud, or rhetorical depending on tone and context. Common in questions or statements: '나 같은 사람?' = 'Someone like me?'.
native_language_example: Is there someone like me here?

meaning: I, me (informal; repeated for emphasis or casual speech)
additional_notes: The base word 나 means 'I' or 'me' (informal, used with friends or younger people). Seeing '나 나' is nonstandard in formal writing — repetition can appear in casual spoken Korean or dialect to add emphasis, hesitation, or a playful tone (like 'me, me' or 'well, I...'). Stick to a single 나 for normal sentences. Use 저 for polite/formal speech.
native_language_example: Me, me — I'll try it.

meaning: I (subject)
additional_notes: 나는 is the topic/subject form of '나' (I). It often marks the speaker as the topic (similar to 'as for me') and is commonly used before verbs or adjectives. In casual speech the topic particle can be shortened or dropped, but 나는 appears in sentences to emphasize the subject. When combined with verbs, it indicates actions or states performed by 'I'.
native_language_example: I study Korean every day.

meaning: 'I' (topic) + 'that' (demonstrative) — literally 'I, that' but often starts a sentence meaning 'As for me, that...'
additional_notes: 나는 is the topical form of 'I' (나 + 는). 그 is a demonstrative meaning 'that' or 'the' (referring to something mentioned or pointed out). Together they can begin a sentence where the speaker contrasts themselves or introduces their opinion about 'that' thing: e.g. 'As for me, that...' or 'I (know) that...'. In the example sentence, 나는 그 구분을 알아, it means 'I know that distinction.' The phrase is compositional and not informal.
target_language_example: 나는 그 문제를 해결할 수 있어.
native_language_example: As for me, I can solve that problem.

meaning: I + him (object). '나는' = I (topic/subject), '그를' = him (object form).
additional_notes: '나는 그를' combines the subject/topic marker 나는 (I) and the object pronoun 그를 (him). Use when the speaker is doing something to or about a male person. The particle 를/을 marks the direct object. In casual speech, 나는 can be shortened or omitted if context is clear. Word order in Korean is typically Subject–Object–Verb, so a verb follows (e.g., 만났다 = met, 돕고 있다 = am helping).
native_language_example: I am waiting for him in the park.

meaning: I (topic) + my — '나는' marks 'I' as the topic; '내' is the informal possessive 'my'.
additional_notes: This is two separate words often used together in casual sentences: 나는 (I as topic) + 내 (my). '내' is the short/informal form of '나의' and is common in spoken Korean. Ensure verb grammar follows (e.g., 숙제를 끝낼 수가 없었다 — correct verb form). In formal writing/speech, use '저는 제...' or '나의' for 'my'.
native_language_example: I (topic) found my glasses.

meaning: 'I' (나는) + 'you' (너) — literally 'I ... you'; often the start of a sentence meaning 'I [verb] you' (e.g., I love you, I know you).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's just the pronouns 나는 (I, topic/subject) and 너 (you, informal). In natural Korean, a verb is usually needed after 너 (e.g., 나는 너를 좋아해 — I like you). 나는 is the casual/formal-neutral spoken form (나는 = 나 + 는 topic marker). 너 is informal; avoid using 너 with strangers or elders. When marking the object, add the object particle 를/을: 나는 너를 ...
native_language_example: I love you.

meaning: 'I am a devil' or 'I am the devil' (literal statement identifying oneself as a demon/devil).
additional_notes: 나는 = 'I (subject) + am' (informal/plain speech). 악마 = 'devil' or 'demon'. This phrase is literal and strong — used in dramatic, fictional, or joking contexts. Tone can be playful, self-deprecating, or serious depending on context and intonation. You can change 나는 to 저는 for more polite speech (저는 악마입니다).
native_language_example: Right, I am a devil!

meaning: me too / I also / even I
additional_notes: Used to express that the speaker shares the same feeling, experience, action, or also wants to do something. Context determines nuance: agreement ("me too"), shared experience ("I've also had that happen"), desire ("I want to too"), or modesty/emphasis ("even I..."). Often follows a verb or clause it agrees with. Informal but common in everyday speech.
native_language_example: I want to go too.

meaning: I don't know either / I don't know (either).
additional_notes: A casual phrase used to say you also don't know something or to express unwillingness to answer. 나도 = 'me too' or 'I also'; 몰라 is the informal present of 모르다 ('to not know'). Common in spoken Korean; can sound blunt or dismissive depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: 어제 누가 왔는지 알아? — 나도 몰라.
native_language_example: Do you know who came yesterday? — I don't know either.

meaning: because of me / due to me
additional_notes: Used to indicate that the speaker (나 = I/me) is the cause or reason for something (often negative). Can express guilt, blame, or concern. Common in questions and statements like "Is it because of me?" or "Don't do X because of me." Tone depends on context—can be apologetic, defensive, or accusatory.
target_language_example: 그 일은 다 나 때문에 일어났어.
native_language_example: That whole thing happened because of me.

meaning: the object form of '나' (I/me) — 'me' (used when something is done to or for me).
additional_notes: 나 is the informal first-person pronoun 'I'. 나를 is 나 + object particle 를 (replaces '가/는' when marking the direct object). Used in casual and polite sentences depending on the verb ending that follows (e.g., 나를 사랑해? / 나를 사랑해요?). In questions like '감히 나를?' it's shortened and rhetorical. Can appear in commands (나를 따라와 — 'follow me') and statements about actions done for or to the speaker (나를 위해 — 'for me').
native_language_example: Can you help me?

meaning: 'only me' or 'just me' (emphasizes that something applies solely to the speaker).
additional_notes: Combines 나 (I/me) + 만 (only). Used to say that something is true only for the speaker or to single themselves out. Can appear in questions (e.g., 'Am I the only one...?') or commands/requests (e.g., 'Just follow me'). Tone depends on context — can be curious, confident, or defensive. Informal everyday usage.
native_language_example: Am I the only one who hasn't seen that movie?

meaning: 'than me' (used for comparisons; literally 'than I')
additional_notes: Combines 나 (I/me) + 보다 (than) to make comparisons. Used before adjectives, verbs, or noun phrases to say someone/something is more/less than the speaker. Word order: [other person/thing] + 나보다 + [adjective/verb/clause]. In casual speech, 나보다 can appear after the speaker as in examples (implying comparison with the speaker).
native_language_example: He is taller than me.

meaning: 'I'm here' or 'me, here' (casual spoken way to say you are here or present).
additional_notes: Informal, contracted speech: '나' = I/me, '여기' = here. Often used when answering roll call, indicating your location, or attracting attention (e.g., calling out in a group). In polite situations use 저는 여기 있어요 or 저 여기 있어요. Tone and context matter—can be followed by a verb or used alone.
native_language_example: I'm here! I'll come right now.

meaning: 'with me' (when attached to a noun or pronoun '나') or the particle '와' following '나'—commonly means 'and I' / 'with me' depending on context.
additional_notes: 나 = 'I' (informal). 와 is a particle that can mean 'and' (joining nouns) or 'with'/'together with' (in conversational contexts). In sentences like '나와 그 여자의 관계라뇨?' it means 'between me and that woman' (i.e. 'my relationship with that woman'). In commands or exclamations like '나와 요괴야!' the structure is colloquial and may mean 'You and I are a monster!' or 'I'm a monster?' depending on tone; context matters. Commonly used in spoken Korean; when politely referring to oneself use '저와'.
native_language_example: Come with me.

meaning: my (possessive form; more formal or literary than 내)
additional_notes: Used before nouns to mean 'my.' 나의 is the full/formal possessive of 나 (I). In everyday spoken Korean, 내 is much more common. 나의 appears in formal, written, poetic, or emphatic contexts (e.g., songs, speeches, exclamations). Placement: 나의 + noun (나의 친구, 나의 사랑).
native_language_example: This is exactly the difference between you and me!

meaning: a casual/demanding way to refer to oneself + soften/request marker; 'me, (please)...' used to ask/command someone to do or stop doing something to you
additional_notes: Combines 나 (I/me) + 좀 (a softener meaning 'a bit' or 'please' in requests). Common in casual speech to make requests, pleas, or commands directed at others about oneself. Tone depends on verb and context: can be pleading (나 좀 살려줘), demanding (나 좀 놔줘), or exasperated (나 좀 내버려 둬). Informal and should be avoided in polite/formal situations.
native_language_example: Let me go! / Leave me alone!

meaning: I (am) now / I'm right now
additional_notes: Casual spoken combination of the subject '나' (I) + time adverb '지금' (now). Common in informal conversation to emphasize current action, feeling, or state. Often followed by verbs or sentence endings and may be contracted in rapid speech. Not polite — use with friends or people you are close to.
native_language_example: I'm going home right now.

meaning: with me; (do something) with me / to me (colloquial)
additional_notes: 나하고 is the casual spoken form of '나와/나랑' meaning 'with me' or used to indicate involvement of the speaker. Common in everyday conversation. Used to invite someone to do something together (나하고 같이 가자), to ask if someone is interacting with the speaker (나하고 장난치는 거야?), or to challenge/compete (나하고 붙자). Polite situations use 나와/저하고/저랑 or the speaker may use the polite forms with -요.
native_language_example: Do you want to eat dinner with me today?

meaning: by myself; alone (I alone)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker is alone or acting without others' help. '나' is informal for 'I'. Often appears in commands or complaints (e.g., '나 혼자 내버려둬!' = 'Leave me alone!'). Can be repeated or followed by particles (e.g., '나 혼자야' = 'I'm alone').
native_language_example: I'll watch the movie by myself.

meaning: with me / to me (casual).
additional_notes: Shortened/colloquial form of 나와/나하고. Used in informal speech to mean 'with me' (doing something together) or in phrases like '나랑 장난하냐?' meaning 'Are you joking with me?' Often used in casual conversations among friends. Avoid in formal situations; use 저와/저하고 instead.
native_language_example: Do you want to go see a movie with me?

meaning: 'with me' or 'together with me'.
additional_notes: Casual way to invite or state being together with the speaker. 나랑 = 'with me' (informal; from 나 + 랑). 같이 = 'together'. Common in spoken Korean; use 나와 같이 or 저와 같이 for more polite forms.
target_language_example: 이번 주말에 나랑 같이 영화 볼래?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch a movie with me this weekend?

meaning: '(to) me' or 'asking/telling me to...'; used when someone is addressing or blaming the speaker about an action or expectation.
additional_notes: 나보고 = 나 + 보고. Here 보고 is a colloquial contraction meaning 'to (me)' or 'about me' in contexts like 'you tell/ask me to do something' or 'you expect me to...'. Often used with verbs/questions to express surprise, refusal, annoyance, or to challenge the expectation (e.g., 나보고 어쩌라는 거야? = 'What do you want me to do?'). Common in spoken/informal Korean.
native_language_example: You're telling me to leave right now?

meaning: 'It's me' or 'I'm the one'.
additional_notes: Casual way to identify oneself or answer when someone calls; contraction of 나 + 이야 (or form of 나이다). Common in spoken Korean. Often used alone as a short reply (e.g., when someone asks who did something) or at the start of a sentence for emphasis. Informal — used with friends, family, or children.
native_language_example: Are you here? It's me!

meaning: to/for me; toward me (dative/benefactive 'to me' or 'for me').
additional_notes: Combination of 나 (I/me) + 에게 (to/for someone). Used to indicate the recipient or target of an action or feeling. Common in spoken and written Korean. Polite/formal speech often uses 저에게 instead. Context determines translation: can mean 'bring to me', 'tell me', or 'to me' as in 'for me'.
native_language_example: Please tell me.

meaning: for me; to me (marks something as being the case for the speaker)
additional_notes: 나에게는 = 나에게 + 는. 나에게 is the dative form of '나' (to/for me). The particle 는 adds topic/contrast, so 나에게는 emphasizes 'as for me' or 'to me' when saying what someone has or what is true for them. Common with_existential phrases (있다/없다) and statements like 'I have...' or 'for me,...'.
native_language_example: I have three friends.

meaning: to/for me; toward me (informal, casual)
additional_notes: 나한테 is an informal contraction of 나에게/나한테서 used to indicate the recipient, target, or direction toward the speaker. Commonly used in spoken Korean. Can appear with verbs like 주다 (give), 말하다 (say), 화나다 (be angry), 보여주다 (show). Use with friends, family, or casual situations; avoid in very formal contexts.
native_language_example: You can tell me.

meaning: 'must leave' or 'have to get out' (informal spoken necessity to go out/leave a place).
additional_notes: Contraction of 나가다 (to go out/leave) + -아/어야 하다 (must/have to). Used to say someone needs to leave now or that leaving is necessary. Common in spoken Korean; can be softened or made more polite with 나가야 해요 or 나가야 합니다. Context often implies urgency.
target_language_example: 지금 상황이 위험해. 우리 당장 나가야 해.
native_language_example: This situation is dangerous. We have to leave immediately.

meaning: will go out / going to leave (short for 나갈 거예요 or 나갈 거야)
additional_notes: Casual future expression formed from the verb 나가다 (to go out/leave) + -ㄹ/을 거(예요) indicating intention or prediction. Without the polite ending, it sounds informal or neutral depending on context. You may hear contractions like '나갈 거예요' (polite) or '나갈 거야' (informal). Can refer to physically leaving a place or stepping outside.
native_language_example: I'm going to go out now.

meaning: I'll/I'm going to go out; (I) will leave.
additional_notes: Casual future tense of 나오/나가다 meaning to go out or leave. Used when the speaker intends to go out or leave a place. With sentence-ending 요 it's informal/polite among friends; can be softened or made more formal by changing ending (나갈 거예요, 나갈 것입니다). Can also be used as a question or negative (안 나갈 거야? = Aren't you going out?).
native_language_example: I'll go out after dinner.

meaning: 'be able to go out' / 'can go out' (ability or possibility to leave/go out)
additional_notes: 나가다 = to go out/leave. '~(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다' is the pattern for ability/possibility. Combine 나가다 + ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다 to say you can/cannot go out. Informal speech often shortens forms (나갈 수 있나? casual question). Use with tense particles: 나갈 수 있었다 (could have gone out), 나갈 수 있을 때 (when you can go out).
native_language_example: If the rain stops, I can go out.

meaning: 'the rest' or 'the remaining (things/people)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains after mentioning something else. Often followed by a comment, instruction, question, or description. The particle 는 marks the topic (the rest). Can refer to people, things, time, etc. Context determines exact translation: 'the rest,' 'what's left,' or 'as for the rest.'
native_language_example: I'll handle the rest.

meaning: the noun '나무' (tree) with the subject marker '가' — 'a/the tree' as the subject of a sentence.
additional_notes: 나무 = 'tree'. 가 is the subject particle used after nouns that end in a vowel (or after the noun form). Together 나무가 marks 'the tree' (or 'a tree') as the subject. Depending on context, it can be literal (an actual tree) or used in figurative/idiomatic expressions. In casual speech, 나무가 can also appear in exclamations or jokes (e.g., '난 나무가 아냐!' = 'I'm not a tree!').
native_language_example: The tree makes a big shade.

meaning: 'tree' marked with the object particle (the tree as the direct object)
additional_notes: 나무 = 'tree'. -를 is the object particle (used after a vowel-ending noun) marking the noun as the direct object of a verb. In sentences it usually corresponds to English 'the tree' or just 'tree' when it's the thing acted on. Example verbs: 타다 (to climb/ride), 보다 (to see), 갖고 다니다 (to carry around).
native_language_example: Tom climbs the tree.

meaning: a bad guy; a naughty/mean person (insult).
additional_notes: A casual/colloquial insult. 놈 is a masculine-sounding word meaning 'guy' or 'fellow' and can be rude depending on tone and context. 나쁜 놈 can be used jokingly among friends or seriously to scold/insult someone. Adding 이 before it (이 나쁜 놈) emphasizes the phrase.
native_language_example: He's really a bad guy.

meaning: a bad person; someone who is mean, immoral, or harmful.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as morally bad, cruel, or simply unpleasant. Can be said seriously or as an insult. Context determines strength — can mean 'a bad person' (character) or 'someone who did something wrong.' Often used with particles or endings (같아 보이지 않아요 = 'doesn't look like a bad person').
native_language_example: He is not a bad person.

meaning: bad deed; wrongdoing; something bad someone did.
additional_notes: Used to refer to harmful, immoral, or naughty actions. Can be literal (crime, misbehavior) or mild (naughty behavior by children). Often used in questions or accusations: 'Did you do something bad?' or 'Is someone doing bad things?' Tone depends on context—can be serious or casual.
target_language_example: 혹시 누가 나쁜 짓을 한 건가요?
native_language_example: Did someone do something bad?

meaning: something that comes out; the act of coming out (appearing, being produced, or being released).
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase: 나오는 is the present progressive/passive form of 나오다 (to come out/appear/be produced) and 거 is a colloquial shortened form of 것 (thing/act). Used to refer to something that appears, is released, is produced, or the result of an action. Exact meaning depends on context (e.g., a product coming out, a result appearing, words coming out of one's mouth).
native_language_example: When will the results come out?

meaning: 'age' used as the subject/topic (the noun 'age' with a subject marker).
additional_notes: 나이 = age. Here 나이가 is the noun plus the subject marker -가, so it's used when talking about someone's age (asking, comparing, or stating it's a lot/too old). Common patterns: 나이가 몇(이에요)? / 나이가 어떻게 되세요? / 나이가 많다/적다 (to be older/younger or 'to be old/young' in age). Polite form often uses 되시죠/되세요. Context determines politeness and formality.
native_language_example: How old are you?

meaning: about someone's age / 'age is' (used when asking or stating age).
additional_notes: 나이는 comes from 나이 (age) + topic particle 는. Used to state or ask about age. In casual speech you might hear short forms like 나이? (Age?) or 오빠 나이는? (How old are you, older-brother/formal-casual). When answering, a full sentence would be 제 나이는 열 살이에요 (I'm ten years old). Particle 는 emphasizes the topic 'as for age'.
native_language_example: My age is 21.

meaning: at (a certain) age; in someone's age
additional_notes: Used after a noun meaning 'age' (나이) to indicate at what age something happens or to refer to people of a certain age. Often appears in questions or comparisons (e.g., criticizing or admiring how someone acts given their age). Common patterns: '그들 나이에?' (At their age?), '젊은 나이에' (at a young age).
native_language_example: Isn't it too early to get married at that age?

meaning: later; afterward; sometime after now.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a time in the future (shortly or at an unspecified later time). Common in everyday speech for plans, requests, or saying you'll do something later. Can mean 'later on,' 'afterward,' or 'see you later' depending on context. Often follows verbs or stands alone in casual farewells.
native_language_example: I'll call again later.

meaning: to see (someone/something) later; to check/look at later.
additional_notes: 나중에 = later. 보다 = to see/look/watch/check. Used to say you'll deal with, look at, or meet something/someone at a later time. Can be used for postponing actions (I'll check it later), or arranging to meet (see you later). Context tells whether it's about checking or meeting.
native_language_example: We'll meet/see each other after the meeting (later).

meaning: I'm okay / I'm fine.
additional_notes: Casual way to say you are okay or don't need help. '난' is contraction of '나는' (I), and '괜찮아' is informal present form of '괜찮다' (to be okay). Used in everyday speech with friends or peers; use more polite forms (괜찮아요 / 저는 괜찮습니다) with strangers or elders.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I'm fine.

meaning: short for '나는 그…' meaning 'I (am) that…' or 'I…' used when starting a sentence about oneself (colloquial/slang).
additional_notes: 난 is a colloquial contraction of 나는 (I). 그 here begins a clause ('that' or 'the one'), often followed by a noun, adjective, or clause (e.g., 난 그 사람이 좋아 = 'I like that person'). By itself '난 그' is incomplete and sounds conversational; you'll usually hear it in spoken Korean followed by more words. Tone is casual — not for formal writing or polite speech.
native_language_example: I already watched that movie.

meaning: I (informal contraction) + him (object); 'I [verb] him.' — subject 'I' with object 'him'.
additional_notes: 난 is the contracted, informal form of 나는 (I). 그를 is the object form of '그' (he/him) using the object particle 를. Together they mark 'I' as the subject (casual) and 'him' as the direct object. Use 난 with friends or casual speech; for polite/formal speech use 저는/나는. The verb that follows completes the sentence (e.g., 몰라 = don't know him, 믿어요 = believe him). Word order in Korean is Subject-Object-Verb, so the verb comes at the end.
native_language_example: I believe him.

meaning: contraction of '나는' + '내' meaning 'I' (topic) + 'my' — used when the speaker refers to themselves and something they own/relate to (I ... my ...).
additional_notes: 난 is the colloquial/contracted form of 나는 (topic marker). 내 is the informal possessive 'my' (short for 나의). Together they commonly start sentences like '난 내 집이 좋아' = 'I, my house, like' → 'I like my house.' This structure is informal and typical in spoken Korean. Use in casual conversation; in formal writing/speech use 저는 제 (or 나는 나의) instead.
target_language_example: 난 내 친구랑 영화 보러 갈 거야.
native_language_example: I'm going to watch a movie with my friend.

meaning: 'I' (subject) + 'you' (object) — a colloquial contraction of 나는 널; used to start sentences meaning 'I [verb] you...' (e.g. I trust you / I won't forgive you).
additional_notes: 난 is the contracted, informal form of 나는 (I). 널 is the contracted object form of 너를 (you). Together they appear at the start of a sentence to emphasize the speaker's action or feeling toward 'you'. This phrase is informal and common in spoken Korean. The verb that follows completes the meaning (e.g. 믿어 = trust, 용서하지 않을 거야 = will not forgive).
native_language_example: I'll help you.

meaning: contraction of '나는 네(가/가 아니야/사부다/etc.)' — 'I am/I'm (your...)' or 'I (do not) ... you' depending on following word; '난' = 나는 (I), '네' = 네(가/가 아니야) depending on context (colloquial).
additional_notes: This is colloquial speech. '난' is the casual contraction of '나는' (topic marker). '네' here is the informal possessive/pronoun 'your' or the informal nominative '네가'/'네는' depending on following words—often used in spoken Korean to directly address someone as 'you' or indicate 'your ...'. Meaning changes with what comes next: e.g. '난 네 사부다!' = 'I am your master!' ; '난 네 오빠가 아니다.' = 'I am not your older brother.' It is informal and can sound blunt or rude in polite situations. Use with friends or when imitating casual speech.
native_language_example: I'm your friend.

meaning: I (short for 나는) you — an informal way to start a sentence meaning 'I (am) you' or more likely 'I (to) you' depending on context; often appears in intimate or poetic expressions.
additional_notes: 난 is the contracted/informal form of 나는 (I). 당신 is a polite form of 'you' but can sound distant or used in formal/romantic/poetic contexts. Together, 난 당신 by itself is incomplete and sounds like the beginning of a sentence such as 난 당신을 사랑해 (I love you) or 난 당신이 그리워 (I miss you). Using 당신 in casual conversation with friends is uncommon — choose 너 for close friends or people younger than you. In written/lyrical language, 난 당신 often appears for emphasis or style.
native_language_example: I love you.

meaning: I (do) not / I won't (short, casual way to say 'I don't' or 'I'm not')
additional_notes: 난 is the casual contraction of 나는 (I). 안 is the basic negation word meaning 'not' or 'don't'. Together 난 안 + verb is a casual/informal way to say you won't do something or you don't do/believe something. Tone can be blunt or emphatic; avoid in very polite/formal situations. For polite speech, use 저는 안 .../안 ...요 or ~지 않아요.
native_language_example: I won't go.

meaning: Why me / Why do I... (expressing self-directed wonder, confusion, or frustration)
additional_notes: Short for 나는 왜; 난 is the casual contraction of 나는 (I). Used to start a rhetorical or emotional question about oneself: 난 왜 + verb/adjective/clause. Tone can be puzzled, self-deprecating, or frustrated depending on context. Common in spoken/informal Korean.
target_language_example: 난 왜 아무 것도 잘 못할까?
native_language_example: Why am I so bad at everything?

meaning: I already (have/know/did).
additional_notes: A casual contraction of 나는 이미. Used to say you have already done, experienced, or know something. '난' is informal; use with friends or in casual speech. '이미' means 'already' and usually comes after the subject. Combine with verbs: 난 이미 먹었어 (I already ate), 난 이미 알아 (I already know).
native_language_example: I'm already ready.

meaning: I now / I'm now (emphatic 'I' + 'now')
additional_notes: 난 is the contracted, casual form of 나는 (I). 이제 means 'now' or 'from now on'. Together, 난 이제 emphasizes a change or new state (e.g., 'I'm different now', 'I'm now ...', 'from now on I'll...'). Common in casual speech. Use with verbs, nouns + 이다, or clauses to state a present change or decision.
target_language_example: 난 이제 운동을 매일 할 거야.
native_language_example: I'm going to exercise every day from now on.

meaning: I'm (right) now / I right now ... — used to state what you are doing or your current state.
additional_notes: 난 is the contracted informal form of 나는 (I). 지금 means 'now' or 'right now'. Together, 난 지금 starts a sentence to say what you are doing at the moment (e.g., 'I'm busy right now', 'I'm at the cafe right now'). Common in spoken/informal Korean; use 나는 지금 in more neutral or polite contexts. You can follow it with verbs (가 — go, 바빠 — busy, 운전 중이야 — driving, 있어요 — polite 'am at').
native_language_example: I'm eating right now.

meaning: a contraction of '나는 것' often meaning 'the thing I ...' or 'what I ...' (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction: '난' = '나는' (I + topic/subject), '거' = '것' (thing/act). Used when referring to something the speaker does, felt, or experienced. Appears in phrases like '난 거 봐' (look at what I...), '난 거 알아' (I know that/what I did). Tone is casual; avoid in formal writing or polite speech.
native_language_example: I know that / I know what I did.

meaning: You're making a fuss / What's all the commotion? (expresses surprise, annoyance, or reproach at someone's noisy/exaggerated reaction)
additional_notes: Informal phrase often used to scold or question someone who is overreacting, causing a scene, or making a lot of noise. Can be directed at a person ("왜 네가 난리야?" — why are you making a fuss?) or used to react to a situation ("이게 웬 난리야?" — what is all this commotion?). Tone depends on context: can be annoyed, incredulous, or mildly joking.
target_language_example: 걱정할 거 없는데 왜 그렇게 난리야?
native_language_example: There’s nothing to worry about — why are you making such a fuss?

meaning: short for '나를 못' — 'cannot (do something to/with) me' or 'not (verb) me'.
additional_notes: In these examples, '날' is the colloquial object form of '나(를)' (me). '못' is the adverb meaning 'cannot' or 'unable to'. Together they appear before a verb (often omitted in the short phrase) to mean 'can't [verb] me' or 'won't [verb] me'. Common in colloquial spoken Korean; tone can be confrontational depending on context and following verb. Word order: subject/topic + (나를) + 못 + verb. In casual speech '나를' is often shortened to '날'.
native_language_example: You can't beat me.

meaning: 'Look at me' (informal; imperative)
additional_notes: Casual/informal command formed from 나 (me, object form 날) + 보다 (to look) in the informal imperative 봐. Used to get someone's attention, to ask someone to look at you, or to check if they hear/understand you. Tone can be urgent, annoyed, playful, or affectionate depending on context and intonation. Not polite — use 저를 보세요/날 좀 봐 주세요 for polite requests.
native_language_example: Look at me for a second, check this out.

meaning: 'how (do you) (verb) me' — asks about someone's action, opinion, or treatment of the speaker
additional_notes: 날 is the shortened, colloquial form of 나를 (me, object). 어떻게 means 'how' or 'in what way'. Together they appear in questions like 'How did you find me?' or 'What do you think of me?'. Word order in Korean often places the object before the verb; the full phrase in a sentence will include the verb (생각한 거야, 찾았지, 생각하는지 알겠어요, etc.).
native_language_example: How did you know about me?/How did you find out about me?

meaning: the day/time (when something happens); 'the day will come' or 'a time will come'.
additional_notes: 날 means 'day' or 'time'. When used with the subject marker -이 (날이), it often appears in phrases like '날이 오다/올 거다/왔다' meaning 'the day/time comes/will come/came' — usually referring to a significant or expected moment. Common patterns: '그 날이 오다' (that day will come), '이런 날이 올 거다' (a day like this will come). Context determines whether it's literal (a calendar day) or figurative (a future opportunity or event).
native_language_example: It was hard, but finally the day has come.

meaning: the weather (subject particle '가' attached) — marks 'weather' as the subject of the sentence.
additional_notes: 날씨 means 'weather'. Adding the subject particle '가' makes it the topic/subject of a sentence like 'The weather is...'. Common in short questions and comments: '날씨가 더워?' (Is the weather hot?), '날씨가 좋죠?' (The weather is nice, right?). In casual speech the verb/adjective often follows directly and endings can change for politeness.
native_language_example: The weather is much nicer.

meaning: 'man' or 'a man' as subject/topic (subject form of 남자).
additional_notes: 남자 = 'man' or 'male'. 남자가 is the noun plus subject particle -가, used when the speaker marks 'a man' or 'the man' as the subject of the sentence (often neutral or emphasizing subject). Context and tone can change meaning (e.g., insulting line 3). In questions or exclamations it appears naturally: '남자가 뭔데?' = 'What is a man?' or 'Who is the man?'.
target_language_example: 저기 서 있는 남자가 제 친구예요.
native_language_example: The man standing over there is my friend.

meaning: 'As for men' or 'men (topic marker)'; introduces or comments about men in general or a particular man.
additional_notes: 남자 = 'man' or 'men'. The -는 particle marks the topic ('as for...'). Used to make general statements about men, contrast men with others, or point to a specific man already in context. Tone can be neutral, conversational, or informal depending on sentence. In English it often translates as 'men...', 'a man...', or 'your man...' depending on context.
native_language_example: Men usually like gifts.

meaning: 'a man' (object form; the noun '남자' with the object particle '를')
additional_notes: 남자 = man. 를/을 is the object particle; 를 is used after vowels or when pronunciation favors it. '남자를' marks 'a man' as the direct object of the verb. In English this corresponds to phrases like 'see a man', 'find a man', etc. Context determines definiteness (a man / the man).
native_language_example: I helped a man.

meaning: boyfriend; a male romantic partner.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to someone's male romantic partner. In Korean, words are often spaced: 남자 (man/male) + 친구 (friend). Can also be used in questions and polite/formal forms (e.g., 남자친구 without a space is also seen). To ask if someone has a boyfriend: "남자 친구 있니?" (casual) or "남자 친구 있어요?" (polite).
native_language_example: My friend has a boyfriend.

meaning: He's a man / it's a man (casual).
additional_notes: 남자 (man) + 야 (informal copula: contraction of 이다). Used in casual speech to state or ask that someone/something is male. Can be declarative or interrogative depending on intonation and punctuation. Avoid in formal situations—use 남자예요/남자입니다 instead. Common in simple identification: "그 애는 남자야." = "That kid is a boy/son/ male."
native_language_example: He's my man.

meaning: husband (as the topic of the sentence).
additional_notes: 남편 means 'husband'. Adding the topic particle 은 indicates the husband is the topic or you're asking/contrasting about him. Used in questions or statements like 'As for (your/my) husband...?' Context often determines whose husband (e.g., 네 남편은 = 'your husband...').
native_language_example: Where is your husband right now?

meaning: 'husband' as the direct object (marked with 를).
additional_notes: 남편 means 'husband'. When combined with the object particle 를 (남편을), it indicates the husband is the object of the verb (e.g., to see, call, bring, kill). Use other particles for different roles (e.g., 남편이 for subject, 남편과/와 for 'with husband'). Context determines the verb and nuance.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for (my) husband.

meaning: the husband (as subject or topic); 'husband' with subject/topic particle -이
additional_notes: 남편 = husband. The particle -이 marks the noun as the subject (or topic after contraction with topic/subject functions) of the sentence. Depending on context, it can mean 'my husband', 'your husband', 'the husband', etc., based on possessive words or context. In casual speech, possessives like 내/당신들/제 can appear before 남편 (e.g., 내 남편 = my husband). When used alone as in these examples, context tells whose husband is meant. Use -가 instead of -이 after vowels (남편이 stays the same because 남편 ends with a consonant).
native_language_example: My husband is at home right now.

meaning: I (subject)
additional_notes: 내가 is the first-person subject pronoun 'I' used before verbs. It can also add emphasis (like 'I did it' or 'I — not someone else') depending on tone and context. In casual speech, 내가 often contrasts with 누가 (who) or responds forcefully to disbelief. Watch register: sentences with 내가 can be rude depending on wording and tone.
native_language_example: I did it.

meaning: 'How can I' / 'What can I (do)?' — expresses inability, surprise, or asking how one should act.
additional_notes: Used to question or object to what the speaker is expected to do or how they could do something. Often appears in conversational Korean to show doubt, helplessness, indignation, or to ask for guidance about the speaker's possible action. Tone depends on context: can be rhetorical (내가 어떻게 하겠어? = What can I do?) or genuine (내가 어떻게 지도자로서 일해야 하나? = How should I act as a leader?).
target_language_example: 그 상황에서 내가 어떻게 해야 해?
native_language_example: What should I do in that situation?

meaning: 'Why would I (do/say/etc.)?' or 'Why me?' (used to express surprise, denial, or to ask why the speaker is involved)
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used when the speaker expresses disbelief, denies responsibility, or asks why they are the subject. Often followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 내가 왜 그런 말을 하지? — 'Why would I say something like that?'). Tone depends on context: can be defensive, surprised, or genuinely inquisitive.
native_language_example: Why would I say something like that?

meaning: my words; what I say; my opinion
additional_notes: Short for 내 말은/내 말이, often used to refer to something you said or to introduce your opinion. Can appear in phrases like '내 말이' (that's what I'm saying / I agree) or '내 말은...' (what I mean is...). Context determines whether it's simply 'my words' or functions idiomatically as 'exactly'/'that's right.'
native_language_example: That's what I'm saying.

meaning: Can you hear me? / Do you hear what I'm saying?
additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase. Literally 'my words (are) heard?' Used to check if someone can hear you (audio connection) or if they understand/listen to what you're saying. Often said when speaking to one person or a group; the name or pronoun can be added before the phrase (e.g., '딜런, 내 말 들려?'). Tone and context determine whether it's about sound (can you hear me) or attention/understanding (are you listening).
native_language_example: Friends, can you hear me?

meaning: 'what I mean' / 'my point' (used to check or emphasize that the listener understands or agrees).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or check understanding/agreement. Can stand alone as 'Exactly!' or 'See?' (e.g., '내 말이!' = 'That's what I'm saying!'). Often followed by explanations or used rhetorically. Informal but common in spoken Korean.
native_language_example: That's what I'm saying!

meaning: Listen to me / hear me out (used to get someone's attention before speaking).
additional_notes: Informal to neutral phrase. 내 말 = 'my words' (what I say). 좀 softens the command, making it more like 'please' or 'just' — used when you want someone to listen, often before giving advice, complaining, or making a point. Can be said firmly (내 말 좀 들어!) or politely with -요 (내 말 좀 들어봐요). Followed by statements or urgings. Tone and context determine politeness.
target_language_example: 내 말 좀 들어봐요, 중요한 얘기예요.
native_language_example: Listen to me, this is important.

meaning: 'to me' or 'for me' (dative form of '나' used in speech/writing).
additional_notes: 내게 is the contracted form of 나에게 (나 = I/me, 에게 = to/for). It's used to mark the indirect object (recipient, target, or experiencer) of an action. Common in both spoken and written Korean; slightly more concise than 나에게. Context determines whether it means 'to me', 'for me', or 'from me' (rare).
target_language_example: 그 소식은 내게 큰 위로가 되었어.
native_language_example: That news was a great comfort to me.

meaning: 'my shop' or 'my store'.
additional_notes: 내 = my (informal); 가게 = shop/store. Used to state ownership or claim over a shop. Context can be neutral (introducing your store) or strong/angry (defending your property). Because 내 is the casual form of 'my', it's commonly used in speech with friends or in heated situations; for polite speech use 제 가게. The example sentences show increasingly aggressive tone—watch your tone and add polite endings if needed.
native_language_example: This is a product sold at my shop.

meaning: 'my bag' (informal, shortened spoken form of '내 가방은/를').
additional_notes: 내 is the informal/casual possessive 'my' (short for 나의). 가방 means 'bag'. In conversation Koreans often drop particles (은/를) and verbs, so you'll hear just '내 가방!' to mean 'my bag!' or to claim/point to it. To be polite or formal, use 제 가방. Use 내 가방은/내 가방이/내 가방을 when you need a subject/object particle.
native_language_example: My bag is here.

meaning: my family
additional_notes: 내 is the informal/casual form of 'my' (short for 나의). 가족 means 'family'. Used to refer to one's family members. In polite/formal speech you might hear 제 가족 instead. Depending on sentence ending, it can be a statement, question, or exclamation (e.g., 내 가족! as an emotional exclamation).
native_language_example: My family is here.

meaning: my (thing); mine.
additional_notes: Contraction of '내 것' (내 + 것) meaning 'my thing' or 'mine.' Common in spoken Korean. Used to claim ownership of an item or refer to something that belongs to the speaker. In casual speech the final consonant often drops, so '내 거' sounds like one unit. To be more polite or formal, use '제 것' or '제 거.'
native_language_example: This is mine.

meaning: will be mine / belongs to me (in the future or as a prediction)
additional_notes: 내 is a short form of 나의 (my). 것이다 is the noun 것 (thing) plus the future/predictive marker -이다, often used to express that something will be or is expected to be yours. Context can imply possession, prediction, or certainty (e.g., 'That will be mine' or 'It must be mine'). In casual speech 나의 것 or 내 거 are more common; 내 것이다 sounds slightly more formal or emphatic.
native_language_example: That item will be mine soon.

meaning: my husband
additional_notes: 내 = my (informal/common). 남편 = husband. Used to refer to one's husband; can be possessive and appears before 남편. Tone can vary with context (proud, protective, angry). Sentences 2–3 show protective/commanding uses: 'stay away from my husband' / 'take your hands off my husband.'
native_language_example: My husband is really good at cooking.

meaning: 'my eyes' (often used idiomatically to mean 'in my view' or 'look at me')
additional_notes: Literally 'my eyes'. Used both literally (talking about one's eyes) and idiomatically: as an imperative telling someone to look directly at the speaker (내 눈 똑바로 봐!), as a colloquial comment about perception/opinion (내 눈엔 — 'to me / in my view'), or in expressions like 놀라움/불신 (내 눈 똑바로 보면서 거짓말을 해? — 'Are you lying while looking me straight in the eye?').
native_language_example: Look me in the eye and tell me honestly.

meaning: my money
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 내 = my (short for 나의), 돈 = money. Used to talk about money that belongs to the speaker. Can appear alone as an exclamation (e.g., surprised or angry) or inside sentences. Neutral in formality; tone depends on context (can be strong or rude when shouted).
native_language_example: Is my money in that wallet?

meaning: my younger sibling / my brother or sister (depending on context).
additional_notes: 내 = my (informal, contraction of 나의). 동생 = younger sibling (can be brother or sister). Used in everyday speech; context tells whether it's brother or sister. Common in questions, exclamations, and statements. Pronunciation: [nae dong-saeng].
native_language_example: My younger sibling is at home right now.

meaning: my younger sibling (as the topic); 'as for my sibling...'
additional_notes: 내 = my; 동생 = younger sibling (can be brother or sister). 은 is the topic particle, used to mark the topic and imply contrast or topic-comment structure. Use when you want to talk about your sibling (e.g., state occupation, location, or ask about them). In casual speech, people may drop 은 and say 내 동생 instead. If you mean 'older sibling', use 형/오빠/누나/언니 instead.
native_language_example: My sibling is at home right now.

meaning: my daughter
additional_notes: 내 = 'my' (informal/neutral possessive), 딸 = 'daughter'. Used to refer to one's daughter; appears in statements, exclamations, questions, and emotional expressions. Context/intonation can change politeness and emotion (e.g., 걘 내 딸이잖아 = That's my daughter, defensive; 내 딸이라고요! = insistence or surprise).
native_language_example: That person is my daughter.

meaning: 'my daughter' as the object of a verb (accusative form).
additional_notes: 내 = my (informal/common). 딸 = daughter. The particle 을 marks the noun as the direct object of the verb. Use when the speaker is talking about doing something to or for their daughter (e.g., see, take care of, release). If the next word begins with a vowel-like sound, 을 may change to 를 in speech depending on phonetics (내 딸을 vs. 내 딸을 돌보다).
native_language_example: I took my daughter to school.

meaning: She's/my daughter (informal, saying someone is your daughter).
additional_notes: 내 = my. 딸 = daughter. 이야 is the informal/contracted form of 입니다/이다 used in casual speech to state identity or relationship: 'She/that is my daughter.' Can be used as a statement or a question depending on intonation. Use with friends/family; not polite. For polite contexts use 제 딸이에요 or 제 딸입니다.
native_language_example: That girl is my daughter.

meaning: 'my words' or used idiomatically as 'what I say' / 'listen to me'.
additional_notes: Literally 'my words' (내 = my, 말 = words/speech). Often used to refer to what the speaker is saying: e.g., as a command ('내 말 잘 들어' = 'listen to me/what I'm saying') or to confirm understanding ('내 말 알겠어요?' = 'Do you understand what I'm saying?'). Tone can be firm or commanding depending on context.
native_language_example: Listen to me carefully.

meaning: Are you listening to me? / Listen to what I'm saying
additional_notes: A casual phrase used to ask if someone is listening or to get their attention. "내 말" = "my words / what I say"; "듣고" is the connective/shortened form of "듣고 있(니/있어/있어요)" or an imperative-like prompt. Tone ranges from casual to neutral depending on sentence ending (e.g., 듣고 있어요? is polite; 듣고 있어? is informal). Often followed by a question ending or a name when calling someone's attention.
native_language_example: Are you listening to me?

meaning: 'Can you hear me?' / 'Do you hear what I'm saying?'
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to check if someone can hear you (physically) or to ask if they understand/are listening to what you're saying. "내 말" = "my words"; "들려?" is short for "들려요?/들리나요?" depending on politeness. Can be used with friends, family, or in casual speech; add polite endings (e.g., "제 말 들리세요?") for formal situations.
native_language_example: Honey, can you hear me?

meaning: '(You) don't (do/understand) what I say' — a clipped way to start questions like 'Can't you hear/understand me?' or 'Didn't you listen to me?'.
additional_notes: This is an informal, conversational fragment used to form questions by adding verbs like 들리냐/들리세요 (can you hear/understand), 들었어/들었어요 (did you hear/listen), 믿죠/믿죠? (you don't believe me?). Alone it feels incomplete; native speakers append the appropriate verb and ending. Tone can be annoyed or surprised depending on context and ending formality.
native_language_example: Didn't you hear/listen to me?

meaning: 'my words' (used in phrases like 'listen to me' or 'hear what I say')
additional_notes: 내 (my) + 말 (word/words). Commonly appears in expressions about speaking or listening, e.g. 내 말을 들어(요) = 'listen to me' or 내 말을 듣지 않았다 = 'didn't listen to me.' Used both literally (my speech) and idiomatically (pay attention to me).
native_language_example: Please listen to me.

meaning: My point / What I said (used to check or emphasize agreement or to ask if someone heard you).
additional_notes: Literally 'my words.' Commonly used to: 1) ask for confirmation/agreement (e.g., 'See? I was right.'), or 2) ask if someone heard you ('Can't you hear me?'). Tone depends on context — can be casual, slightly confrontational, or simply checking. Often appears in questions like '내 말이 맞지?' or '내 말이 안 들려?'.
native_language_example: I'm right, aren't I?

meaning: my head
additional_notes: Literally 'my head'. Used both for the physical head and figuratively (e.g., hairstyle, hair, or when someone touches or messes with you). Context determines if it's about hair, hairstyle, or the actual head. Informal phrasing (내 is casual for 'my'). To be more polite, use 제 머리.
native_language_example: How is my hair/head?

meaning: my body
additional_notes: Used to refer to one's physical body or personal space. Can be literal (physical body) or figurative (one's own situation/health). Often appears in commands or warnings (내 몸 건드리지 마! 'Don't touch my body!'). '내' is the casual/informal possessive 'my'.
native_language_example: You should take care of my body. / I should take care of my body.

meaning: 'my room' (the room that belongs to me)
additional_notes: 내 = 'my' (informal/casual; short for '나의'). 방 = 'room'. Used to talk about one's private bedroom or personal room. Common in everyday speech. When giving commands or strong requests, Korean often uses 내 방에서 꺼져! ('get out of my room!'). To be more polite or formal, use 제 방 (humble) or 제 방이에요/제 방입니다.
native_language_example: I'm studying in my room right now.

meaning: 'my love' — an affectionate address or phrase for someone you love.
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a loved one (romantic partner, close family member, or sometimes playfully to a friend). Can be used as a direct form of address (like 'my love!') or in statements ('my love is...'). Tone can be romantic, dramatic, or affectionate depending on context. Informal but polite enough in many situations; not a literal legal phrase.
target_language_example: 내 사랑, 오늘 저녁에 뭐 할래?
native_language_example: My love, what do you want to do tonight?

meaning: my thought / my opinion
additional_notes: Commonly used to state or introduce your opinion. Can be followed by a verb like '에는' (내 생각에는) to mean 'in my opinion' or by a clause (내 생각이야) to emphasize it's what you think. Neutral register—suitable in both casual and polite speech when combined with appropriate endings.
target_language_example: 내 생각에는 이 계획이 좋아 보여.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this plan looks good.

meaning: my birthday
additional_notes: 내 means 'my' (informal/casual). 생일 means 'birthday'. Together they refer to the speaker's birthday. For polite situations you can use 제 생일 instead of 내 생일. Commonly used with particles (에 for 'on' a date, 에서/까지 for location/time ranges) or with verbs like 있다, 아니다, 축하하다, 열다 (파티를 열다).
native_language_example: My friends prepared a party for my birthday.

meaning: my hand
additional_notes: 내 is the informal/casual form of 'my' (from 나의). 손 means 'hand'. Commonly used when asking someone to hold or grab your hand (physically or metaphorically). Because 내 is casual, use with friends, family, or people younger than you; use 제 손 or 제 손을 with polite speech. In spoken commands you may hear the object particle omitted (내 손 잡아 = 'hold my hand').
native_language_example: Hold my hand, let's go together.

meaning: 'in my hands' / 'by me' (used to threaten or say someone/something will be dealt with by the speaker)
additional_notes: Literally 'in my hand(s)'. Often used in spoken Korean to threaten or warn someone (e.g., "내 손에 죽을 줄 알아" = 'you'll die by my hand' / 'I'll deal with you'). Can be followed by verbs like 있다/있어, 죽다, or expressions meaning punishment. Tone is aggressive; not for polite contexts.
target_language_example: 조용하지 않으면 내 손에 죽을 줄 알아!
