additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition or persistence. Often attached to verbs or actions to mean doing something multiple times or 'no matter how many times.' Can express frustration, determination, or encouragement depending on context. Similar to 몇 번이나 but with slightly stronger emphasis on repetition.
target_language_example: 그 문제는 몇 번이고 설명했는데 아직 못 이해하네.
native_language_example: I've explained that problem many times, but they still don't understand.

meaning: 'how old (are you/they/etc.)' or 'what age'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about someone's age. Often appears with a subject and polite/casual endings: 몇 살이에요? (polite), 몇 살이야? (casual), 몇 살이죠? (polite/formal question), 몇 살인데? (confrontational or surprised). Can be used about people or things (e.g., age of an object). Literal components: 몇 = 'how many/what number', 살 = 'years (of age)'.
native_language_example: How old are you?

meaning: What time (is it)? / At what time?
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time. Can be combined with polite endings: '몇 시예요?' (polite), '몇 시에요?' (alternate spelling), '몇 시야?' (casual). To ask 'at what time' for events, add a verb or marker: '몇 시에 만나요?' (What time shall we meet?).
native_language_example: What time does the subway come?

meaning: 'at what time' or 'what time (at)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time when something happens. 몇 시 means 'what time'; adding 에 marks the time (at). Polite/formal variations include 몇 시예요? (What time is it?) and 몇 시에 오실 거예요? (What time will you come?).
native_language_example: What time does the meeting start?

meaning: 'What time is it?' (casual/informal)
additional_notes: Informal way to ask the time. Used with friends, family, or people of same/lower social status. For polite situations use '몇 시예요?' or '몇 시입니까?'. Can be followed by a subject (e.g., 시합이 몇 시야? — What time is the match?) or stand alone.
native_language_example: What time is it now?

meaning: how many hours; a few hours (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about an amount of time measured in hours. Can be a question (몇 시간이 걸려요? — How many hours does it take?) or a vague amount (몇 시간 — a few hours). Often appears with verbs like 걸리다 (to take time) or 함께 with time markers like 동안.
target_language_example: 이 일을 끝내는 데 몇 시간이 걸려요?
native_language_example: How many hours does it take to finish this work?

meaning: 'what score/points' or 'how many points' (asking about a numeric score or points).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a score, grade, points left, or current points in games/tests. '몇' = 'how many/what number', '점' = 'point/score' or 'mark' (also 'dot' in other contexts). Polite form: '몇 점이에요?' Casual/informal: '나 몇 점이야?'
native_language_example: What score did you get on the exam?

meaning: 'which floor?' / 'how many floors?' (used to ask what floor someone or something is on)
additional_notes: Used when asking or confirming a floor number in a building (e.g., in elevators, at hotels, offices). Often followed by a particle: '몇 층이에요?' or shortened in casual speech to '몇 층?' or '몇 층이야?'. Use polite forms with '-세요?' or '-이에요?'.
native_language_example: In the elevator: Which floor would you like?

meaning: everyone; all of it / all together (emphatic)
additional_notes: A colloquial emphatic phrase combining 모두 ('all/everyone') and 다 ('all/everything' or emphasis). Used to mean 'everyone' (people) or 'everything/all of it' depending on context. Often used for encouragement, permission, or to emphasize inclusiveness: 'everyone go', 'take everything', 'all together'. Common in spoken Korean; can sound more emphatic than just 모두 or 다 alone.
native_language_example: Let's all leave together.

meaning: everyone; everybody (subject marker attached).
additional_notes: 모두 means 'everyone' or 'all'. When followed by the subject particle -가, 모두가 marks 'everyone' as the subject of the sentence. Used in statements about what all people do, know, think, etc. Colloquial register; can appear in formal and informal contexts depending on verb endings.
native_language_example: I hope everyone is happy.

meaning: 'everyone' or 'all (of them)' as an object (accusative form)
additional_notes: 모두 means 'everyone' or 'all'. 모두를 is used when 'everyone' is the object of the sentence (followed by verbs like 믿다, 숨기다, 알다). In casual speech you may also hear 그냥 '모두' without 를 when context makes the object clear. Use 모두를 when you want to emphasize that the action affects all people/items.
native_language_example: I will help everyone.

meaning: everything; all things.
additional_notes: Used to refer to all items, situations, or aspects collectively. Often appears as '모든 것' (noun phrase) or with subject particle '모든 것이' / object particle '모든 것을'. Can be used alone as a short answer or in questions (e.g., '모든 것이?' meaning 'Everything?').
native_language_example: We tried everything.

meaning: 'everything' or 'all (things)'.
additional_notes: 모든 것 means 'everything'; 모든 것을 uses the object particle 를/을 (것을) so it's used when 'everything' is the object of a verb. Common in sentences like 'I will do everything', 'I risked everything', or exclamations 'Yes, everything!'.
target_language_example: 나는 모든 것을 시도해 볼 거예요.
native_language_example: I will try everything.

meaning: 'everything' (subject form)
additional_notes: 모든 것 = 'everything'; adding -이 marks it as the subject (모든 것이 ~). Used to talk about all things or the whole situation. Can appear alone as a question (모든 것이?) meaning 'Everything?'. Common in statements like 'everything stopped/changed/seemed...'.
native_language_example: Everything will be okay.

meaning: 'everything' or 'all of it' (colloquial contraction of 모든 것이).
additional_notes: 모든 게 is the casual spoken form of 모든 것이. Use it to refer to all things/situation(s) in context. It can describe concrete things ('everything in the box') or abstract situations ('everything is over'). Common in everyday speech and written dialogue. Followed by verbs like 있다, 끝나다, 잘되다, 아니다, etc.
native_language_example: Everything will be okay.

meaning: to not know (used as part of a larger clause; expresses that someone wouldn't know or is unlikely to know)
additional_notes: 모르다 = to not know. 줄 here is from 줄 알다/모르다 construction indicating expectation or assumption about someone's knowledge or behavior (e.g., '~할 줄 알다/모르다' = know how to / don't know how to). In many cases 모를 줄 appears inside sentences like '그가 올 줄은 모를 줄 알았다' or more commonly '그가 올 줄은 몰랐다' (I didn't expect he would come). 모를 줄 by itself is incomplete and needs context (what someone doesn't know or wouldn't know).
native_language_example: I didn't think (you) would not know that news. / I didn't expect they wouldn't know about the news.

meaning: Do you think I don't know? / You think I wouldn't know?
additional_notes: A colloquial, slightly confrontational expression used to challenge someone's assumption that the speaker is unaware of something. Often used rhetorically and can imply annoyance, disbelief, or warning. Common in spoken Korean; can be said with rising intonation. The neutral verb stem is 모르다 (to not know) + 줄 알다 (to think/assume) in negative form.
target_language_example: 네가 학교에서 마약 파는 걸 내가 모를 줄 알아?
native_language_example: Do you think I wouldn't know that you're selling drugs at school?

meaning: to/at (a) meeting or gathering
additional_notes: 모임 means 'meeting' or 'gathering'. Adding 에 marks direction/place ('to' or 'at' a meeting). Often used with verbs like 가다 (go), 나오다 (attend/come out), 오다 (come), 나가다 (go out/attend). Context decides translation: 모임에 가? = 'go to the meeting?' 모임에 오다/나오다 = 'come to/attend the meeting'. Informal speech often drops particles or shortens verbs.
target_language_example: 다음 주 모임에 꼭 올 거죠?
native_language_example: Will you definitely come to the meeting next week?

meaning: topic marker 'as for a hat' / 'about hats' (모자 + 는)
additional_notes: 모자 means 'hat'. The particle 는 marks the topic and can imply contrast or emphasis (e.g., 'as for the hat...'). In spoken Korean, sentences may drop verbs, so 모자는 안 쓰고 있는데 can mean 'I'm not wearing the hat (but...)'. Context determines nuance: contrast, topic, or slight disagreement.
native_language_example: As for the hat, leave it here and go.

meaning: the hat (object) — '모자' in the accusative form (direct object).
additional_notes: 모자 means 'hat'. 모자를 is used when the hat is the direct object of a verb (marks with object particle -를 after a vowel-ending noun). Common verbs: 사다 (to buy) → 모자를 샀다 (bought a hat), 쓰다 (to wear/put on) → 모자를 쓰다 (to put on a hat). In spoken Korean, object particle can sometimes be omitted if context is clear.
native_language_example: I bought a new hat.

meaning: wearing a hat / with a hat on
additional_notes: 모자 (hat) + 쓰다 (to wear, for head items). 쓰고 is the connector form (present participle or '-ing') used to link to another verb or to describe someone currently wearing a hat. Commonly used in sentences like '...모자를 쓰고 있다' (is wearing a hat) or '...모자를 쓰고 ...' (doing something while wearing a hat). Pronunciation: mo-ja-reul sseu-go.
target_language_example: 그는 파란 모자를 쓰고 공원에 갔어요.
native_language_example: He went to the park wearing a blue hat.

meaning: to wear a hat (to put on/to have a hat on)
additional_notes: 모자 means 'hat' and 쓰다 in this context means 'to put on' or 'to wear' (used for items worn on the head). With 쓰다 the focus can be on putting the hat on or simply having it on. For other clothing items, different verbs are used (입다 for clothes, 신다 for shoes). Politeness and tense are shown by conjugating 쓰다 (e.g., 써요, 쓸게요, 썼어요).
target_language_example: 모자를 쓰다 보면 시야가 좁아질 수 있어요.
native_language_example: If you wear a hat, your field of vision can become narrower.

meaning: the (subject) voice / someone's voice (with subject marker -가).
additional_notes: 목소리 means 'voice' or 'sound of a voice'. Here it appears with the subject marker -가 (목소리가), so it marks 'voice' as the subject of the sentence. Used to talk about the quality, presence, or audibility of a voice (e.g., 'your voice is nice', 'I can hear a voice', 'why can't I hear the voice?'). Common verbs and adjectives used with 목소리가: 좋다 (to be good/nice), 들리다 (to be heard), 안 들리다 (not heard), 어떻다/그러다 (to be like).
native_language_example: That person has a warm voice.

meaning: 'one's life' used as the object (with an action like give, risk, save).
additional_notes: 목숨 means 'life' (one's existence). When followed by the object particle 을, it marks 'life' as the direct object of a verb (e.g., give one's life, risk one's life, save someone's life). Common verbs with 목숨을: 주다 (give), 걸다 (risk), 구하다 (save). Often used in strong or dramatic contexts.
target_language_example: 나는 친구를 위해 내 목숨을 바치겠다.
native_language_example: I'll give my life for my friend.

meaning: purpose; objective (with subject particle -이).
additional_notes: 목적 means 'purpose' or 'goal'. Adding -이 marks it as the subject (목적이 ...?). It commonly appears in questions asking about someone's purpose (e.g., '목적이 뭐야?' = 'What's the purpose?'). In polite speech you'd use 무엇/뭘/뭐 and polite endings: '그 목적이 뭘까요?' or '목적이 무엇입니까?'.
native_language_example: What is that purpose?

meaning: on/for the body; affecting the body (physically).
additional_notes: 몸 (body) + 에 (particle) — used to say something is on someone's body (touching them) or that something affects someone's health/physical state. In commands, it appears in phrases like '몸에 손대지 마!' (Don't touch their body). For health comments, it's used with adjectives: '몸에 나쁘다/좋다' = 'bad/good for the body'.
target_language_example: 이 약은 식사 후에 먹어야 해. 공복에 먹으면 몸에 안 좋아.
native_language_example: You should take this medicine after a meal. If you take it on an empty stomach, it's not good for your body.

meaning: 'as for (your) body' / 'about (your) health' — topic marker + 'body/health'.
additional_notes: 몸 means 'body' and 은 is the topic particle. Used to ask or talk about someone's physical condition or health. In questions it's a casual/neutral way to ask 'How are you feeling?' Adjust politeness with verb endings (e.g., 괜찮아? casual, 괜찮으세요? polite). Not used alone — usually followed by adjectives or verbs about health (괜찮다, 어떻다, 어때요).
native_language_example: How is your health? / Are you feeling okay?

meaning: the noun '몸' (body) with the object particle '을' (marks the direct object).
additional_notes: 몸 = body. 을 is the object marker used after a noun ending in a consonant (here '몸'). '몸을' appears whenever 'body' is the direct object of a verb (e.g., 버리다, 부르다, 얻다, 숙이다). In English sentences you often translate the whole clause (e.g., 'throw away the old body', 'bow your body' = 'bow down'). Word order in Korean is typically Subject–Object–Verb, so verbs come at the end.
native_language_example: John, bow your body! / John, bend down!

meaning: 'body' used as the subject (with subject particle 이) — often refers to one's health or physical condition.
additional_notes: 몸 means 'body'. When combined with the subject particle 이 (몸이), it typically introduces statements about physical state, symptoms, health, or appearance (e.g., 몸이 안 좋아 = (my) body/health is not good). Context and verb/adjective determine whether it's about illness, feeling, or appearance. Pronoun 'my' is often implied by context; Korean frequently omits explicit possessive pronouns.
native_language_example: My health/body hasn't been good lately.

meaning: can't go / unable to go (informal, short for 못 가다)
additional_notes: Used to say someone cannot go or is unable to do something that involves going/moving. '못' is placed before a verb to indicate inability (cannot). In casual speech the dictionary form '못 가다' is shortened to '못 가'. Can be used as a command/statement depending on intonation and context (e.g., '넌 못 가!' = 'You can't go!').
native_language_example: I can't go today because I have work.

meaning: 'I didn't hear (it)' / 'Didn't you hear (it)?' (casual)
additional_notes: 못 = cannot / did not; 들었어 is past casual form of 듣다 (to hear). Used in casual speech to say you didn't hear something or to ask someone if they didn't hear. Can be a question (with rising intonation) or a statement. For polite situations use 못 들었어요.
native_language_example: What did you say? I didn't hear well.

meaning: '(You) don't (or can't) trust (me)?' / 'I can't believe (it).' depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly used in conversational Korean. As a question directed at someone (e.g., '날 못 믿어?'), it means 'Don't you trust me?' Literally 못 = cannot/not, 믿어 = (you) trust/believe (informal present). Can also be used to express disbelief about something (e.g., 못 믿어! = 'I can't believe it!'). Informal tone — used with friends, family, or when not using polite speech.
native_language_example: Why don't you trust me?

meaning: so that (someone) cannot see (someone/something); to prevent meeting/seeing
additional_notes: 못 is the negation 'cannot' and 보게 is the connective form of 보다 (to see) meaning 'to be able to see' or 'to see (someone)'. Together used after verbs like 막다 (to prevent) to mean 'prevent from seeing' or 'make it so they can't see/meet'. Often appears in contexts about blocking contact or meetings (e.g., 가족이 못 보게 하다 = to stop someone seeing a family member).
native_language_example: He was forbidden from seeing the child.

meaning: can't/won't see (something happen); can't tolerate/allow (a certain situation).
additional_notes: 못 is a negator meaning 'cannot' or 'won't'; 봐 comes from 보다 ('to see'), but in these sentences it's idiomatic: '~는 꼴을 못 봐' means you can't stand watching that happen (you refuse to let it happen or can't bear to see it). Alone, '난 절대 못 봐' can mean 'I absolutely won't tolerate/see that.' Context decides whether it's literal (can't see) or emotional (won't tolerate).
target_language_example: 난 친구가 울면서 헤어지는 꼴은 못 봐.
native_language_example: I can't stand seeing my friend break up while crying.

meaning: I didn't see (them/it), but... / I haven't seen (someone/something).
additional_notes: 못 봤다 is the past negative of 보다 (to see): 'didn't see' or 'haven't seen.' Adding -는데 softens the statement, can imply contrast, expectation, surprise, or invite a response (English: '...but' / 'though' / tag question). Context and intonation determine whether it's a simple report, a mild complaint, or a question.
native_language_example: I didn't see that person—who is it?

meaning: Did (you) not see (someone/something)? / I didn't see (someone/something).
additional_notes: Casual/informal spoken form. 못 = cannot / did not (negation), 봤어 = past tense of 보다 (to see). Depending on intonation and context, it can be a question (Did you not see...?) or a statement (I didn't see...). Used when asking if someone has seen a person or thing, or reporting that you didn't see them. For polite speech, use 못 봤어요 or 못 봤습니다.
native_language_example: Did you not see Rachel? / Haven't you seen Rachel?

meaning: Didn't see/meet; haven't seen (something or someone).
additional_notes: Polite past-negative of '보다' (to see). Used to say you did not see or meet someone/something, or to ask if someone hasn't seen them. Context determines whether it's a question ('Haven't you seen...?') or a statement ('I didn't see...'). Common in everyday speech. To make it less formal, use 못 봤어? (informal) or 못 봤습니다 (more formal).
native_language_example: I didn't see that movie yesterday.

meaning: I/I can't stand it; I can't take it anymore.
additional_notes: A colloquial expression meaning one can no longer tolerate something (pain, annoyance, delay, etc.). Often used alone as an exclamation or followed by what the speaker wants (e.g., '빨리 내려!' = 'get down quickly'). '못' is the negation ('cannot') and '참아' is the informal present of '참다' (to endure). Use with friends or in informal situations.
native_language_example: I really can't stand this noise!

meaning: I can't (do it) / I can't handle (it).
additional_notes: Casual/informal way to say you are unable or unwilling to do something, or that you can't understand or cope with a situation. Derived from 못 (cannot) + 하겠어 (colloquial future/ability expression) — often expresses inability, refusal, or frustration. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be a strong exclamation (I can't!) or a question (You can't?) when used in questions.
target_language_example: 이 일은 나 혼자서 못 하겠어.
native_language_example: I can't do this job by myself.

meaning: 'cannot' or 'to be unable to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used before a verb (or verb phrase) to indicate inability or that something cannot be done. 못 is a negative adverb (cannot); 하다 is 'to do' but here appears as part of verbs or support verb constructions (못 + verb). Combine with a verb stem or with 하다 compounds: 못 + verb (e.g., 못 가다 = cannot go) or 못 하다 as the predicate after a noun+하다 verb (e.g., 운동을 못 하다 = cannot exercise). Can express physical inability, lack of permission, or circumstances preventing an action. For prohibition or simple negation of doing by choice, use 안 하다 instead of 못 하다.
native_language_example: to be unable to exercise / cannot exercise.

meaning: 'cannot' or 'cannot do' (cannot perform an action).
additional_notes: 못 + 하다 = 'unable to do' or 'cannot'. Used after a verb stem; here examples shorten to '못 해' (I/you/he/etc. can't do it). Informal/conversational; negative ability (not the same as refusing). Polite speech would be 못 해요/못 합니다. Can be used alone as a brief reply ('I can't').
native_language_example: I can't do that.

meaning: couldn't (do something) / did not manage to do (something).
additional_notes: Combines 못 (cannot/not able to) + past polite form 했어요 of 하다 (to do). Used to say you were unable to do something or didn't do it. Common in spoken Korean; often followed by the verb's object or activity before 못 했어요. Can express inability, lack of opportunity, or failure to complete an action.
native_language_example: I couldn't do my homework.

meaning: will not be able to do (something) / probably can't do
additional_notes: Combination of 못 (cannot) + 할 거(예정/추정) from 하다 (to do). Used to express inability or expectation that someone/something won't be able to do an action. Often followed by a verb or clause context (e.g., 못할 거야, 못할 거 같은데). Polite endings can be added (못할 거예요).
native_language_example: I probably won't be able to finish it by tomorrow.

meaning: 'weapon(s)' with topic/contrast marker - 'as for weapons' or 'weapons...?'
additional_notes: 무기 = 'weapon' (noun). -는 is the topic/contrast particle attached to 무기 (weapon). So 무기는 is used to bring up or ask about weapons, to contrast them with something else, or to emphasize the topic. In questions it often implies expectation or contrast (e.g., 'what about weapons?' or 'you didn't bring weapons, right?').
native_language_example: I left the weapons at home.

meaning: 'weapon' in the object form (used when doing something to/with a weapon).
additional_notes: 무기 (武器) means 'weapon'. 무기를 is the accusative/object form (무기 + 를) used when commanding, requesting, or describing actions involving a weapon (e.g., put down, pick up, throw away, give). You'll often see it in imperative sentences: 모두 무기를 내려놔! (Put down your weapons!), 무기를 들어라! (Raise your weapons!).
native_language_example: Please put down your weapon(s).

meaning: 'on/onto the stage' (location or movement toward the stage)
additional_notes: 무대 (stage) + 에 (location/goal particle). Used to say someone is physically on the stage (무대에 있다) or goes onto the stage (무대에 오르다/서다). Context decides whether it's static (on) or action (onto). Common verbs with it: 서다 (to stand), 오르다 (to go up/perform), 있다 (to be).
native_language_example: The actors went on stage and received applause.

meaning: 'what game' / 'which game' (used to ask what game someone is playing or referring to)
additional_notes: Common, casual phrase to ask about the game someone is playing or to express confusion about a game. Can be used in polite, neutral, or informal forms depending on sentence ending (예: 무슨 게임이에요? polite; 무슨 게임이야? informal). Often followed by verbs like 하다 (to play) or 있어/있다 (to be).
native_language_example: What game are you playing now?

meaning: What (kind of) smell?/What is that smell?
additional_notes: Used to ask about an unknown smell. 무슨 means 'what (kind of)' and 냄새 means 'smell' or 'odor'. Can be used alone as a short question (무슨 냄새?) or with verb endings for politeness/nuance (나? 니? 지?). Tone can show surprise, concern, or curiosity.
native_language_example: What is that smell coming from the kitchen?

meaning: 'what (is the) meaning' or 'what does (this) mean'
additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning or significance of a word, phrase, sentence, or situation. Common in questions: 무슨 뜻이야? (casual), 무슨 뜻인가요? (polite). Can be followed by 이/그/저 (this/that) or a noun/phrase to ask about that specific item.
native_language_example: What does this word mean?

meaning: What does (this/that) mean?
additional_notes: Casual/informal way to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, sentence, or situation. '무슨' = what/which kind of, '뜻' = meaning, and '-이야' is the informal casual ending used with friends or people younger than you. For polite situations use '무슨 뜻이에요?' or '무슨 뜻입니까?'. Can point to something (이게/그게) or be used alone when context is clear.
native_language_example: What does this word mean?

meaning: What does (this/that) mean?
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask for the meaning or explanation of something. 무슨 = what kind of/what; 뜻 = meaning; -이죠 is a polite ending (slightly softer than -이에요/-예요, often used when addressing someone respectfully). Can be used about words, situations, or actions. Add context words if needed: 이게 무슨 뜻이죠? (What does this mean?), 그게 무슨 뜻이죠? (What does that mean?).
native_language_example: What does this sentence mean?

meaning: 'what (something) means' or 'whether/if (you) know the meaning'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the meaning of something. Often appears in questions like "무슨 뜻인지 아세요?/알겠어요?/알지?" depending on formality. It literally combines 무슨 (what) + 뜻 (meaning) + -인지 (subordinating ending indicating indirect question or uncertainty). Common in both direct questions and embedded clauses (e.g., "내가 무슨 뜻인지 말했어").
native_language_example: Do you know what this word means?

meaning: 'what (words/thing someone said)' or 'what do you mean? / what are you talking about?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the content or meaning of someone's words. Common in questions like 'What did you say?' or 'Do you know what they mean?'. Can stand alone as a short question: '무슨 말?' = 'What? / What do you mean?'. Often followed by verbs like 하다/하려고 하다/하는지 알다.
target_language_example: 그가 무슨 말 하려는지 잘 모르겠어.
native_language_example: I'm not sure what he was trying to say.

meaning: 'what (words/thing) —' used to ask or refer to what someone said or what was said.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before verbs like 하세요/했지/한 거야/들었지 to ask about or mention speech/things someone said. Can be shortened in casual speech (무슨 말). Often followed by a verb (하다, 듣다, 하다). In sentence 5 it introduces a clause meaning 'whatever the author says' (무슨 말을 하든 = 'no matter what he says').
native_language_example: What did you say like that?

meaning: 'what (you/someone) are saying' or 'what do (you/they) mean?'.
additional_notes: A phrase used to ask or question the content or meaning of someone's words. Often appears in questions like '무슨 말을 하는 거예요?' (What are you saying?) or in exasperated forms like '무슨 말을 하는 건지 몰라' (I don't know what you're talking about). Can be followed by particles/ending (거야/거예요/건지) depending on formality and nuance.
target_language_example: 무슨 말을 하는지 다시 말해 주세요.
native_language_example: Please say again what you are saying / what you mean.

meaning: 'What do you mean?' or 'What are you saying?'.
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase used to ask someone to clarify, express surprise, or show disbelief about what was just said. Common in spoken Korean. Can be shortened to '뭐?' or '무슨 말?' depending on tone. With rising intonation it's a question; with sharper tone it can express shock or challenge.
target_language_example: 그들이 서로 죽이고 있다는 게 무슨 말이야?
native_language_example: What do you mean they are killing each other?

meaning: 'what (someone) means' or 'what (this) means' (used when checking understanding).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the meaning or intent of something someone said. Often appears in questions or tags asking if the listener understands (e.g., '무슨 말인지 아세요?'). Can be followed by verbs like 알다/모르다 (to know/not know) or by sentence endings that check comprehension. Informal form may drop polite endings (알아?).
target_language_example: 제가 천천히 말하면 무슨 말인지 알겠어요?
native_language_example: If I speak slowly, will you understand what I mean?

meaning: 'what (are you) saying?' or 'what do you mean? (polite/formal)'
additional_notes: Used in polite/formal speech to ask someone to repeat or clarify what they said, or to express surprise/disbelief at their statement. Often appears with polite endings like -이시죠, -이세요, or as part of a question. '말씀' is the honorific form of '말' (word/speech).
native_language_example: Sorry, what did you say?

meaning: 'what problem' or 'what's the problem?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask whether there is a problem or what's wrong. Can be casual or polite depending on sentence ending (있어?/있어 요?/있나?/있냐?). Often shortened to just '무슨 문제?' in casual speech. Not asking for a description of 'which problem' but rather 'is there a problem?' or 'what's wrong?'.
native_language_example: Is there a problem?

meaning: Is there any problem? / Is something wrong?
additional_notes: Polite/neutral phrase used to ask if someone has any problem or concern. '무슨' = 'what/any kind of', '문제' = 'problem', and '-이라도' adds a sense of 'even/any' (emphasizing 'any problem at all'). Common in questions like '무슨 문제라도 있어요?' or more polite '무슨 문제라도 있으신가요?'.
native_language_example: Is there any problem?

meaning: what does (it/them/this) have to do with (me/you/this)? / what relevance/relationship (does it have)?
additional_notes: Used to ask about relevance or to dismiss something as not related. Often appears as 무슨 상관이에요? or 무슨 상관이지? Can be neutral (asking relevance) or dismissive/critical depending on tone and context (e.g., '죽든 말든 걔들이 무슨 상관인데요?' = 'Why should I care if they die?'). Often followed by particles indicating the person or thing: ~와/과 무슨 상관 (with), ~랑 무슨 상관 (colloquial).
native_language_example: What does that news have to do with us?

meaning: What's it to me? / What does it matter? (expresses indifference or that something is none of one's business)
additional_notes: Casual/neutral phrase used to show indifference, dismissiveness, or to say something is not one's concern. Often follows a statement or question about someone else's actions. Tone can be blunt or rude depending on context and intonation. Formal alternative: '무슨 상관입니까?'
native_language_example: What does it matter if you're late?

meaning: What's it to me? / What does it have to do with (me/this)? (asking why something matters/why it's relevant)
additional_notes: Used to question relevance or importance—often a bit confrontational or dismissive. Can be used politely depending on tone and context (adding -요 makes it polite). Replace -죠 with -야? or plain form for informal speech (무슨 상관이야, 무슨 상관이니) or make more formal with -습니까 (무슨 상관입니까). Commonly followed by a topic (e.g., 그게 릴리아나와 무슨 상관이죠? 'What does that have to do with Liliana?').
native_language_example: What does that matter to me?

meaning: What's it to me? / How is that my concern? (expressing that something is not one's business)
additional_notes: Informal, often blunt or confrontational. Used to question why something matters to the speaker or to dismiss relevance. Common in spoken Korean; tone can be rude depending on context. Can be used with different subjects (나랑, 니가, 경찰이랑) to ask why the relation matters.
native_language_example: What does that have to do with me?

meaning: 'what (kind of) thought' — used to ask 'what are you thinking?' or 'what do you mean?'
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions like '무슨 생각 해?' (= What are you thinking?/What are you doing in your head?). Short form '무슨 생각?' can be used alone to ask someone to explain their idea or to express surprise at their thoughts/behavior. Informal; often followed by 해? or 해요? in polite speech: '무슨 생각 해?' → casual, '무슨 생각 해요?' → polite.
native_language_example: What are you thinking?

meaning: with what thought/intention; 'what were you thinking (when...)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask (often angrily or incredulously) about someone's motive, intention, or thought process behind an action. Common in spoken Korean. Tone can be critical or surprised. Often followed by verbs like 했니/왔니/그랬죠/부른 거야. Can be softened with polite endings.
native_language_example: What were you thinking when you did that?

meaning: 'what thought' (used to ask or refer to what someone was thinking; part of the question phrase '무슨 생각을 하다' = 'to think what').
additional_notes: Often appears in questions about someone's thoughts or intentions. Usually followed by a verb like 하다 (하다/했죠/했어/한 거야). Informal forms drop particles or change endings (무슨 생각을 했어요? / 무슨 생각을 했어?). Can express surprise or criticism when used with 도대체 or in an exasperated tone.
native_language_example: What were you thinking?

meaning: 'what (kind of) thought(s) (you) are having' — used to ask or refer to someone's thoughts.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of phrases like "무슨 생각을 하고 있(는)지" or "무슨 생각을 하고 있어요?" to ask or state what someone is thinking. Politeness is shown by verb endings: 하고 있어요/있어요 (polite), 하고 있어? (casual), 하고 계신가요? (honorific). Often followed by verbs like 있다/있나 (to be doing) or 알다/모르다 (to know/don't know).
native_language_example: What are you thinking right now?

meaning: 'What are you talking about?' / 'What do you mean?'/expression of disbelief
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is saying or to show disbelief/surprise/annoyance at a statement. Polite form: '무슨 소리입니까?' Casual/angry: '무슨 소리 하는 거야!' Can be used both as a genuine question (what did you say?) and as a reaction (That can't be true / What nonsense).
target_language_example: 무슨 소리 하는 거야? 그게 사실이라고?
native_language_example: What are you talking about? Is that really true?

meaning: "What are you talking about?" / "What do you mean?" (expressing disbelief, confusion, or disagreement)
additional_notes: Casual, spoken phrase used to question or reject what someone just said. Often part of a longer sentence like "무슨 소리 하는 거야?" or asked directly as a retort. Tone can be surprised, annoyed, or disbelieving depending on context. Use with friends or informal situations; avoid with strangers or in formal contexts.
target_language_example: 무슨 소리 하는 거야? 그게 사실이야?
native_language_example: What are you talking about? Is that true?

meaning: "What are you talking about?" / "What do you mean?" (expresses disbelief, confusion, or asks for clarification)
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase used to challenge, show surprise, or ask for clarification about what someone said. Tone can be incredulous ("No way!") or simply questioning depending on context and intonation. Use with friends or people of same/lower social level; for polite situations use 무슨 말씀이세요? or 무슨 말이에요?.
native_language_example: You say that's true? What are you talking about?

meaning: 'What are you talking about?' / 'What do you mean?'/ 'What is that noise/sound? (context-dependent)'
additional_notes: Common polite/formal spoken phrase. Used to express surprise, disbelief, or to ask for clarification about what someone just said or about an unexpected statement or situation. Tone and context change meaning: can be genuine question, shocked disbelief (often with rising or exclamatory intonation), or literal question about a sound. Often follows something surprising (e.g., '새 여자라니 무슨 소리예요?' = 'What do you mean by a new woman?').
native_language_example: You’re saying you were that late? What do you mean?

meaning: What is that sound? / What do you mean by that sound?
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to ask about an unfamiliar or surprising sound, or to ask for clarification about what someone means (especially when reacting to something heard). Often shortened from "무슨 소리야?" or "무슨 소리지?" and used with rising intonation. Can be used alone or with a gesture toward the sound/source.
native_language_example: Wait, that noise over there—what is that sound?

meaning: 'what are you talking about' / 'what do you mean' (part of phrases expressing confusion or disbelief about someone's words)
additional_notes: Literally 'what sound/words'. Used when asking what someone means, expressing confusion, or showing disbelief/strong disagreement. Commonly appears in full phrases like '무슨 소릴 하는 거야?' (informal/neutral) or exclamations '무슨 소릴!' (I don't agree / nonsense). Politeness is adjusted by ending (해/해요/합니까/etc.).
target_language_example: 무슨 소릴 하는 거야? 지금 무슨 말 하는 거야?
native_language_example: What are you talking about? What do you mean right now?

meaning: what use; what's the point
additional_notes: Used to ask rhetorically about the usefulness or purpose of something, often implying doubt, frustration, or that it's pointless. Common in questions like '무슨 소용이야/있어/있겠어?' and can be softened with polite endings (예: 무슨 소용이죠?).
native_language_example: What's the point of going now?

meaning: by what means / how (will something be done)?
additional_notes: Used to ask or challenge the method, means, or possibility of doing something. Often expresses disbelief, doubt, or demand for an explanation (e.g., 'How could (you) do that?' or 'By what means will you...'). Common in questions and rhetorical expressions.
native_language_example: How are you going to go alone? / By what means will you go alone?

meaning: What trick/scheme (are you doing)?; What are you up to?
additional_notes: Used to express suspicion or anger about someone's actions—asking what trick, scheme, or nonsense they are trying. Often confrontational; can sound rude depending on tone. Common in casual speech. Not a literal question about a 'work'—수작 here means 'trick' or 'ploy'.
native_language_example: If you say that, what are you trying to pull?

meaning: 'what (are you) talking about' / 'what (is the) story/topic'
additional_notes: Used to ask about the topic, content, or meaning of what someone said. Common in questions: 무슨 얘기 하는 거야? (casual), 무슨 얘기 하세요? (polite), 무슨 얘기죠? (neutral/polite). 얘기 is an informal form of 이야기 (story/talk). Often followed by verbs like 하다 (to do/say) or 했어/했어요 (did/said).
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

meaning: 'what (kind of) story/talk/things (are you) ...' — used to ask about the content/topic of what someone is saying or wants to say.
additional_notes: 무슨 = what/which kind of; 얘기(를) = story/talk/thing said. Often appears in questions like '무슨 얘기를 해요?' (What are you talking about?) or '무슨 얘기를 듣고 싶어?' (What do you want to hear?). The object marker 를 can be omitted in casual speech. Tone can be surprised (대체 무슨 얘기를 하는 거예요? = What on earth are you talking about?) or curious (무슨 얘기를 할 것 같아요? = What do you think they'll talk about?).
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

meaning: what (talk/speech) / what are (you) talking about; "무슨 얘기(를)" contracted — asks about the content of a conversation or what someone wants to say.
additional_notes: 얘길 is a colloquial contraction of 얘기(를). Used to ask or refer to the topic/content of speech. Common in questions: "무슨 얘길 할까요?" (What should we talk about?), "무슨 얘길 하는 건가?" (What on earth are you talking about?). Polite forms replace 해/하겠어요 with appropriate endings; the meaning stays the same.
native_language_example: What are you going to tell your friend? / What will you talk about with your friend?

meaning: 'what meaning' → 'what does (it) mean?' / 'what is the meaning (of...)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask about the meaning, purpose, or significance of something. Commonly appears with particles or endings: '무슨 의미냐?' (casual/strong), '무슨 의미죠?' (polite), '무슨 의미가 있나?' (asks if there is any point/meaning). Often followed by '인지', '인지 아세요', or '있다/있나' depending on grammar.
target_language_example: 그 말이 무슨 의미인지 잘 모르겠어요.
native_language_example: I don't really know what that means.

meaning: 'what story' / 'what are you talking about?' — used to ask what someone is talking about or to express disbelief.
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase. Can be used as a direct question (무슨 이야기야?/무슨 이야기예요?) to ask what topic someone is discussing, or alone (무슨 이야기?) to show surprise or confusion, similar to 'What are you talking about?' or 'Come on / No way' depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: 너 지금 무슨 이야기 하는 거야?
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

meaning: what (happened)
additional_notes: Used to ask about an event, situation, or what someone is doing. In casual speech it can mean 'What happened?' (무슨 일 있었나?), 'What's up?' or 'What are you doing?' (지금 무슨 일 해?). Tone and context determine whether it's about a past event, current situation, or ongoing activity. Can be followed by 있다/없다, 해, 있어? etc.
native_language_example: Is something going on right now?

meaning: 'for what reason' or 'why' (polite/contextual: 'what brings you')
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone came or did something. Can be casual or polite depending on sentence endings and context. Common in questions like '무슨 일로 왔어?' (Why did you come?/What brings you?) or more polite '무슨 일로 오신 거죠?'. Not used for asking 'what job' (that would be '무슨 일').
native_language_example: Sir/Madam, what brings you here?/What did you come for?

meaning: 'what (kind of) work/thing' or 'what (is someone) doing/going to do'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's job, actions, plans, or what kind of thing is being done. Often followed by a verb like 하다/하니/하는데/할 거다. In casual speech the particle '을/를' after 일 may be dropped (무슨 일). Can mean 'what's going on' or 'what are you up to' depending on context.
native_language_example: What do you do? / What kind of work do you do?

meaning: 'what (kind of) thing' or 'what happened' (used to ask about an event or problem).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to ask about events, problems, or reasons. Often appears in questions: 무슨 일이야? / 무슨 일이 있었어? Can be casual or polite depending on ending (있나요, 있었나, 있었지, 있었니). Not a fixed literal phrase — combines 무슨 ('what/which') + 일 ('thing/affair').
native_language_example: What happened last night?

meaning: no matter what happens; under any circumstances
additional_notes: Used to emphasize determination or that something will be done regardless of events. Often followed by a clause describing the action or promise (e.g., 하겠다, 가겠다, 지켜라). Tone can be strong — common in promises, warnings, or vows.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I will keep my promise.

meaning: what happened / whether something happened (used when asking or reporting about events)
additional_notes: Built from 무슨 일 (what/what kind of thing) + 있었는지 (whether/that there was). Common in questions or indirect questions: asks for information about an event or situation. Can be used directly (무슨 일이 있었는지 말해) or with verbs like 기억나? 말해 줄 수 있나요? Often shortened in casual speech (무슨 일 있었어?).
target_language_example: 무슨 일이 있었는지 자세히 말해 줘.
native_language_example: Tell me in detail what happened.

meaning: 'what happened' (describing that something occurred)
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to an event or situation that occurred. Often appears in questions with endings like -거야/거죠/거지 to indicate different levels of politeness or certainty (casual, polite, wondering). Can be combined with pronouns or place markers (e.g., 여기서 무슨 일이 있었던 거야? — What happened here?).
native_language_example: What happened here?

meaning: 'What happened?' (past; polite/neutral)
additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or situation that occurred. Polite/neutral tone because of the sentence ending -죠 (short for -지요). Can be used by itself or with time/place (e.g., 그날 밤, 저녁에). Literal parts: 무슨 (what kind of), 일 (thing/event), 있었다 (there was), -죠 (seeking confirmation or polite question).
native_language_example: What happened that night?

meaning: 'Is something wrong?' or 'Is there a problem/anything going on?'.
additional_notes: Casual phrase used to ask if something is wrong, if someone needs help, or if there's a situation happening. Often used when you notice unusual behavior or worry about someone. Can be shortened from '무슨 일이 있어?' (more grammatically complete). Tone can be concerned, surprised, or inquisitive depending on context and intonation.
native_language_example: Wait, is something wrong?

meaning: What is the matter? / How can I help you?
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask what is going on or why someone has come. Often used by staff (receptionists, customer service) or when addressing a visitor politely. Contains honorific ending '-시-' and polite question ending '-죠'. Use with strangers or customers. For less formal situations, use '무슨 일이야?' or '무슨 일이에요?'.
native_language_example: Hello, how can I help you?

meaning: 'What's going on?' or 'What's the matter?' (informal)
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase used to ask what is happening or why someone looks upset/surprised. Common in spoken Korean among friends or people of same age. Can be softened or made polite: '무슨 일이에요?' or '무슨 일이세요?'. Used alone as a question or with a name (e.g., '지민아, 무슨 일이야?').
native_language_example: Hey, what's going on? Why are you crying?

meaning: 'What's going on?' or 'What's the matter?'
additional_notes: Polite/formal spoken form used to ask about a situation, problem, or reason. Can be used to check if something is wrong or to ask for an explanation. Slightly more polite than casual 무슨 일이야. Often said with concern or curiosity; tone and context determine urgency.
target_language_example: 오늘 왜 이렇게 시끄러워요? 무슨 일이에요?
native_language_example: Why is it so noisy today? What's going on?

meaning: 'What's going on?' or 'What happened?' (polite/informal-polite)
additional_notes: Used to ask about a situation or problem. Polite because of the ending -죠; can express surprise, confusion, or a request for explanation. Can be said to someone you don't know well or in neutral contexts. For more casual speech, people might say '무슨 일이야?' and for more formal '무슨 일입니까?'.
target_language_example: 여기서 왜 모여 있어요? 무슨 일이죠?
native_language_example: Why are you all gathered here? What's going on?

meaning: 'What's going on?' or 'What is this/about?'
additional_notes: Casual to neutral phrase used to ask about a situation, problem, or surprising event. Often expresses confusion, surprise, or demand for explanation. Can be used alone or addressed to someone (e.g., '무슨 일이야?' is similar; '이지' adds a softer/reflective tone).
target_language_example: 여기 왜 이렇게 사람이 많지? 무슨 일이지?
native_language_example: Why are there so many people here? What's going on?

meaning: What's going on? / What's the matter?
additional_notes: A slightly formal or neutral way to ask what is happening or if something is wrong. Used to ask about a situation or someone's problem. Can be used alone as an attention-getting question or followed by a person's name. Similar to '무슨 일이야?' which is more casual.
native_language_example: What's going on — why are you so late?

meaning: What's going on? / What's the matter?
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase used to ask what is happening or why someone is acting a certain way. Often used with surprise, frustration, or urgency. Can be shortened to '무슨 일이야?' in more neutral speech. Adding '대체' (e.g., '대체 무슨 일인데?') increases emphasis—'what on earth is going on?'.
native_language_example: What's going on? Tell me quickly.

meaning: what (is) going on / what's the matter (is).
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the reason, situation, or what happened. Often appears in questions or indirect statements with verbs like 알다, 모르다, 보다, 대답하다. The literal parts: 무슨 (what/kind of), 일 (matter/event), 인지 (whether/if or indirect question marker). Common in both casual and polite speech; tone changes with ending (e.g., 아나? / 알아? casual, 알고 계신가요? polite).
native_language_example: Please tell me quickly what's going on.

meaning: what crime/what fault (did someone commit)?
additional_notes: Used to ask or wonder what wrongdoing, blame, or reason someone is responsible for. Common in questions like "What did they do?" or rhetorical expressions like "What fault could they have?" Can be followed by particles: 무슨 죄가 있습니까? (formal), 무슨 죄로? (asking 'for what reason/crime?'). Tone can be accusatory, confused, or sympathetic depending on context.
native_language_example: What crime could that person have committed?

meaning: what kind of act/thing (often negative or surprised: 'what did you do?').
additional_notes: Used to ask about or scold someone's action. Often implies disapproval, shock, or confusion about the action. Can be shortened to a sharp question (무슨 짓?) or used in full questions (너 무슨 짓 했어?). Tone and context determine politeness; add -요/죠 for more polite forms (무슨 짓이에요?/무슨 짓이죠?). Not typically neutral — usually negative or accusatory.
native_language_example: What are you doing here?/What do you think you're doing here?

meaning: what kind of thing/action (often with negative or disapproving nuance)
additional_notes: Used when asking or complaining about someone's actions, often implying surprise, judgment, or suspicion. Commonly followed by 하다/했나/하는지/etc. Can be rhetorical. Tone can be accusatory or frustrated depending on context.
target_language_example: 너는 도대체 무슨 짓을 한 거야?
native_language_example: What on earth did you do?

meaning: what kind of thing (did [someone] do)? / what have (I/you) done?
additional_notes: Used to express shock, disbelief, or self-reproach about an action. Often follows a subject or is used alone with a verb ending (e.g., 거지? 거냐! 거니! 거요?). '짓' here means 'act' or 'deed' and can be negative or neutral depending on context and tone. Common in informal and emotional speech.
native_language_example: What have I done?

meaning: 'What did (you) do?' (often with shock, anger, or blaming tone)
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, anger, or accusation about someone's actions. Tone can be strong—implies the speaker thinks the action was bad, harmful, or unexpected. Can be said to one person (informal) or to ask broadly. The subject is often omitted because context or names indicate who. Informal/colloquial language (반말).
target_language_example: 너 무슨 짓을 한 거야? 왜 이렇게 망가뜨렸어?
native_language_example: What did you do? Why did you ruin it like this?

meaning: What are you doing?/What kind of thing is that? (expressing shock, anger, or disbelief)
additional_notes: Casual/colloquial phrase used to show surprise, anger, or disapproval at someone's action. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be accusatory ("What are you doing?" as in "How could you do that?") or incredulous. Typically used in spoken Korean; not polite. You can soften or make polite by changing ending (e.g., 무슨 짓이에요?).
native_language_example: What on earth are you doing!/What did you do?!

meaning: What kind of actions/things (have been done)? — expresses shock, disbelief, or anger about someone's actions.
additional_notes: Plural form of '무슨 짓' (what deed/action). Used to react strongly to bad, surprising, or unacceptable behavior. Tone depends on ending: casual (야), polite (죠), or emphatic (냐고요). Often rhetorical and carries negative judgment.
native_language_example: What on earth have you been doing?

meaning: 'what' as the object of a verb (what + direct object)
additional_notes: Used when asking about the thing someone wants, sees, does, etc. 무엇 means 'what'; when followed by the object particle 을/를 it becomes 무엇을 (object form). Use 무엇을 with verbs that take a direct object. Informal spoken Korean may use 뭐를 or 뭐 instead.
native_language_example: What will you do after graduation?

meaning: 'what' as the subject of a sentence (what + [verb]).
additional_notes: 무엇 is 'what'. Adding the subject particle 이 marks it as the subject (what is doing/being something). Used in questions to ask about the thing that causes or is involved in the action. Common in both casual and formal questions (verb endings or honorifics change politeness). You will often see 무엇이 필요해? / 무엇이 문제입니까?; in spoken Korean native speakers may shorten 무엇이 to 뭐가.
native_language_example: What is the problem?

meaning: 'what is (it)?' — a slightly formal/neutral way to ask what something is or what the purpose/meaning is.
additional_notes: 무엇 means 'what' and -인가 is a formal or literary copula/ending used to form a question (similar to '인가?' = 'is it?'). Often used in definitions, philosophical questions, or formal contexts (e.g., 'X란 무엇인가?' = 'What is X?'). In casual speech, people usually say '뭐야?', '무엇이야?', or '무엇이죠?' instead.
native_language_example: What is happiness?

meaning: 'What is ...?' (formal/polite question)
additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask 'what is ...?' in Korean. Used in questions asking for identification, definition, name, occupation, etc. Common in formal speech, written language, or when speaking respectfully. It combines 무엇 (what) + 입니다 (formal copula) + question particle (implicit). For less formal situations, use '뭐예요?', '뭐야?', or '무엇이에요?'.
native_language_example: What is this?

meaning: Open the door (informal/command).
additional_notes: Casual imperative used to tell someone to open a door. '문' = door, '열어' is the informal present imperative of '열다' (to open). Common in urgent situations or between friends/family. To be polite, use '문 열어 주세요' or '문을 열어 주세요.' You may also hear '문 열어라' (rougher) or '문을 열어 주시겠어요?' (formal).
native_language_example: Open the door, please!

meaning: Please open the door / (You) open the door (polite)
additional_notes: Polite present tense form of '문을 열다' (to open the door). Commonly used to ask or tell someone to open a door. Context and intonation decide whether it's a polite request ('Please open the door') or a direct command in polite speech. For more casual speech you might hear '문 열어' and for more formal '문 열어 주세요' (please open the door).
native_language_example: Open the door quickly, it's cold.

meaning: toward/through the door (to/through a door)
additional_notes: 문 means 'door'. -으로 is a directional particle indicating movement toward or via something. Use 문으로 when you want to say 'to the door', 'through the door', or 'via the door' depending on context. If the noun ends in a vowel, use -로; if it ends in a consonant, use -으로. Context and verbs determine whether it implies 'toward' (가다), 'out through' (나가다), or 'into/through' (들어오다/들어가다).
native_language_example: Let's go out through the side door.

meaning: 'the door' (with topic/contrast marker -은) — used to talk about or ask about the door
additional_notes: 문 means 'door'. When followed by the particle 은 (topic/contrast marker), 문은 emphasizes or marks 'the door' as the topic or contrast in the sentence. Context determines nuance: it can be a simple topic ('as for the door...'), a contrast ('the door, (but...)'), or used in questions to ask about the door (e.g., location, action, or manner). In casual speech, short utterances like '문은?' mean 'What about the door?' or 'Where is the door?'.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: the door (as the object of a verb) — marks 'door' in a sentence as the direct object
additional_notes: 문 means 'door'. 을 is the object particle attached to nouns that end in a vowel (or after consonant? actually 을 after consonant, 를 after vowel). Wait: In Korean, 을 is used after a noun ending in a consonant; 를 after a vowel. 문 ends with consonant 'ㄴ', so 을 is correct. It indicates that the noun '문' is the direct object of the verb. Used in commands and statements about opening, closing, kicking, etc. Examples often appear with verbs like 열다 (open), 닫다/잠그다 (close/lock), 차다/발로 차다 (kick). In casual speech, particles can be dropped, but including 문을 is common and natural.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: to open a door (literally); also used figuratively for opening a business or beginning something.
additional_notes: Literally 'open the door' (문 = door, 열다 = to open). Common everyday phrase for physically opening doors. Can be used figuratively: e.g., '가게를 문을 열다' = to open a shop (start a business). Use appropriate object before 열다 (문을 열다, 창문을 열다).
target_language_example: 그녀가 문을 열다 그리고 방에 들어왔다.
native_language_example: She opened the door and entered the room.

meaning: the door (as the subject of a sentence) — '문' (door) + subject marker '이'.
additional_notes: Used when talking about a door as the subject. '이' is the Korean subject particle attached to nouns ending in a consonant. Examples show surprise, description, or state (e.g., locked). Replace '이' with '가' after vowel-ending nouns; with '가' also used in spoken Korean. You will often see sentences like '문이 없어요' (There is no door) or '문이 잠겼어요' (The door is locked).
native_language_example: The door is open.

meaning: 'the door' + polite/softening 'please' (used when asking someone to do something with the door, e.g. 'please open/close the door')
additional_notes: 문 means 'door'. 좀 is often used to soften or make a request more polite (like 'please' or 'a bit'). In speech you usually attach a verb after 문 좀 (열어, 닫아, 열어 줄래?) to ask someone to do something with the door. The overall phrase is casual; add more polite endings (열어 주세요) for formal situations.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: 'text (message)' as an object (accusative form) — short for 문자 메시지 (text message).
additional_notes: 문자 is short for 문자 메시지 (text message). In these examples 문자를 is used with verbs like 보내다 (to send), 읽다 (to read), 하다 (to do/contact) and appears in the object position (hence -를). Commonly used in everyday speech to talk about sending, receiving, or reading texts. Informal contexts often drop 메시지 and just say 문자.
native_language_example: I sent a text to my friend.

meaning: the sentence (object form) — '문장' (sentence) with the object particle '-을/를' (here '문장을').
additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific sentence as the direct object of a verb (e.g., 읽다, 설명하다, 원하다). '문장' means 'sentence'. In speech/writing the object marker is '-을' after consonant; when spoken, '문장을' often sounds like one unit. For polite requests, verbs change (보세요, 주세요, 주십시오).
native_language_example: Please read this sentence.

meaning: 'problem' as the subject (the noun 문제 in subject form with topic/subject particle -가).
additional_notes: 문제 (問題) means 'problem', 'issue', or 'matter'. When followed by -가 it marks the noun as the subject of the sentence. Common usages: asking '문제가 뭐야?' (What's the problem?), saying '...이/가 문제가 아니다' (it's not the problem), or '문제가 있어' (there's a problem / I have a problem). Context determines whether it's a literal problem, an obstacle, or a personal issue. Pronunciation: [mun-je-ga].
native_language_example: Money isn't the problem right now.

meaning: to have a problem; there is a problem
additional_notes: Common phrase to say something is wrong or that an issue exists. Used for concrete problems (a broken item) and abstract issues (a plan or situation). Politeness varies by ending: '문제가 있어요' (polite), '문제가 있어' (casual). To specify the problem, add details after: '문제가 있다: ...'. Often appears with particles indicating the affected thing (e.g., '컴퓨터에 문제가 있다').
native_language_example: There is a problem with the computer.

meaning: the object form of '문제' (problem/question) — 'the problem' or 'the question' (used as the direct object).
additional_notes: 문제 = problem, question, issue. 문제를 is the accusative/object particle form (문제 + 를). It marks 문제 as the thing affected by the verb (e.g., 풀다 'solve', 해결하다 'resolve'). Common verbs with 문제를: 풀다 (solve a question/problem), 해결하다 (solve/resolve an issue), 제기하다 (raise a problem). Word order: Korean typically places the object before the verb: 이 문제를 풀 수 없다 = 'cannot solve this problem.'
native_language_example: He resolved that problem quickly.

meaning: There is no problem; it's okay; no worries.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is fine, acceptable, or not a problem. Common in everyday conversation to reassure someone or to agree that something can be done. Can be expressed in polite forms like '문제 없습니다' or '문제 없어요' and informal '문제 없어'. Often used after a proposal, apology, or when confirming availability.
native_language_example: It's okay to do it that way; there's no problem.

meaning: Is there a problem? / Do you have a problem?
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase using the verb 있다 (to exist) with 문제 (problem). Depending on tone and context, it can be a neutral question (Is there a problem?) or a confrontational challenge (Got a problem?). Often used in spoken Korean. For polite situations use 문제가 있어요? or 문제가 있나요?.
native_language_example: What's wrong? Is there a problem?

meaning: It's a problem / (What's) the problem?
additional_notes: 문제야 is the copula form of 문제 + 이야 (informal/plain speech). Used to state that something is a problem (e.g., '엔진 문제야' = 'It's an engine problem') or in questions to ask what's wrong (usually with 뭐가/무슨/너). It's casual — used in spoken, informal contexts. For polite speech use 문제예요/문제입니다.
native_language_example: Is the food the problem?

meaning: It's a problem / Is it a problem?
additional_notes: 문제 (problem) + 예요 (polite copula). Used to describe that something is a problem or to ask whether something is a problem. Context and intonation determine statement vs. question. Polite but neutral — suitable in many situations. Formal alternative: 문제입니다. Casual: 문제야.
native_language_example: Is that the problem right now?

meaning: a casual spoken ending meaning 'that's the problem' or 'the issue is...'
additional_notes: 문제지 is a colloquial contraction of 문제지(요) used in spoken Korean. It's often attached to a sentence to point out a problem, express puzzlement, or emphasize what the issue is. Context and intonation determine nuance: can be accusatory (놈만 스타가 되니 문제지!), surprised/questioning (뭐가 문제지?), or contemplative (좋은 보석인데 뭐가 문제지?). Not the same as 문제지 meaning 'test paper' (which is spelled the same but used in formal/written contexts).
native_language_example: There's no time, so who's going to clean up is the problem.

meaning: in/into/on the water; to the water (location or direction - indicates location or movement related to '물' = water).
additional_notes: 물에 is the noun 물 (water) plus the particle 에. Use when saying something is in water (location: ~에 있다/떠 있다) or when something goes into water (direction: ~에 빠지다/들어가다). Context and verb determine whether it means 'in' (location) or 'into' (movement). For emphasis or contrast you might see 에는 (물에는).
native_language_example: The child goes into the water.

meaning: the object form of '물' — 'water' (accusative particle attached: 'water' as the thing being acted on).
additional_notes: 물을 = 물 + 을. 을 is the object particle used after a noun ending in a consonant to mark the direct object. You'll see it in sentences like '물을 마시다' (to drink water), '물을 주다' (to give/water plants), or '물을 가져오다' (to bring water). In spoken Korean the particle can be dropped when context is clear, but beginners should learn to recognize it.
native_language_example: Please give me (some) water.

meaning: 'water' as the subject (with the subject particle -이).
additional_notes: 물이 is the noun 물 (water) plus the subject particle -이. Use it when water is the subject of the sentence (e.g., describing water coming out, being cold, running out). In speech the particle -이 contracts with vowels? (No—-이 attaches after consonant-ending nouns like 물). Common verbs with 물이: 나오다 (to come out), 많다 (to be many/much), 차갑다 (to be cold), 안 나오다 (not come out/run).
native_language_example: The tap water smells too much.

meaning: a polite/softened way to ask for or offer water; 'some water' or 'water, please' (with a softening particle).
additional_notes: 물 means 'water'. Adding 좀 (literally 'a little' but used as a softener) makes requests/offers more polite or less direct. Depending on sentence ending, it's used to ask someone to give water, offer water, or tell someone to drink. Common in casual and polite speech. Tone and verb ending determine politeness level (e.g., 주세요 = please give; 줄까 = shall I give; 가져다 드릴까요 = would you like me to bring).
native_language_example: Please give me some water.

meaning: 'as for the item/thing' — topic-marked '물건' using the topic particle 은.
additional_notes: 물건 means 'item, thing, belonging'. Adding the topic particle 은 (물건은) sets 'item' as the topic and often contrasts or asks about it (e.g., location, status, possession, whether it's used). Common in questions and statements: '그 사람 물건은 어떻게 됐죠?' (What happened to that person's things?). In conversation you can drop parts after 물건은 and leave it implied.
native_language_example: As for the remaining items here, I'll take them.

meaning: 'of course' or 'sure'.
additional_notes: Used to agree or give a positive, often friendly response. Slightly more casual than the formal 물론입니다; can be used with friends or acquaintances. Adding a name/ending (e.g., 넌? 자네는?) turns it into a question back to the other person. Tone can be enthusiastic or simply confirming.
native_language_example: Of course, I'll help you.

meaning: May I ask (you)? / Is it okay if I ask?
additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission to ask a question. Built from the verb 묻다/물어보다 (to ask) + -아/어도 되다 (may/can). Common in spoken Korean; can be shortened to 물어도 돼요 or 더 politely 물어봐도 될까요?. Use when you want to check if it's okay to ask someone something.
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask just one thing?

meaning: what (subject)
additional_notes: 뭐 means "what". The particle 가 marks the word as the subject of the sentence, so 뭐가 is used when "what" is the subject (e.g., "What is there?", "What is wrong?"). Common in questions. In casual speech you may also hear 뭐가 or 뭐가 ~지? depending on ending. Not a fixed idiom—compositional from its parts.
native_language_example: What is the problem?

meaning: 'What's there to worry about?' or 'What are you worried about?'
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase using 뭐가 (what + subject) + 걱정 (worry). Often appears with particles like -이야/인데/이시죠 to make questions: 뭐가 걱정이야? (casual), 뭐가 걱정인데? (slightly confrontational/curious), 뭐가 걱정이시죠? (polite). Use with friends/family in casual form; add polite endings when speaking respectfully.
target_language_example: 뭐가 걱정이야? 다 잘 될 거야.
native_language_example: What's there to worry about? Everything will be fine.

meaning: What's so (something)? / What is it that's so ...?
additional_notes: Used to ask why something is considered notable (funny, good, problematic, etc.). '뭐가' = 'what (subject)', '그렇게' = 'so/that much'. Tone can be neutral, curious, or slightly critical depending on intonation and context. Common in spoken Korean; add an adjective or verb after it (e.g., 재밌어, 좋아, 문제예요).
native_language_example: What's so amazing about it?

meaning: What's so (—)? / What about it is so (—)?
additional_notes: Used before adjectives or verbs to ask why something seems to have that quality (e.g., urgent, funny, important). Conveys surprise, mild irritation, or curiosity. Common in spoken Korean; follow with an adjective/verb (급해, 우습지, 중요해).
native_language_example: What's so strange about it?

meaning: 'What's the problem?' or 'What's wrong?'.
additional_notes: Casual/questioning phrase asking what the problem or issue is. Often used to ask for clarification or to challenge someone. Can be polite with appropriate endings (e.g., '뭐가 문제죠?') or informal/rough with plain endings (e.g., '뭐가 문제야?', '뭐가 문제니?'). The literal parts: 뭐 (what) + 가 (subject particle) + 문제 (problem).
native_language_example: What's wrong with you? / What's the problem?

meaning: What's the problem? / What's wrong?
additional_notes: Casual/informal phrase used to ask what the issue is or to challenge someone (sometimes with a confrontational tone). '뭐' = what, '가' marks the subject, '문제' = problem, '야' is informal/provocative ending. Can be softened with polite forms (e.g., 뭐가 문제예요?). Context and intonation determine whether it's a genuine question or a sharp remark.
native_language_example: What on earth is the problem?

meaning: What's there? / What is (it) that...?
additional_notes: Used to ask or challenge about the existence or content of something. Context determines nuance: simple question about what's inside/there (e.g., 안에 뭐가 있는데? = What's inside?), or a confrontational/ rhetorical challenge asking what reason or thing someone has (e.g., 내가 싫다고 한 게 대체 뭐가 있는데? = What exactly is it that makes you dislike me?). '뭐가' = 'what (subject)', '있는데' = present/past background or contrast marker from 있다 + -는데. Tone depends on intonation and context.
native_language_example: What's inside?

meaning: What's there? / What's the point? (depends on context)
additional_notes: 뭐가 (무엇이) + 있어 (있다). Can be used literally to ask 'what is there?' or colloquially/ rhetorically to mean 'what's the point/what's the use?' Tone depends on intonation and context: with a question mark it's a genuine question; with exclamation or flat statement it can express disbelief, dismissal, or resignation. Often casual/informal.
target_language_example: 그렇게 걱정할 필요 없어. 거기서 뭐가 있어?
native_language_example: You don't need to worry. What's there?

meaning: I wonder what there is / What else is there?
additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase combining 뭐(what) + 가(subject marker) + 있다(to exist) + 지 (sentence-ending particle expressing wonder or thinking). Used when thinking aloud or asking what items/people/situations exist or what else is available. Can be used alone or with location (여기/여긴). Informal, common in conversation.
native_language_example: I wonder what is here / What's here?

meaning: why; for what reason
additional_notes: Casual phrase combining 뭐 (what) + 때문에 (because of). Used to ask for the reason or cause of something. Can be direct or slightly blunt depending on tone; often used in spoken Korean. In formal contexts, use 왜 (or 왜 때문에 is not standard) or 어떻게 된 이유인지 묻다.
native_language_example: Why are you saying/doing that?

meaning: with/using what; by what (method or thing)
additional_notes: Contraction of 뭐 + 로. Used to ask what instrument, material, method, choice, or reason is used. Common after verbs like 하다, 하실까, 드릴까요, 알다, 하다. Can ask about items (What will you use?), choices (Which one?), or reasons (How do you know?). Tone is neutral; polite forms add polite endings.
native_language_example: What will you use to wrap the gift?

meaning: 'what' as an object (colloquial contraction of 무엇을/뭘 + object particle 를)
additional_notes: 뭐를 is a spoken/colloquial form used when asking or referring to the object of a verb (what someone fears, sees, wants, etc.). It's identical in meaning to '무엇을' or the contracted '뭘' + 를. Often appears in casual conversation; polite speech would use 무엇을 or use honorific/particle forms (e.g., '무엇을 원하세요?').
native_language_example: What do you want for your birthday present?

meaning: So what? / What does it matter? / How about it?
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to dismiss concern, show indifference, or ask for someone's opinion casually. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be confrontational ('So what?') or neutral/inviting ('How about it?'). Common in spoken Korean among friends.
native_language_example: Fine, so what?/Alright, how about it?

meaning: 'Is there anything?' or 'Do you have anything?' (informal)
additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase. 뭐 = 'what/anything'; 있어 comes from 있다 ('to exist/have'). Use with friends or family. Depending on context and intonation it can ask if something exists (Is there anything?) or if someone has something (Do you have anything?). To be more polite, use 뭐 있어요? or 뭐 있어요? / 뭐 있어요 instead of 뭐 있어. To ask 'What's up?' you might hear 뭐 있어? with a different intonation.
native_language_example: Is there anything for dinner tonight?

meaning: something wrong / did I do/say/eat something wrong?
additional_notes: 뭐 (what/something) + 잘못 (wrong). Used in casual questions to ask whether something is wrong, whether you made a mistake, or whether something went wrong (e.g., food made you sick). Often appears with verbs: 말했어 (said), 됐어요 (went wrong), 먹었나/먹었어 (ate). Tone can be defensive or concerned depending on context. Politeness is adjusted by verb ending (e.g., 했어? vs 했어요?).
native_language_example: Did I say something wrong?

meaning: something / a little something (used to offer or ask for/offer something politely or casually)
additional_notes: 뭐 means 'what' and 좀 softens the request/offering — together they mean 'something' or 'anything (small)'. Common in offers/questions: 'Do you want something to drink/eat?' or 'Shall I show you something?' Polite forms often add -래요? or -까요?. Can be casual depending on verb form.
native_language_example: Shall I help you with something?

meaning: 'what (are you) doing' — used to ask what someone is doing or was doing
additional_notes: 뭐 = 'what'; 하고 comes from the verb 하다 ('to do') plus connective. Common in questions: 뭐 하고 있어요? (What are you doing?), 뭐 하고 있었어? (What were you doing?). Can be followed by different endings for politeness (있어/있어요/있었어/있었소) or tacked onto other verbs (뭐 하고 싶나? = What do you want to do?). Informal/casual uses often drop 있어요. Not a fixed idiom—compositional.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'What are you doing?' (casual/informal)
additional_notes: A casual way to ask someone what they are doing right now. Used in informal situations with friends, family, or close acquaintances. Often appears with sentence-ending particles/punctuation (뭐 하고 있어? or 뭐 해?). Can be softened or made polite by using 뭐 하고 있어요? or 뭐 해요?.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'What are you doing?' (casual/rude)
additional_notes: Informal, casual or blunt way to ask what someone is doing. Common among friends or when annoyed; can sound rude if used with strangers or superiors. Literally 'what do (you) do?' — subject and politeness level are omitted. Use polite forms like '뭐 하세요?' or '뭐 해요?' in formal situations.
native_language_example: What are you doing today?

meaning: 'what (are [you/we/they]) doing' or 'what (is this place) for'.
additional_notes: 뭐 하는 combines 뭐 (what) + 하는 (doing/that does). Often appears in casual questions about someone's action or the purpose/function of a place/thing. Tone depends on sentence ending: can be neutral, surprised, or annoyed. Common full patterns: '뭐 하는 거예요?' (polite), '뭐 하는 거야?' (informal), '뭐 하는 건데?' (asking for explanation), '뭐 하는 곳이에요?' (what kind of place).
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'what (are you) doing' or 'what is (someone) doing' (casual)
additional_notes: Casual, conversational phrase used to ask what someone is doing now or what an action/purpose is. Often appears as '뭐 해?' or '뭐 하는 거야?' depending on level of formality and tone. Can be shortened/contracted in speech; context determines subject (you, someone else, or a general situation). Not polite — use more polite forms (e.g., '뭐 하세요?') with strangers or elders.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: "What are (you) doing?" (casual/informal)
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to ask what someone is doing right now or to express surprise/annoyance at their action. Typically used with friends, family, or when scolding; not polite. Can be said with different intonation to be curious, irritated, or accusatory. For polite situations, use 뭐 하세요? or 지금 뭐 하세요?.
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing right now?

meaning: 'What are (you) doing?' / 'What is (this) person doing?'.
additional_notes: Polite/formal question used to ask what someone is doing right now or to express surprise/annoyance at someone's actions. Literally: 'what doing (thing) is it?'. Subject (you, he, she, they) is often omitted and understood from context. Can be said with varying tone — neutral curiosity, or stronger reproach depending on delivery.
target_language_example: 지금 그거 집어 넣지 마세요. 뭐 하는 거예요?
native_language_example: Don't put that in now. What are you doing?

meaning: What are you doing?/What kind of thing are you doing? (expresses shock, disapproval, or anger)
additional_notes: Colloquial and often used to scold or express strong surprise/disapproval at someone's action. Tone can be angry, shocked, or incredulous depending on context and intonation. Can be directed at someone (informal) and may sound rude if used with strangers or superiors. The literal components: 뭐 (what) + 하는 (doing) + 짓 (act/behavior) + 이야 (casual copula/question).
target_language_example: 지금 뭐 하는 짓이야? 그걸 왜 부숴?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now? Why did you break that?

meaning: 'What are (you) doing?'
additional_notes: Casual/informal way to ask someone what they are doing right now. Used with friends, younger people, or informal situations. 너 뭐 하니? and 너는 뭐 하니? are equivalent; adding 여기서 ('here') asks 'what are you doing here?'. The punctuation and intonation can make it sound surprised (e.g., '뭐 하니!') or a neutral question ('뭐 하니?'). For more polite speech use 뭐 하세요? or 뭐 하십니까?.
native_language_example: What are you doing here?

meaning: why (do something)
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone would do something or what the purpose is. Often informal/conversational. Can sound surprised, doubtful, or dismissive depending on tone. Commonly appears in questions like '그건 뭐 하러 봐요?' ('Why would you watch that?') or '뭐 하러 나가?' ('Why go out?'). Followed by a verb (often action being questioned).
target_language_example: 너 지금 뭐 하러 거기에 가?
native_language_example: Why are you going there now (what for)?

meaning: What are (you) trying to do? / What do you intend to do?
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's intention or purpose, often somewhat blunt or confrontational depending on tone. Context determines formality; with friends it can be casual, but in more polite speech you'd use 뭐 하려고요? or 무엇을 하려고 하세요?. Can be used alone (What's your plan?) or followed by an object (이걸로 뭐 하려고? — What are you going to do with this?).
native_language_example: What are you going to do with this?

meaning: what are (you) trying to do / what do (you) intend to do
additional_notes: Casual phrase used to ask about someone's intention or purpose. Often appears in questions like '뭐 하려는 거야?' with varying politeness/forms: - 거야 (informal/rough) - 거예요 (polite) - 거죠 (confirming/soft) - 거지 (thinking to oneself). Can express surprise, annoyance, suspicion, or confusion depending on tone and context. The subject (you) is usually implied.
native_language_example: What are you trying to do? Stop that.

meaning: "What are you doing?" (polite/formal)
additional_notes: Used to ask someone (often older or not close to you) what they are doing or what their plans are. Can be used about current actions (What are you doing right now?) or about plans (What do you do on Sunday?/What are you doing on Sunday?). Polite form: 하세요 (하세요 form). For casual speech with friends, use 뭐 해?; for very polite/formal contexts, use 뭐 하십니까?.
native_language_example: What are you doing on Sunday?

meaning: polite/formal way to ask 'what are (you) doing' or 'what do (you) do (right now)'.
additional_notes: Used before polite sentence endings (거예요, 겁니까, 거죠) to ask what someone is doing right now or what their action/occupation is. '뭐' = what, '하시는' is the honorific/polite form of 하다 (to do). Common when speaking respectfully to someone of higher status or to be polite. For casual speech with friends use '뭐 해' or '뭐 하고 있어?'.
native_language_example: Excuse me, what are you doing right now?

meaning: 'What are (you) doing?' or 'What will (you) do?'
additional_notes: Casual/informal short form of '뭐 해요?' or '뭐 하니?'. Used to ask what someone is doing now or what they plan to do (context determines tense). Common in spoken Korean between friends or people of the same age. To be polite, use '뭐 해요?' or '무엇을 하세요?'.
native_language_example: What are you doing (this) evening?

meaning: 'What are (you) doing?' or 'What do (you) do?'.
additional_notes: Polite/formal (요-form) question using 뭐 (what) + 하다 (to do). Can ask about current action ('What are you doing?') or habitual/occupation ('What do you do?') depending on context and intonation. When directed at a group or with question tone, it can sound surprised or slightly confrontational (e.g., 'What are you doing here?').
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'What did (you) do?' (informal/casual)
additional_notes: Casual way to ask what someone did. Used with friends, family, or younger people. subject 'you' is implied; to be polite use 뭐 했어요? or 뭐 하셨어요? Can refer to general actions (e.g., last weekend) or specific location (e.g., upstairs).
native_language_example: What did you do last weekend?

meaning: 'What did (you/he/she/they) do?' or 'What did (someone) do?'.
additional_notes: Casual polite question asking what someone did (past tense). 뭐 = 'what'. 했어요 is the polite past form of 하다 (to do). Use with different subjects depending on context (어제 뭐 했어요? = What did you do yesterday? 그 친구는 뭐 했어요? = What did that friend do?). Common in conversation; can be made more formal (뭐 하셨어요?) or informal (뭐 했어?).
native_language_example: What did you do for lunch today?

meaning: 'What is it?' or 'What's (something)?' — informal, blunt question form.
