meaning: '(be) on (someone's) side' / 'be an ally/supporter'
additional_notes: Informal contraction: 편이야 is the casual spoken form of '편이다' or part of the phrase '(~의) 편이야' meaning 'I'm on (someone's) side' or 'someone is on the side of...'. Used to express support or which side someone belongs to. Often follows a noun or pronoun (e.g., 네 편이야 = I'm on your side). Tone is casual/friendly; avoid in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: 걱정하지 마, 난 항상 네 편이야.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'm always on your side.

meaning: 'letter' (with the topic particle -는) — used to mark 'letter' as the topic of the sentence.
additional_notes: 편지 means 'letter' (a written message). The attached particle 는 marks it as the topic, often implying contrast or the subject of comment. In English you usually omit an explicit particle, so translate based on context (e.g., 'As for the letter,' 'The letter...,' or simply 'letter').
native_language_example: Who are you going to send the letter to?

meaning: 'letter' marked as the object (accusative) — the noun 편지 with the object particle -를/을.
additional_notes: 편지를 is 편지 (letter) + the object particle -를 (used after a vowel). It indicates that the letter is the direct object of the verb (what is read, written, found, sent, brought, etc.). Depending on context, it can refer to a specific letter or letters in general. Use 편지를 with verbs like 읽다 (to read), 쓰다 (to write), 찾다 (to find), 보내다 (to send), 가져오다 (to bring). If the noun ends in a consonant, use 을 (e.g., 책을).
native_language_example: I wrote a letter yesterday.

meaning: 'peace' (object form — the noun 평화 with the object particle -를/-을)
additional_notes: 평화 means 'peace'. 평화를 is 평화 + the object particle -를 (pronounced 'reul') used when 평화 is the direct object of a verb (e.g., 원하다 'to want', 지키다 'to protect'). In polite speech you may see 원합니다/원한다; casual uses drop polite endings. Use 평화가 when 'peace' is the subject, and 평화에/에서 for location/target uses.
native_language_example: We want peace.

meaning: 'grass' or 'weed' as the direct object (object marker -을 attached)
additional_notes: 풀 means 'grass', 'weeds', or 'herb'. When you add the object particle -을 (after a consonant-final noun) it marks 풀 as the direct object of a verb: 풀을 먹다 (eat grass), 풀을 뽑다 (pull up weeds). Use 풀을 when the verb that follows acts on the grass/weed.
native_language_example: The cow is eating grass.

meaning: 'French' (as the topic of the sentence); literally 'as for French' or 'French is/..., French (language) + topic marker'.
additional_notes: 프랑스어 = 'the French language'. 는 is the topic particle used to mark the topic of a sentence (contrast or general statement). Together, 프랑스어는 introduces a statement or opinion about the French language (e.g., 'As for French, ...' / 'French is ...'). Use 는 when you want to talk about or contrast the language; for simple subject statements, 이/가 could appear instead in other contexts.
native_language_example: As for French, it's fun to learn.

meaning: in French / into French (by means of the French language).
additional_notes: 프랑스어 = 'French (language)'. The particle -로 indicates direction, means, or language used. Use 프랑스어로 + 말하다/얘기하다/쓰다/읽다 to say 'speak/talk/write/read in French.' Can also mean 'into French' for translation (e.g., 번역해서 프랑스어로). If you want to emphasize exclusivity, add 만 (프랑스어로만).
native_language_example: Please speak in French here.

meaning: the Korean particle-marked noun 'French (language)' with the object marker '-를' (marks the direct object).
additional_notes: 프랑스어 = 'French (language)'. Adding -를 marks it as the direct object of a verb (what is taught, learned, understood, etc.). In sentences like '프랑스어를 배우다' (to learn French) or '프랑스어를 가르치다' (to teach French). The form changes with particles (e.g., '프랑스어를' object, '프랑스어가/는' subject/topic).
native_language_example: I teach my friend French.

meaning: to do/speak French (partial phrase; usually continued as 하다 → '프랑스어를 하다' = 'to speak French')
additional_notes: This is an incomplete verb phrase. Korean often uses '언어(를) 하다' to mean 'to speak [a language]'. The full expression is '프랑스어를 하다' or more naturally '프랑스어를 할 줄 알다' (to be able to speak French) or '프랑스어를 배운다' (to learn French). Alone '프랑스어를 할' requires completion (e.g., '프랑스어를 할 수 있어요?' = 'Can you speak French?').
native_language_example: Can you speak French?

meaning: A name/nickname (Frodo) — used as a character name or affectionate nickname in Korean.
additional_notes: 프로도 is the Korean phonetic spelling of 'Frodo' (from The Lord of the Rings) and is also used as a cute nickname for someone (often a pet or child) or as a character name in comics/cartoons. In the example sentences, '프로도 나리' uses a playful honorific '나리' (similar to 'your highness' or 'sir') attached to the name, so the phrase is addressing 'Frodo' in a joking/polite way. Not a common everyday word — mainly a proper noun.
native_language_example: Frodo (or Frodo) will go to the park today.

meaning: 'blood' as the subject (nominative form) — used when blood is doing or being something (e.g., there is blood, blood is coming out).
additional_notes: 피 means 'blood.' Adding -가 marks it as the subject of the sentence (nominative particle). You will see sentences like '피가 났다/나요' (blood came out/I'm bleeding) or '피가 많다/적다' (there is a lot/little blood). In descriptions, it can appear with verbs like 묻다 (to be stained), 있다 (to exist/there is), 나다 (to come out), or with quantifiers (많이).
native_language_example: Blood is coming from my hand.

meaning: the noun '피' (blood) in the object case (marked by 를) — 'blood' as the direct object
additional_notes: 피 = blood. 를 is the object particle (받침/받침 여부와 관계없이) attached to a noun to mark it as the direct object of a verb. 피를 appears in sentences where someone is bleeding, someone eats blood, likes blood, etc. Use 피가 when you want to say 'blood (as the subject) is ...' (e.g., 피가 흐른다 = blood flows).
native_language_example: He was injured and was bleeding.

meaning: the piano (as a direct object; with object particle 를)
additional_notes: 피아노 = 'piano' (noun). 피아노를 is 피아노 + 를, the object marker used when the piano is the thing being acted on (e.g., 치다 = to play/hit). Commonly used with verbs like 치다 (to play an instrument). In casual speech 난 is short for 나는. Context determines tense and politeness from the verb ending, not from 를.
native_language_example: He practices the piano every day.

meaning: 'need' (as a noun marker: 'the need to ...' or 'need for ...')
additional_notes: 필요 is a noun meaning 'need'. When combined with the subject particle -가 (필요가), it often appears before verbs like 있다/없다 or in questions to talk about whether something is necessary (e.g., "필요가 있다/없다" = 'there is/isn't a need'). Common patterns: '필요가 있다/없다', '필요가 있겠어?', '필요가 있을 수도 있다'.
native_language_example: Do we need to prepare?

meaning: to need to (do something); there is a need to ...
additional_notes: Used after a noun or verb stem (often with -을/ㄹ) to say that something is necessary or required. In spoken Korean, it's common to say verb stem + 필요가 있어 (e.g., 공부할 필요가 있어 = 'need to study'). Can be used neutrally to state necessity or sometimes more forcefully depending on tone/context (e.g., 'Do you really need to...?').
target_language_example: 오늘 오후에 병원에 갈 필요가 있어.
native_language_example: I need to go to the hospital this afternoon.

meaning: 'need to' with a nuance of 'it's not necessary to' (used to say something is unnecessary or not required)
additional_notes: 필요 means 'need' or 'necessity'. When combined with 는 (topic marker) after 필요 and followed by a negative verb form (e.g., 없다/없지/없었어), it expresses that something is not necessary. Common patterns: '필요는 없다/없지/없었어' meaning 'there's no need to...' or 'it's not necessary to...'. Politeness and tense come from the verb that follows. Can be used in both formal and informal contexts depending on ending.
native_language_example: You don't need to do that.

meaning: 'not necessary' / 'don't need (it/them)'
additional_notes: Casual/informal way to say something is unnecessary or that you don't need someone/something. Often follows a verb (e.g., ~할 필요 없어 = don't need to ~) or stands alone as a blunt dismissal. Tone can be rude depending on context and intonation. To be more polite, use 필요 없어요 or 필요 없습니다.
native_language_example: You don't need to worry like that.

meaning: I don't need (it); it's unnecessary.
additional_notes: Polite/formal-ish negative phrase from 필요하다 (to need). Used to refuse something, say you don't want or don't need an item or offer. Can be spoken alone as a short rejection. Tone can be firm depending on context; add 안 or 아니에요 for different nuances (e.g., 필요하지 않아요).
native_language_example: I don't need that money.

meaning: 'something you need' or 'anything needed'.
additional_notes: Casual phrase used to ask if someone needs anything. 거 is a colloquial short form of 것 ('thing'). Often appears in questions with 있다/없다 (있어요?/없어요?) and can be shortened in casual speech (필요해요? / 필요한 거 있어요?). Polite forms use -요; very casual may drop 요 (필요한 거 있어?).
target_language_example: 여기 있어요. 필요한 거 있으면 말하세요.
native_language_example: It's here. If you need anything, tell me.

meaning: what is needed / the thing(s) needed
additional_notes: Combines 필요하다 (to be needed) with 건 (short for 것 + topic/contrast marker), used to point to a needed thing or to ask if anything else is needed. Often followed by topic-comment structure: '필요한 건 + (noun/clause)' or in questions '더 필요한 건 없어요?' ('Is there anything else you need?'). Tone can be neutral or polite depending on the verb ending.
target_language_example: 우리가 지금 필요한 건 더 많은 정보야.
native_language_example: What we need right now is more information.

meaning: 'what is needed' or 'the necessary thing(s)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that is needed or necessary in a situation. Can refer to a specific item, action, or quality depending on context. Often follows a clause or noun phrase (e.g., '딱 필요한 것' = 'exactly what's needed').
native_language_example: This is exactly what we need right now.

meaning: ‘what is needed’ or ‘something needed’ (colloquial)
additional_notes: A casual way to ask or refer to things someone needs. 게 is a contraction of 것이 (thing), and 필요한 is the adjective 'needed' (from 필요하다). Common in questions: 필요한 게 뭐예요?/뭔데요? or with 있다/없다 to ask if there is anything needed. Polite forms add -요 (뭐예요?). Tone can be neutral to casual depending on ending.
native_language_example: What do you need right now?

meaning: Do you want to (do something)? (informal, asks someone's desire/preferences)
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 하고 싶다 (to want to do) in the casual/informal question form. Used to ask what someone wants to do or if they want to do a specific action. With pronouns or question words: '뭘/무엇을 하고 싶니?' = 'What do you want to do?' Polite forms: 하고 싶어요 (polite) / 하고 싶습니까 (formal).
native_language_example: What do you want to do right now?

meaning: to want to do (something); 'would like to do'
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to express desire to perform that action. Conjugate the verb into its stem (remove -다) then add 하고 싶다. For polite speech, use 하고 싶어요 (present) or 하고 싶었습니다/하고 싶었어요 (past). To negate, use 하고 싶지 않다 (하고 싶지 않았어요 for past). When describing someone else’s desire, use -고 싶어하다/-고 싶어해요 (e.g., 하고 싶어해요) rather than directly quoting their internal state with 하고 싶다 in polite contexts.
native_language_example: I want to eat Korean food.

meaning: want to do (something) — casual/informal
additional_notes: Combines a verb stem + 하고 (and/do) + 싶어 (want) to express desire to do an action. Used in casual speech among friends or people of equal/lower status. Polite forms: 싶어요 or 싶습니다. With many verbs, the connector is -고 (e.g., 먹고 싶어). Often the subject is omitted when clear from context.
native_language_example: What do you want to say?

meaning: want to (do) — expresses desire to do something or want to say something
additional_notes: Combines the verb 하다 (to do) + -고 싶다 (to want to). Use before a noun or verb stem to show desire: 하고 싶은 말 (things you want to say), 하고 싶은 것 (things you want to do). Often shortened in speech to 하고 싶어/싶어? in questions. Polite forms require conjugating the main verb or using 하고 싶어요.
target_language_example: 나한테 하고 싶은 말 있으면 지금 해.
native_language_example: If you have something you want to say to me, say it now.

meaning: something (someone) wants to say; words one wants to say
additional_notes: Literally 'words you want to do/say' (하고 싶은 = want to do; 말 = words/speech). Used to ask or tell someone about things they wish to say—can be questions, encouragements to speak up, or commands to say everything. Common in casual and polite forms depending on verb endings that follow (있어요?, 다 해봐, 하라고).
target_language_example: 네가 하고 싶은 말 있으면 지금 해.
native_language_example: If you have something you want to say, say it now.

meaning: a colloquial phrase meaning 'the thing (someone) is doing' or 'what (someone) is doing' (progressive/nominalizer)
additional_notes: Combines the verb 하다 (to do) in the progressive form 하고 있다 (doing) with 거 (a contraction of 것, 'thing') to refer to an action or situation currently happening. Used in casual spoken Korean to talk about what someone is doing, often as part of questions or explanations. Can be attached after other verbs (V + -고 있는 거) to mean 'the thing of V-ing.'
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'to be doing' — expresses an ongoing action or current continuous state (present progressive).
additional_notes: Attach 하고 있다 to a verb stem (usually after 하다 verbs or after a noun + 하다) to indicate someone is currently doing something or that a state continues. For many verbs not ending in 하다, the progressive is formed with -고 있다 (e.g., 먹고 있다). In casual speech, forms like 하고 있어(요) are common; past/future contexts use 하고 있었다 / 하고 있을 것이다. Context can also make it describe a repeated or habitual action. When speaking politely, use 하고 있어요 or 하고 있습니다.
native_language_example: I am doing my homework right now.

meaning: am/are/is doing (something); in the middle of doing
additional_notes: Present progressive form of 하다 (to do) used after a verb stem or noun+하고 to say someone is currently doing something. Common in casual and neutral speech. When used alone (e.g., '하고 있어!') it emphasizes that you are already doing it or that something is in progress. In questions (뭐 하고 있어? / 지금 뭘 하고 있어?) it asks 'What are you doing?'.
native_language_example: I'm doing my homework right now.

meaning: “One, two, three” — a simple counting sequence used to start an action together.
additional_notes: Used to count off before doing something simultaneously (e.g., start moving, jump, lift, turn). Often said aloud by a group leader to coordinate timing. Can be shortened to just the numbers or used with a verb like 가자 (let's go) or 돌려 (turn). Very common in casual and neutral contexts.
native_language_example: Ready? One, two, three — let's go!

meaning: one more; another one
additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate an additional item, action, or wish. Common in everyday speech. Can be used with objects, actions (e.g., make one more wish), or commands. Place after a number word (하나) and before verbs or at the end of a sentence. Tone and context determine if it's a question, suggestion, or command.
native_language_example: Please give me one more drink.

meaning: not even one / none (emphatic negation)
additional_notes: Used with negative verbs/adjectives to emphasize there is not a single one. Often appears before verbs like 없다, 보이지 않았다, 못하다, or with commands to stress 'not miss even one'. In casual speech you may hear 하나도 followed by 안/없다/etc.
native_language_example: There aren't any stars at all.

meaning: 'not ... at all' or 'not ... even one' (emphatic negation)
additional_notes: Used before verbs/adjectives to strongly negate something — emphasizes zero degree or complete absence. Common in spoken Korean. Often appears as '하나도 안 + (verb/adjective)' or with past/colloquial forms (e.g., '하나도 안 들었지?'). Can be followed by particle/ending for questions or exclamations.
native_language_example: I'm not hungry at all.

meaning: just one / only one (please/asking for one thing)
additional_notes: 하나 means 'one'. -만 is a particle meaning 'only' or 'just'. 하나만 is used when requesting, offering, or emphasizing a single item or action. Common in polite requests (…하나만 주세요/주실래요?), questions (하나만 물어봐도 돼요?), and casual commands (하나만 대 봐요). Tone and politeness come from the rest of the sentence, not 하나만 itself.
native_language_example: Please give me just this one.

meaning: Shall we do/play/have one? (suggesting doing one of something)
additional_notes: Used to suggest doing one instance of an activity or item together (e.g., play one game, have one match, make one bet). Polite/soft suggestion using -까요. Context determines verb meaning (하다 = do/play/have). Often used when proposing to start a single round, game, bet, etc.
native_language_example: Shall we play one game?

meaning: 'the thing (that) someone does' / a nominalizer: turns a verb into 'doing something' or 'the fact of doing...'
additional_notes: Common spoken Korean pattern: verb stem + 하는 거 (or ~는 거) nominalizes the verb, making it a noun phrase meaning 'doing X' or 'the fact that X happens'. Used in casual and neutral speech. Can express an action, habit, situation, or something being discussed/pointed out. Often shortened in speech to '하는 거' with pronunciation changes (e.g., '하는 거 아니야' → '하는 거 아니거든').
native_language_example: Stop doing that.

meaning: colloquial/questioning ending: 'what are (you) doing?' or 'are (you) doing...?' (used to ask/criticize what someone is doing)
additional_notes: Informal, often blunt or confrontational. '하는 거냐' follows a verb stem (e.g., 뭐 하는 거냐? = 'What are you doing?'). Used in spoken Korean with friends or when expressing surprise/annoyance. Equivalent to the polite question '하는 거예요?' but much more direct. Not appropriate for formal or polite situations.
native_language_example: What are you doing here?

meaning: colloquial way to ask or emphasize 'what are (you/they) doing?' or 'is it that ...?' (expresses questioning or emphasis).
additional_notes: A casual, spoken form combining the verb stem + 하는 (doing) + 거야 (short for 것이야). Used to ask what someone is doing (뭘 하는 거야?), to express surprise or criticism (무슨 짓 하는 거야?), or to confirm understanding (이제 이해하는 거야?). Tone depends on context and intonation — can sound blunt or emotional, so avoid with strangers or in formal situations. Can appear with question marks or as a rhetorical/emphatic statement.
native_language_example: What are you doing here?

meaning: polite spoken form meaning 'are (you) doing / is (someone) doing / do (you) ...?' or 'what are (you) ...?' depending on context.
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + -는 (present participle) + 거예요 (polite ending) to ask or state in present tense. Commonly used to ask what someone is saying or doing (e.g., '무슨 얘기를 하는 거예요?' = 'What are you talking about?'). Can be used for asking how to do something when attached to 하다 (e.g., '이거 어떻게 하는 거예요?' = 'How do you do this?'). Polite and neutral—suitable for most everyday situations. With different verbs the nuance changes: asking about action (뭘 하는 거예요?), asking for clarification (뭐라고 하는 거예요?), or asking reason/intent (대체 무슨 얘기를 하는 거예요?).
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: used to ask for clarification or confirmation about an action or statement (roughly 'what are (you/we) doing?' / 'is that what you mean?').
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 하는 (doing) with 거죠 (contraction of 것 + 죠) to make a polite/soft question seeking explanation, confirmation, or surprise. Common in spoken Korean. Tone can be curious, confused, or mildly critical depending on context and intonation. Replace 하는 with other verb stems to ask about different actions (e.g., 어떻게 하는 거죠?, 왜 하는 거죠?).
target_language_example: 이 버튼을 누르면 어떻게 하는 거죠?
native_language_example: If I press this button, how do I do it?

meaning: used to ask for confirmation, express surprise, or question someone's action (roughly 'are/you doing...? / why are... doing...?').
additional_notes: Informal spoken ending attached to verb stem + 하다/other verbs. Can soften a question, show disbelief, or ask for clarification about purpose or reason. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be curious, annoyed, or confirming. Often shortened from '하는 거예요/하는 거지요.'
target_language_example: 왜 우리한테 이런 얘길 하는 거지?
native_language_example: Why are they telling us this?

meaning: the act of doing (something); 'doing' as a noun/topic (emphasizing the action).
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 하는 (present participle) with 건 (short for 것은) to nominalize the action and make it the topic or object of discussion. Used to emphasize who does something, to suggest or consider an action, or to say that an action is trivial. Context decides nuance (ownership, suggestion, minimization).
target_language_example: 그 일은 내가 하는 건 어때?
native_language_example: How about I do that job?

meaning: used to ask (often rhetorically or bluntly) 'what are (you/they) doing/saying?' or to question whether an action is actually happening
additional_notes: A conversational ending combining the verb stem + 하는 + 건가 (short for 것인가). It turns a statement into a question that can express genuine inquiry, irritation, disbelief, or surprise depending on tone and context. Common after verbs like 말하다 (얘기하다) — e.g., '무슨 얘기를 하는 건가?' = 'What are you talking about?' Not formal; often used in spoken Korean. Can be softened by changing intonation or using polite forms (하는 건가요?).
native_language_example: What on earth are you doing here?

meaning: used to give background, explain something, soften/contrast a statement, or ask for clarification; roughly 'it's that (someone) is doing...', 'but...', or 'how do you do...?' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is a conversational grammar pattern: 하다 (to do) + 는 (present participle) + 건데 (short for 것인데). It can (1) provide background or an explanation ('it's that...'), (2) express mild objection/contrast ('...but.../and yet'), (3) soften commands or complaints, or (4) form informal questions asking for clarification about what someone is doing. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation. Common in spoken Korean.
target_language_example: 지금 내가 하는 건데 잠깐만 기다려.
native_language_example: I'm the one doing it now, so wait a moment.

meaning: polite/question form meaning 'what are (you) doing?' or 'how do (you) do (something)?' (asks about the action)
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 하다 → 하는 with 겁니까, a polite and slightly formal question ending used to ask about an action or how something is done. Use with present tense actions. Can be used with different verbs (e.g., '뭐 하는 겁니까?' = 'What are you doing?' or '어떻게 하는 겁니까?' = 'How do you do it?'). Suitable in formal/polite situations; less casual than -아/어? or -니? endings.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: 'the act of doing' — a nominalized form meaning 'doing (something)' used to suggest, ask about, or comment on an action
additional_notes: 하는 게 is formed from the verb stem + 하는 (present participle) and 게 (short for 것이) to nominalize the verb: 'the act of doing...'. Common uses: suggestions/questions (e.g., '하는 게 어때?'), asking whether something is appropriate ('하는 게 좋을까요?'), rhetorical or critical comments, and everyday casual remarks. Formality depends on the verb endings and overall sentence; the phrase itself is neutral but frequently appears in casual speech.
native_language_example: Would doing that be better?

meaning: 'words said' / 'what (someone) says' (the things someone is saying)
additional_notes: Combines the verb 하다 (to do/say) in its modifier form 하는 + 말 (words). Used to refer to someone's utterance(s) or the content of what someone is saying. Can point to a specific recent statement or to habitual speech. Often appears in phrases like '네가 하는 말' (what you say) or '내가 하는 말' (what I am about to say).
target_language_example: 네가 지금 하는 말이 무슨 뜻이야?
native_language_example: What do the words you're saying now mean?

meaning: a person who does (something); someone who performs a specified action
additional_notes: Attach to a verb stem (verb stem + 하는 사람) to describe someone who performs that action. Can be used generally or to point out a specific person. To specify the action, place the object or phrase before the verb: 예: 요리하는 사람 (a person who cooks), 수리하는 사람 (a person who repairs). In casual speech, the form can be shortened or replaced with other relative constructions depending on register.
native_language_example: The person who is cooking is in the kitchen.

meaning: 'work; job; the things someone does' (what someone does / their occupation or tasks).
additional_notes: Used to ask or describe someone's job, duties, or what they do regularly. Can refer to occupation (profession) or everyday tasks depending on context. Common in questions: '하는 일이 뭐예요?' ('What do you do?'). Often follows a subject: '제가/내가 하는 일은...'.
native_language_example: My job is cooking.

meaning: 'do you know ...?' or 'know whether/what/when someone does something' (literally: 'know if/what someone does').
additional_notes: Combines a verb/adjective stem + -는지 (question/complementizer meaning 'whether/what/...') and 알아 (from 알다, 'to know'). Used to ask whether someone knows about an action, manner, time, etc. English rendering depends on context: 'Do you know how...?', 'Do you know whether...?', 'Do you know what/when...?'. Common in spoken Korean; politeness is adjusted by changing 알아 to 아세요/알아요/아십니까, or by adding polite endings.
native_language_example: Do you know how I do it?

meaning: 'in a day' or 'per day' (indicates frequency within one day).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens during one day (e.g., times per day). Can be followed by a number + 번 (times) or verbs/phrases about routines. Common in questions and answers about frequency.
target_language_example: 나는 하루에 세 번 커피를 마셔.
native_language_example: I drink coffee three times a day.

meaning: all day; the whole day
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for the entire day or for a long continuous period during the day. Can be followed by verbs (e.g., 일하다, 찾다) and often appears before the verb phrase. Neutral register; common in speech and writing.
native_language_example: I studied all day.

meaning: 'must not' / 'should not' (used to say an action is not allowed)
additional_notes: Short form of 하면 안 되다. Attach to verb stem + 하면 안 (or 하면 안 돼/하면 안 돼요) to forbid or warn. Can be softened with 안 돼요 (polite) or made stronger with 안 돼 (casual). Common in spoken Korean. Negation focuses on prohibition, not inability.
target_language_example: 여기서 사진을 찍으면 안 하면 안 돼요.
native_language_example: You must not take photos here.

meaning: Why don't you (do it)? / You should do it (suggestion or mild urging).
additional_notes: Casual to neutral suggestion or encouragement telling someone to do something. Often follows a verb stem (V + 하지 그래). Can be used helpfully, teasingly, or impatiently depending on tone and context. Not strongly formal — avoid using with superiors in formal situations.
native_language_example: Why don't you do it yourself?

meaning: 'Don't (do that)'.
additional_notes: A short, direct negative command using the verb 하다 (to do) + 지 마 (do not). Used to tell someone not to do something. Tone can be strong or scolding depending on context and intonation; add polite forms (하지 마세요) for respectful requests. Can be followed by commas or exclamation for emphasis.
native_language_example: Don't lie!

meaning: Don't (do it). A polite/formal negative command (please don't).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to do something politely or firmly. '하지' is the verb stem of 하다 (to do) + negative marker '지 말다' in the polite/formal imperative '마세요'. Can be combined with other verbs by replacing 하다 with the verb stem + 지 마세요 (e.g., 가지 마세요 = don't go). Tone can range from gentle request to strong prohibition depending on context and repetition.
native_language_example: Please don't do that.

meaning: do not (do something); don't.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to perform an action. Attach the verb stem (without -다) + 지 말다 to form a negative command or prohibition. Can be softened with polite endings (e.g., 하지 마세요) or casual (하지 마). In narrative contexts, alternative negative forms may be used; this pattern specifically expresses prohibitions or 'don't' instructions.
native_language_example: do not take pictures

meaning: '(to) tell someone not to (do something)'; reported command/request in colloquial Korean
additional_notes: Combines 하지 말다 (to not do) with the quotation/indirect speech marker -라고 to report an order or request. Used when saying you told someone (or told someone to tell another) not to do something, or as a quoted/direct command (e.g., 하지 말라고 해! = 'Tell them not to!'). Common in spoken/informal contexts and can convey anger or forcefulness depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: 그걸 하지 말라고 톰한테 말한 게 너야?
native_language_example: Did you tell Tom not to do that?

meaning: 'to not do' (negation of 하다 = to do).
additional_notes: Used to negate verbs by attaching 않다 after the verb stem (or by placing 안 before the verb). 하지 않다 is often used in more formal or written contexts; casual spoken form is 안 하다. 않다 is conjugated to reflect tense and politeness (e.g., 하지 않아요, 하지 않았어요, 하지 않겠습니다).
native_language_example: I do not do my homework today. / I will not do my homework today. (depends on conjugation; this sentence uses the dictionary form 하지 않다)

meaning: but/however, that (or that thing); used to contrast or object to the previous statement focusing on 'that'.
additional_notes: Combination of '하지만' (but/however) + '그건' (that + topic/subject). Used to introduce a contrasting point about a specific thing or idea just mentioned. Tone can be neutral or defensive depending on context. Followed by a clause giving the contrasting information (e.g., it's fake, wasn't enough, shouldn't have been a problem).
native_language_example: But that isn't true.

meaning: 'but I' — used to contrast previous clause, emphasizing the speaker (난 = 나는).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 하지만 (but/however) with the contracted subject 난 (나는). Common in spoken or informal written Korean. Use when contrasting your own state, opinion, or action with what was said before. If you want to be more formal, use 그러나 저는 / 하지만 저는.
target_language_example: 사람들은 포기하라고 했어. 하지만 난 포기하지 않을 거야.
native_language_example: People told me to give up. But I won't give up.

meaning: 'but I' / 'however, I...'
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 하지만 (but/however) with the subject pronoun 내가 (I). Used to introduce a contrast or objection about the speaker or the speaker's action/feeling. Often followed by verbs or adjectives describing what the speaker does, feels, knows, etc. Common in casual and neutral speech.
native_language_example: But I said it first.

meaning: 'but (still)' or 'however, not yet / still (something hasn't happened)'.
additional_notes: Combines 하지만 (but/however) + 아직 (yet/still). Used to contrast a previous statement and emphasize that something is not finished, not true yet, or continues to be the case. Common in everyday speech. Tone can be neutral or slightly defensive depending on context.
native_language_example: But it's not ready yet.

meaning: 'as for school' / 'school (topic marker)'.
additional_notes: 학교 (school) + topic particle 는. Used to set 'school' as the topic of the sentence — to contrast, ask about, or give information about school. In English this often becomes 'as for school,' 'what about school?', or simply the subject 'school' at the start of a sentence. Common in questions and statements: short replies can be just '학교는?' meaning 'And school?' or 'How about school?'.
native_language_example: As for the school, it will move to a new building next year.

meaning: to/at school (marks destination or location: 'to school' or 'at school').
additional_notes: 학교 = school. The particle -에 after a place marks either direction/destination ('go to school') or location ('be at school'), depending on the verb. With verbs of motion (가다, 오다) it usually means 'to (the) school'. With existence/state verbs (있다, 있다 안 가다) it means 'at school'. Polite endings and tense go on the verb, not on -에.
native_language_example: I'm going to school tomorrow morning.

meaning: must/go to school; have to go to school.
additional_notes: 가야 is the verb 가다 (to go) plus the ending -아/어야 which expresses obligation or necessity ('must' or 'have to'). 학교에 가야 is often finished with polite endings: 가야 돼요/됩니다/합니다 (polite/formal) or 가야 해 (casual). Use 학교에 (to school) before 가야. Tone ranges from casual to very formal depending on the final ending.
native_language_example: I have to go to school tomorrow morning.

meaning: at/from school; in school (location or source).
additional_notes: 학교 (school) + 에서 (location particle indicating where an action happens or where something comes from). Use 에서 to say 'at school' (doing something there) or 'from school' (e.g., coming from). Context determines translation: '학교에서 왔어요' = 'I came from school', '학교에서 공부해요' = 'I study at school.'
native_language_example: I met a friend at school.

meaning: 'student' as the topic (the student... / speaking about students).
additional_notes: 은 is the topic particle attached to 학생 (student). Using 학생은 marks 'student' as the topic of the sentence and often implies contrast or general statement about students. In English you can think of it as 'as for the student' or simply 'the student...'. For specific or new information (subject focus) you might use 학생이/학생가 instead.
native_language_example: As for students, if they have a question, they raise their hand.

meaning: the student (as the subject or topic; 'student' with subject particle 이).
additional_notes: 학생 = student. The particle 이 is the subject marker used after a consonant-ending noun (marks subject or introduces someone/something in a sentence). In spoken Korean you may also hear 학생이 pronounced naturally with linking. Compare with 학생은 (topic marker) or 학생가 (not used).
native_language_example: The student from Korea is the kindest.

meaning: I am / (someone) is a student. (Polite declarative/question form)
additional_notes: 학생 (student) + 이어요/예요 is the polite ending for 'to be' used after a noun. Use '이에요' after nouns ending with a consonant and '예요' after vowels; however many learners see 학생이에요 as the common polite sentence 'I am a student' or asking/confirming 'Are you a student?'. It can be used with 저는 (I) or with names/pronouns. Rising intonation makes it a question.
native_language_example: I am a Korean language student.

meaning: one (unit) for countable machines or cigarettes; 'one (item)' for vehicles or items counted with the counter 대.
additional_notes: 대 is a Korean counter used for vehicles, machines, and also colloquially for cigarettes (한 대/한 대 피다). When ordering or asking for cigarettes, 한 대 means 'one cigarette'. For cars, computers, TVs, etc., 한 대 means 'one (vehicle/machine)'. Colloquial speech may shorten or drop particles (e.g., '한 대 줘?').
native_language_example: Is there one car?

meaning: one (animal); a single animal (counter for animals).
additional_notes: 한 마리 uses the counter 마리 to count animals. It follows a number (한 = one) and is used for most animals (dogs, cats, cows, sheep, etc.). For other quantities, replace 한 with the number (예: 두 마리, 세 마리). In everyday speech, '한' is often shortened to '한' (not dropped) but pronunciation may run together.
native_language_example: I adopted one puppy.

meaning: once; one time; try (once).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a single occasion (once) or to soften a request/suggestion by meaning 'give it a try once' or 'try it for me.' Placed after verbs or alone as a short phrase. In negative structures it can appear as '한 번도' meaning 'not even once.' Tone is casual to neutral.
native_language_example: Let's try it once.

meaning: one more time; once again
additional_notes: Used to ask for or suggest repeating an action, giving another chance, or doing something one additional time. Common in questions and requests. Tone can be casual or polite depending on sentence ending; add polite endings (e.g., -요) for formality.
native_language_example: Please say it one more time.

meaning: 'just once' or 'only one time'.
additional_notes: Used to request or state that something happens or should happen a single time. Often combined with 딱 (exactly) for emphasis: 딱 한 번만 = 'just exactly once'. Can be used in statements, questions, or pleas (e.g., asking someone to do something one more time).
native_language_example: Help me just once.

meaning: one (drink); a glass/cup (of something) — used when offering or ordering a single serving of a beverage, often alcoholic.
additional_notes: 한 is the native Korean numeral for 'one' (before counters). 잔 is a counter for cups/glasses. Commonly used when offering drinks (술 한 잔? = 'Shall we have a drink?') or ordering/asking for a single serving (커피 한 잔 = 'a cup of coffee'). Can be used with 궁금한 tone: casual to polite depending on sentence; add polite endings as needed.
target_language_example: 저녁 먹고 와서 맥주 한 잔 할래요?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a beer (one) after dinner?

meaning: one sheet / one (flat) piece — counter for flat objects (paper, photos, tickets, etc.).
additional_notes: 한 is the native Korean numeral 'one' used before counters. 장 (張 / 장) is a counter for flat, thin objects like paper (종이), photos (사진), tickets (표), napkins, etc. Use number + 장 (e.g., 두 장, 세 장) to count such items. When speaking casually, the particle (을/를) may be dropped: 사진 한 장 찍어! = 'Take one photo!'
native_language_example: I need one sheet of paper.

meaning: colloquial past-action clause: '(did) ...?' or 'did (someone) do ...?' (used to ask or confirm about a completed action)
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 한 (past modifier) + 거야 (casual/colloquial ending from 것이다/거야) to talk about a completed action or to ask for confirmation or clarification. Common in spoken Korean. Tone can be surprised, accusatory, or simply inquisitive depending on context and intonation. Use with subject/context already understood; for polite situations use -한 거예요/했어요 instead.
native_language_example: Did you say that?

meaning: '(I/you/they) did (it), right?' — a past-action phrase used to ask for confirmation, clarification, or to express surprise about something someone did.
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + past participle 한 (did) with the sentence-ending particle -거죠 (short for 거지요), which softens the question and asks for confirmation or explanation. Common in spoken Korean. Use with subject/context: e.g., 내가 뭘 한 거죠? (What did I do?), 도대체 누가 그런 짓을 한 거죠? (Who on earth did such a thing?). Tone can express surprise, disbelief, confusion, or insistence depending on intonation.
target_language_example: 그 사람이 이 파일을 삭제한 거죠?
native_language_example: That person deleted this file, right?

meaning: colloquial tag meaning 'the one who did (it)' or used to ask/clarify 'did (someone) do (it)?' / 'what did (someone) do?'
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle/verb stem + 한 (did) with 거지 (a casual sentence-ending/noun phrase often meaning 'thing' or used to confirm/ask). It appears in two main uses: 1) as a short confirmation/exclamation: 내가 대신 한 거지! ('I did it instead, right!' / 'I was the one who did it!'); 2) in questions asking for clarification about an action: 내가 뭘 한 거지? ('What did I do?') or 대체 어떻게 한 거지? ('How on earth did (someone) do that?'). It's informal and common in spoken Korean. Use with friends or casual contexts, not formal situations.
native_language_example: How did (someone) do that?

meaning: what (someone) said; the words someone spoke
additional_notes: Literal components: 한 (did) + 말 (words). Used to refer back to speech someone has just or previously said. Often follows a noun or pronoun (e.g., 내가 한 말 = what I said; 의사가 한 말 = what the doctor said). Common in questions (Did you hear what I said?) and statements about remembered or reported speech.
target_language_example: 네가 한 말 다시 말해 줄래?
native_language_example: Can you say again what you said?

meaning: indicates a past experience of doing (or saying) something — 'have (you) ever ...?' or 'did (you) ever ...?'.
additional_notes: Used after the verb's past participle (verb stem + -한) plus 적 있다/없다 to talk about whether someone has ever done or said something in the past. Often appears in questions and negative statements. Context here: quoting speech ('...한다고/안 된다고 한 적') — 'have you ever said ...?'
native_language_example: Have you ever asked him?

meaning: the thing (someone) did; an action or behavior someone performed (often with negative tone).
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem or a subject+verb phrase to refer back to an action someone has done. Often expresses annoyance, blame, or criticism (e.g., 'the thing you did'). Common in spoken Korean. '나한테 한 짓' = 'what you did to me.'
native_language_example: Apologize for what you did to me.

meaning: the action/deed (that someone) did — used when talking about something someone has done (often negative).
additional_notes: 한 짓 is a noun phrase from 하다 (to do) + 짓 (act, deed). 한 짓을 is the object form (with object particle 을) and usually appears before verbs like 보다, 말하다, 책임지다, etc. Often used with a negative or accusatory tone to point out someone's (bad) actions: 'the thing you did'.
native_language_example: Tell me right now what you did.

meaning: colloquial ending meaning 'did (it)?' or emphasizing 'have/has done' (question or exclamation).
additional_notes: 한거야 is the casual spoken contraction of '한 거야' (하다 + 거 + 이야). It appears at the end of questions or exclamations to ask how/what someone did or to emphasize that something was done. Used in informal contexts; common in everyday conversation. In questions it often expresses surprise, confusion, or challenge (e.g., 'How did you do that?' / 'What did you do?').
native_language_example: How on earth did you do that?

meaning: one thing; one kind; one item.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a single thing, option, or kind among others. Common in questions and requests (e.g., ordering or asking for one item) and in statements (e.g., 'one reason', 'one way'). Can be followed by a noun or used alone as a brief reply.
native_language_example: Please give me only one kind of drink.

meaning: 'one (item)'; a counter phrase meaning a single unit of something
additional_notes: 한 is the native Korean numeral for 'one'. 개 (gae) is the most common general counter for countable objects (things, items). Together 한 개 means 'one (thing)'. Use when counting or requesting a single item. For quantities use: 한 개, 두 개, 세 개, 네 개. In casual speech you may hear just '하나' or shortened forms like '한 개만' = 'just one'.
native_language_example: Please give me just one (item).

meaning: one (animal); a single animal (counter for animals).
additional_notes: 한 is a number word meaning 'one'. 마리 is a counter used for animals (dogs, cats, horses, birds, insects, etc.). Put a number before 마리 (e.g., 두 마리 = two animals). Use with particles: 한 마리가 (subject), 한 마리를 (object), 한 마리야/예요 (identifying).
target_language_example: 고양이 한 마리가 창밖을 보고 있어요.
native_language_example: One cat is looking out the window.

meaning: 'one person' (a single person).
additional_notes: Used to count people. Attach to verbs or nouns to indicate exactly one person. Often appears with particles (이/가, 은/는) or with words like 만 (only), 씩 (each). Pronounced as '한 명' [han myeong].
target_language_example: 우리 집에 아이가 한 명 있어요.
native_language_example: There is one child in our family.

meaning: 'one blow' or 'one hit' (used figuratively to mean a decisive hit, strong comeback, or getting tricked/defeated once)
additional_notes: Literally 'one blow/shot.' Used both literally (a single punch) and figuratively. Common uses: shouting encouragement to strike once (얼굴에 한 방 날려!), describing someone being hit/defeated/surprised (한 방 먹었어 = I got hit/shot down), or saying someone got tricked/took a loss (한 방 먹었나?). Context determines whether it's physical, verbal, or metaphorical.
target_language_example: 그 팀이 마지막에 한 방으로 경기를 뒤집었다.
native_language_example: That team turned the game around with one decisive play.

meaning: 'once', 'one time', or used to mean 'give it a try' / 'just once' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literally means 'one time'. Used both to count occurrences (한 번 = once) and idiomatically to suggest trying something or softening a request/offering (e.g., '한 번 해 봐' = 'try it once'). Can combine with particles: 한 번도 (not even once), 한 번쯤 (about once/at least once), 한 번밖에 (only once). Tone/context decides whether it's literal counting or a casual prompt/request.
target_language_example: 한 번 와 봐. 분위기 좋을 거야.
native_language_example: Come once/try coming once. The atmosphere will be nice.

meaning: one more time; once again
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to do something one more time or to indicate repeating an action. Common in questions and requests (e.g., '한 번 더 할래?' '한 번 더 읽어줘.'). '한 번' means 'one time' and '더' means 'more', so the phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
native_language_example: Can you do it one more time?

meaning: 'not even once' / 'never (in expressions with past tense or negative)'.
additional_notes: Used with negative verbs or negative past expressions to emphasize that something has not happened even a single time. Often appears as '한 번도 ... 없다/없었다', '한 번도 못/안 ...'. It cannot stand alone without a negative verb.
target_language_example: 나는 한 번도 해외여행을 간 적이 없다.
native_language_example: I have never been on an overseas trip.

meaning: just once; only one time
additional_notes: Used to request or emphasize that something happen one time only. Common in polite requests when combined with -을까요/해 주세요 (e.g., 한 번만 해 주세요) and in emphatic commands or pleas (e.g., 한 번만 더, 한 번만 말한다). Often shortened in speech; tone can be pleading, urgent, or firm depending on context.
native_language_example: Could you help me just once?

meaning: one hour; an hour
additional_notes: Used to indicate a duration of 60 minutes or 'one hour from now' depending on context. Can appear with verbs like 걸리다 (takes), 남다 (remain), 후 (after) to show time remaining or time until an action. Korean spacing: 한 시간 (two words) is standard.
target_language_example: 버스 타면 집까지 한 시간 걸려요.
native_language_example: If you take the bus, it takes one hour to get home.

meaning: 'one (drink)' — a single glass/cup of a drink (often alcoholic); can be used as 'have a drink' or 'want a drink?'.
additional_notes: Commonly used when offering, requesting, or referring to a single serving of a beverage (especially alcohol like soju or beer). Can be literal ('one glass') or part of casual invitations: 한 잔 할래? / 한 잔 마실래? Polite forms add ~요 (한 잔 주세요). In negative or surprise questions, 잔 can emphasize quantity (한 잔도 안 하시게요? = You don't even have one?).
native_language_example: Shall we have a drink after dinner?

meaning: 'Korean (language)' as the direct object marker (marks what the verb acts on).
additional_notes: 한국어 means 'Korean (language)'. 를 is the object particle used after a noun that is the direct object of a verb (used after a vowel-ending noun). In these examples it marks 'Korean' as what is learned, spoken, wanted, or done. When the noun ends with a consonant, 을 is used instead. In casual speech the particle can sometimes be dropped, but including it is grammatically correct and clear.
native_language_example: I am reading Korean (texts).

meaning: 'Try it once' / 'Give it a try.'
additional_notes: A casual phrase inviting someone to try something one time. Often appears as '한번 해 볼래?' (Would you like to try?), '한번 해 봐' (Try it), or simply '한번 해' as an encouragement. '한번' = 'one time/once', '해' is the informal imperative of '하다' (to do). Use with friends or informal situations.
native_language_example: Try it once.

meaning: to try/attempt once; to take a look; to give something a try (casual suggestion).
additional_notes: 한번 (also written 한 번) means "one time/once." When combined with 보다 (to see/do/try) it often functions as a casual suggestion meaning "try it once," "take a quick look," or "give it a try." Common in spoken Korean; often appears in imperative forms like "한번 해봐" (try it once) or in phrases like "한번 보자/한번 보세요." Tone and formality depend on the verb ending used with 보다.
native_language_example: Should we try it once to see if it's a good method?

meaning: go to (someone) / go towards someone (spoken, casual)
additional_notes: 한테 is an informal particle meaning 'to' or 'toward' a person (used with people or animals). 가 is the verb stem of 가다 ('to go'); in casual spoken Korean you might hear 한테 가 (e.g., command or statement like 'go to them' or 'go to (that person)'). For polite speech use 한테 가요/한테 가세요 or to indicate direction to a place use 에 가다 (not 한테).
native_language_example: Go to the child and give them candy.

meaning: 'to/for (someone) + topical/contrastive marker' — indicates the person as the topic or contrasted focus (casual spoken form).
additional_notes: 한테 is a colloquial dative particle meaning 'to' or 'for' (used with people/animals). Adding 는 (topic particle) makes 한테는 emphasize or contrast that person or mark them as the topic. Used in spoken, informal contexts; avoid using 한테 with honorifics for elders or strangers (use 에게/께 instead: 에게는/께는).
native_language_example: To/for my mom (as for my mom), it's the dish I cook best.

meaning: to/for (someone) too; also to someone (casual dative marker).
additional_notes: 한테 is an informal dative particle meaning 'to' or 'from' when referring to people (similar to 에게/께 for polite/written). -도 adds 'also/too'. Use 한테 with people in casual speech; use 에게/께 for formal writing or polite speech. Examples: 친구한테 (to a friend), 친구한테도 (to a friend too).
native_language_example: Tell the friends too!

meaning: 'what (thing) to/for someone' — used when asking or wondering what someone has or will say/do (to someone).
additional_notes: 한테 = to/for (a person) (colloquial form of 에게). 무슨 = what/which (used before nouns). Together 한테 무슨 is often followed by a noun (e.g., 말, 질문, 생각) or a verb phrase to ask what someone said/did/will do to another person. Common in casual speech. Example structures: '한테 무슨 말 해?' (What did you say to them?), '한테 무슨 일이야?' (What's the matter with them?).
native_language_example: What did you say to Mom?

meaning: 'what (to/for) someone' — asks or refers to what (object/action) concerning someone
additional_notes: 한테 is an informal particle meaning 'to' or 'from' (with people) and is used to indicate the person affected. 뭘 is the contracted spoken form of 무엇을 (what + object marker). Together, 한테 뭘 is often used in questions or short phrases to ask what someone did for/said to someone, what to give someone, or what someone received. It's informal and common in spoken Korean (e.g., '네가 한테 뭘 줬어?' → 'What did you give them?'). In more polite/formal speech you might hear 에게 뭘 or 누구에게 무엇을.
native_language_example: What did you give (to) Mom?

meaning: 'to (someone) why' — used when asking why to/about someone (casual)
additional_notes: 한테 is an informal particle meaning 'to' or 'towards' (used with people). 왜 means 'why'. Together 한테 왜 is often used in casual speech to ask 'Why (to/at) someone?' or 'Why did you tell/ask them?' depending on context. Word order and tone matter: it can be part of a question (한테 왜 그래? — Why are you (doing that) to them/me?) or a short surprised complaint (한테 왜...?). For polite speech use 누구한테 왜 or add polite endings (예: 누구한테 왜 물어봤어요?).
native_language_example: Why did you ask that person?

meaning: will do / going to do (future tense, informal/plain speech)
additional_notes: Used to express future intention or plan. Commonly appears after a verb stem (하다 → 할 거야) in casual speech. Can also be used in questions to ask about someone's future action (뭐 할 거야? = What will you do?). Tone can be firm, surprised, or questioning depending on context and intonation. For polite/formal speech use 할 거예요 / 할 것입니다.
target_language_example: 오늘 오후에 영화 볼 거야? 아냐, 집에 있을 거야. 하지만 친구랑 저녁은 할 거야.
native_language_example: Are you going to watch a movie this afternoon? No, I'll stay home. But I will have dinner with a friend.

meaning: will do / going to do (future tense polite)
additional_notes: Polite future tense ending attached to a verb stem (하다 → 할 거예요). Used to express future actions or intentions, or to ask about someone's future plans. In questions it means "Will you...?/Are you going to...?" Contraction of 하다 + (것) + 예요; literal idea: "will do (thing)."
native_language_example: Are you going to do your homework tomorrow?

meaning: Are you/we going to do (it)? / What will (we/you) do?
additional_notes: Casual/informal future-intention/question form. Combines the verb 하다 (to do) + 건가 (short for 것인가), used to ask about plans, decisions, or what someone intends to do about a situation. Tone can be neutral or slightly blunt; context and subject (뭘, 어떻게, 우리, 자네 등) clarify who is acting. Often used in spoken Korean.
native_language_example: What are we going to do about this problem?

meaning: will do / planning to do (used to ask or state what someone intends to do)
additional_notes: Combination of future marker '-(으)ㄹ 건데' used to talk about future plans or intentions, often appearing in questions to ask someone's intended action or in statements to contrast or give background. In casual speech it can sound slightly blunt or confrontational depending on tone. When used in questions (e.g., '어떻게 할 건데?') it asks 'How are you going to do that?' or 'What will you do?'
native_language_example: So how are you going to do that?

meaning: thing to do
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs (dictionary form stem + '할 것') to refer to an action or task (a 'thing to do'). Can indicate a plan, instruction, or obligation depending on context. In speech it often appears in phrases like '할 것 같아' (seems like will do) or '할 것 같다' (looks like will do). When used alone, it often implies 'you should do it' or 'it's something that must be done.' Not a fixed verb form—'할' is the future/attributive form of '하다' + '것' (thing).
native_language_example: You will do this work.

meaning: seems like (someone) will do / probably will do
additional_notes: Used to express the speaker's judgment or prediction that someone will do something or that something is likely. Conjugates to match formality (e.g., 할 것 같아요 polite, 할 것 같아 casual). Appears after verb stem + -ㄹ/을 것 같(다) to show probability. Often follows an action verb to indicate that the action is likely to occur.
target_language_example: 넌 프랑스어를 공부해야 할 것 같아.
native_language_example: I think you should study French (You probably need to study French).

meaning: when (doing something); at the time of doing (something).
additional_notes: Attach to a verb stem (V + 할 때) to indicate 'when' or 'while' performing that action. Used for general times, specific moments, or to say it's not the right time (e.g., '할 때가 아니다'). Can be followed by clauses describing actions, feelings, or judgments about that time.
native_language_example: Turn your phone off when you study.

meaning: something to say; words to say (things one wants to say)
additional_notes: Literally 'to-do words' (할 = to do, 말 = words). Commonly used in questions or statements about whether someone has anything to say. Often appears in phrases like '할 말 있어?' (Do you have anything to say?) or '할 말 없어' (I have nothing to say). Tone can be neutral, curious, or confrontational depending on context.
native_language_example: Do you have anything to say?

meaning: things to say; something to say (often used to ask if someone has anything to say).
additional_notes: Literally 'words to do' (하다 + 말 + subject particle 이 omitted). Common in questions and statements: 할 말이 있어? (Do you have something to say?), 할 말이 없어 (I have nothing to say/I'm speechless). Often used informally but also in neutral contexts. Can be followed by verbs like 없다/있다/없냐/있느냐. When used imperatively (할 말이 있는 사람은 줄을 서!), it calls for those who have something to say to come forward.
target_language_example: 할 말이 있는데, 지금 말해도 돼요?
native_language_example: I have something to say — can I say it now?

meaning: to have something to say; to want to speak up
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to express an opinion, complaint, explanation, or important information. Often appears before directly addressing someone (e.g., 할 말이 있어요?). Can be neutral or slightly confrontational depending on tone and context. Commonly used in conversational Korean and polite forms add 요 (할 말이 있어요).
native_language_example: I have something to say.

meaning: to have something to say; to want to say something (often important, urgent, or complaining)
additional_notes: Commonly used when someone intends to speak up, express an opinion, or confront someone. Appears in various forms depending on politeness/intonation: e.g., '할 말 있어?' (informal/colloquial), '할 말 있어요?' (polite), or '할 말 있다' as a blunt statement. Tone can be neutral, assertive, or confrontational depending on context.
native_language_example: I have something to say to you.

meaning: Do you have something to say? / Is there something you want to say?
additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase. Literally 'have words to say' (하다 = to do, 말 = words, 있어 = have/exist). Used to ask if someone wants to speak or to challenge/comment (e.g., 'What more do you want to say?'). Tone depends on context and intonation — can be neutral, curious, or confrontational. For polite situations, use '할 말 있으세요?' or '할 말 있으신가요?'.
native_language_example: Do you have something to tell Dad?

meaning: can; to be able to (do something).
additional_notes: Combined with a verb stem + 있다/없다 to express ability or possibility. Common patterns: '할 수 있다' (can/able to do), '할 수 없다' (cannot). '할 수 있는' is the attributive form (able to ... / possible). Often contracts in speech (e.g., '할 수 있어' → '할 수 있어요').
target_language_example: 할 수 있는 건 다 해볼게요.
native_language_example: I'll try everything I can.

meaning: 'cannot' or 'can't' (unable to do something)
additional_notes: Casual/informal way to say you cannot do something or are unable to. From 하다 (to do) + 수 (way/possibility) + 없다 (there is not). Use with friends or in informal situations. Polite forms: 할 수 없어요 (polite), 할 수 없습니다 (formal). Can express inability (I can't) or emotional impossibility (I can't live without you).
native_language_example: I can't (do it) without you.

meaning: able to do; that which can be done
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem (하다 → 할) plus 수 있는 to describe ability or possibility. It can modify nouns (할 수 있는 방법 = a way that can be done) or stand in phrases like '할 수 있는 게 있나?' (Is there anything we can do?). Often translated as 'can' / 'able to' / 'possible'. Context determines whether it's ability, possibility, or suggestion.
target_language_example: 우리가 지금 할 수 있는 걸 먼저 하자.
native_language_example: Let's do first what we can do now.

meaning: the things one can do; what one is able to do
additional_notes: Used to talk about the actions or efforts someone is capable of or has done. Often appears with 다 했어 (did all one could) or 다 했다 (did everything possible). 건 is a casual spoken contraction of '것은'/'것' here. Common in past tense to express completion ('I did all I could').
target_language_example: 나는 할 수 있는 건 다 했어.
native_language_example: I did everything I could.

meaning: to be able to do; can / able to
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to express ability or possibility. Conjugates depending on tense and politeness (e.g., 할 수 있어요, 할 수 없습니다, 할 수 있었다). When negated, use 못 하다 or 할 수 없다. Common and essential for expressing capability or permission.
native_language_example: I can speak Korean.

meaning: can / able to (formal polite)
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to say you can do something or someone is able to do something. Combine with a verb stem: [verb stem] + 할 수 있습니다. For abilities (e.g., languages, skills) or possibility. Use less formal forms in casual speech (할 수 있어요 / 할 수 있어).
native_language_example: I can speak Japanese.

meaning: can do it / you can do it (able to do)
additional_notes: Present informal/neutral form of '할 수 있다' used to say someone is able to do something or to encourage someone ('You can do it!'). Use with verb stem before '할 수 있어' for specific actions (e.g., '수영할 수 있어' = 'can swim'). Casual speech — to be polite, use '할 수 있어요' or '할 수 있습니다.'
native_language_example: You can do it!

meaning: can / able to do (polite)
additional_notes: Polite form used to say someone can do something or to ask if they can. Combine verb stem + '할 수 있다' (to be able to do) conjugated politely as '할 수 있어요'. Use with different verbs by replacing '할' with the verb stem + '을/를' as needed (e.g., '말할 수 있어요' → can speak). Common for asking ability or offering encouragement.
native_language_example: Can you speak Korean?

meaning: You can do it / It's possible (isn't it?)
additional_notes: Used to state that something is possible or someone is able to do something. Can be a confident assertion ('you can do it') or a rhetorical tag question seeking agreement ('...right?'). Context and intonation determine whether it's affirmative, encouraging, or questioning. Informal, commonly used in speech.
target_language_example: 걱정 마, 천천히 하면 할 수 있지.
native_language_example: Don't worry, if you go slowly you can do it.

meaning: time to do (something); time for doing
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem or noun+하다 to indicate there is time to perform that action (literally 'time to do'). Often followed by 있어(요)/없어(요) to ask or state whether someone has time. Can be used in questions or exclamations. Compositional: 할 (do) + 시간 (time). Polite forms add 있어요/없어요 or combined with verb endings for formality.
target_language_example: 그나저나 다른 것도 좀 이야기할 시간 있어?
native_language_example: By the way, do you have time to talk about other things?

meaning: something to say; topic to talk about
additional_notes: Literally 'talk to do' (할 = to do, 얘기 = talk). Used when referring to things one wants to say or discuss. Common in phrases like '할 얘기가 있어요' (I have something to tell/discuss) or '할 얘기 없어요' (nothing to say). Polite/formal level depends on the verb ending used with 있어요/있습니다/etc.
native_language_example: I have something to tell the boss.

meaning: things to say; something to talk about (to tell someone).
additional_notes: From 하다 (to do) + 얘기 (talk/story). Used when asking or stating whether someone has something to say, tell, or discuss. Common in questions (할 얘기가 있어?/할 얘기가 뭐야?) and in statements (할 얘기가 있어 — I have something to tell you). Often followed by a verb or a clause (e.g., 있어?, 뭐야?, 있어서요). Polite forms add 요 (있어요).
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

meaning: something to do; tasks or plans (things one will/should do)
additional_notes: Literally 'things to do' (할 = to do, 일 = thing/work). Used for tasks, plans, or activities. Can be asked to mean 'do you have plans/are you busy?' (e.g., 오늘 밤에 할 일 있어? = Do you have plans tonight?). In casual speech can be shortened to '할 일 있어?' or used with particles: '할 일 알지?' (you know what to do), '할 일이라도 있어?' (Do you at least have something to do?).
target_language_example: 주말에 할 일이 많아서 못 가요.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do on the weekend, so I can't go.

meaning: 'things to do' / 'work to do' (tasks or things someone should/needs to do)
additional_notes: Literally from 하다 (to do) + 일 (thing). Used to talk about tasks, duties, or whether someone has something to do. Commonly appears in phrases like 할 일이 있다/없다 (to have/not have things to do) and can be used rhetorically (e.g., criticizing someone's behavior: '그게 엄마가 할 일이 아니면 뭐야?').
target_language_example: 오늘 할 일이 많아서 저녁에 못 갈 것 같아요.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today, so I don't think I can go tonight.

meaning: can do / know how to (do something).
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to ask or state whether someone has the ability, skill, or knowledge to do that action. Often appears in questions with (알다/모르다) or (아세요/있어요). Common in spoken Korean. The full pattern is '[verb] 할 줄 알다' = 'to know how to [verb] / be able to [verb]'.
native_language_example: Do you know how to speak English?

meaning: can do (able to do something); knows how to do
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to say someone has the ability or skill to do that action. Often appears in questions or descriptions (e.g., "~할 줄 아는 사람" = "a person who can do ~"). Can be polite or neutral depending on sentence ending. Commonly contrasted with "모르다/모르세요" for not knowing how to do something.
target_language_example: 불어나 영어를 할 줄 아는 분 없나요?
native_language_example: Is there anyone who can speak French or English?

meaning: to know how to do (something) / to be able to do
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to ask or state whether someone has the ability or skill to do that action. In casual speech it often appears as '할 줄 알아?' for questions. Can be used positively (할 줄 알아) or negatively (할 줄 몰라) to say you can or can't do something. Polite forms: '할 줄 아세요?' or '할 줄 알아요?'.
native_language_example: Do you know how to speak Korean?

meaning: Can (do something); know how to do (a skill).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone has the ability or skill to do an action (often followed by a verb or a noun indicating a skill). Polite/formal speech. Structure: [verb or noun] + 할 줄 알아요? = 'Can you [verb/skill]?' For negatives: 못 할 줄 알아요 or 잘 못 해요. Not used for factual knowledge (use 알다/모르다 for knowing facts).
native_language_example: Can you speak Korean?

meaning: will do / are you going to do (future, informal)
additional_notes: Informal contraction of 하 + (으)ㄹ 거야. Used to express future intention or ask about someone's future plan. Tone can be direct; commonly used in casual speech. For questions, word order and context determine nuance (e.g., surprising, impatient, neutral).
native_language_example: Are you really going to do this job?

meaning: 'grandmother' as the subject (with subject particle -가).
additional_notes: 할머니 means 'grandmother.' Adding the subject particle -가 marks her as the subject of the sentence. Used in questions and statements (e.g., asking for confirmation, describing actions). For beginners: recognize 할머니 (noun) and -가 (subject marker). In polite speech the verb form may change (하셨어요, 계세요).
native_language_example: Grandmother went to the market.

meaning: to try doing something; to give something a try (doesn't guarantee success).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 하다 (to do) with 보다 (to see/try) to indicate attempting an action. Used after a verb stem: V + -아/어/해 보다 (for 하다 verbs the form is 해 보다). Often expresses a suggestion, attempt, or willingness to experiment (e.g., '한번 해 봐' = 'try it once'). Tense and politeness are marked on 보다: e.g., 해 봤어? (have you tried?), 해 볼게요 (I'll try). In writing the verb can appear as one word (해보다) or separated (해 보다); both are understood.
native_language_example: Try doing it once.

meaning: try to do (something); attempt to do
additional_notes: Combines the verb 하다 (to do) in its stem form 하 + -아/어 보다 (here contracted to 볼) meaning 'to try/attempt'. Used to suggest or ask about trying something, or to express intention to try. Commonly appears as 해 볼까요?, 해 볼게요, 해 볼래?, 해 볼까?, 해 볼 거야? Informal in some forms depending on ending.
native_language_example: I'll try doing it once.

meaning: Try to do (it); give it a try.
additional_notes: Colloquial imperative/request form combining the verb 하다 (to do) + 보다 (to try) in the informal/banmal style. Used to tell or encourage someone to try something, ask them to attempt or check something, or demand they do it (tone depends on context and intonation). For polite speech, use 해 보세요 or 해 보십시오. Can be followed by objects or verbs (e.g., 전화 해 봐 = try calling).
native_language_example: Try a little harder one more time.

meaning: Have you tried (doing) ...? / I have tried (doing) ... (polite past)
additional_notes: From 하다 (to do) + 보다 (to try) in past polite form. Used to ask if someone has ever tried or experienced doing something or to state that you have tried it. Context and the verb or noun before 해 봤어요 determine the specific action (e.g., cooking, thinking, sexual or violent acts). Common in yes/no questions and short answers. Polite but conversational (standard polite speech).
native_language_example: Have you tried cooking eggplant dishes?

meaning: to do something for someone; to perform an action as a favor or on behalf of someone
additional_notes: Attach to a verb stem (verb stem + 아/어/해 주다) to indicate doing an action for someone’s benefit. Politeness depends on sentence ending (e.g., 해 주세요 for requests). Common contractions in speech: 줘(요), 줬다, 줘서. Can indicate obligation, permission, or gratitude depending on context and tense.
target_language_example: 책을 들어 줘서 고마워요. 내일 일찍 와 줘(요)서 도와줘요. 숙제 좀 해 주다 줄래요?
native_language_example: Thanks for holding the book for me. Please come early tomorrow and help. Could you do my homework for me?

meaning: Please do (something) for me / do (something) (imperative request).
additional_notes: Combines the verb stem + 주다 (to give) in an imperative/command form. Used to ask someone to do or allow something for you — softer than a plain command because it implies doing a favor. Can be attached to any verb stem: e.g., 보게 해 줘 (let me see / please show me), 설명해 줘 (please explain). Informal (used with friends or people of equal/lower status). For polite requests use ~해 주세요.
native_language_example: Please explain (it) to me!

meaning: the sun (with subject particle '가')
additional_notes: 해 = 'sun'. 해가 is the noun plus the subject marker 가, so it's used when 'the sun' is the subject of a sentence (e.g., 'the sun rises', 'the sun is visible'). Common verbs: 뜨다 (rise), 지다 (set), 보이다 (be visible). For beginner learners, treat it as 'the sun' in sentences where something happens to or by the sun.
native_language_example: The sun rose brightly today.

meaning: 'be able to accomplish' or 'can pull (something) off'.
additional_notes: 해내다 = to accomplish, to pull off, to manage to do something. 해낼 수 is the stem plus the ability/modal '수 있다' (can). Used to ask or state whether someone can complete or succeed at a task. Common in spoken and written Korean. Often appears with particles or endings: 해낼 수 있을까? (Can [they] do it?), 잘 해낼 수 있니? (Can you do it well?).
target_language_example: 우리가 이 프로젝트를 제시간에 해낼 수 있을까?
native_language_example: Can we finish/complete this project on time?

meaning: Can I/you do (this)? / Is it okay to do (this)?
additional_notes: Casual way to ask or give permission. Often follows a verb stem or stands alone as a shortened question. Structure: [verb stem] + 해도 돼? = 'May I/you do [verb]?' For more polite speech use -해도 돼요? or -해도 될까요?. When used alone (해도 돼?), it asks broadly 'Is this okay?' or 'May I?'.
native_language_example: Can I ask a favor?

meaning: May I / Is it okay to do (this)? / You don't have to do (this) (depending on context).
additional_notes: Polite/casual polite phrase used to ask permission or to say something is allowed. Literally 'do (it) + ok'. Can be used to grant permission (e.g., '해도 돼요' = 'You may do it') or to ask (with rising intonation) 'May I do this?'. With negation '안 해도 돼요' it means 'You don't have to do it' or 'It's okay not to do it.' Common in everyday conversation.
native_language_example: May I ask a question?

meaning: May I (do something)? / Is it okay if I (do)...?
additional_notes: Polite/informal-polite expression to ask for permission or check acceptability. Attach to a verb stem or use with pronouns/nouns as in examples (e.g., 내가 해도 될까요? 부탁 하나 해도 될까요?). Used in polite situations; softer than a direct demand. Can be used for requests, permission to act, or to ask to speak.
native_language_example: May I take a photo?

meaning: 'have (ever) tried/done (something)'; expresses whether someone has past experience of doing or trying something
additional_notes: Formed from 하다 (to do) + 보다 (to try/experience) in past participle 해본 plus 적 (occasion/experience). Often appears in questions or statements about prior experience and is commonly followed by 있어요/없어요, 있니/없니, or other particles. Can be used with modifiers and topics (e.g., ~해본 적 있어요?, ~해본 적은 없는데).
native_language_example: Have you ever had a thought like this?

meaning: 'must' / 'have to' (expresses obligation or necessity)
additional_notes: Common spoken form of 해야 하다; used after a verb stem to indicate that something needs to be done. Conjugates following 되다 (e.g., 해야 돼요, 해야 됐어요) and is slightly more colloquial than 해야 하다 but widely used in everyday speech. Can express obligation, necessity, or expected outcome. Note: some speakers and prescriptive grammarians prefer 해야 하다 as the more 'standard' form.
native_language_example: I must do my homework today.

meaning: Do I/should I have to (do this)? — expresses doubt or questioning about whether an action should be done.
additional_notes: Casual/questioning form combining the verb stem + 해야 (must/should) + 하나 (rhetorical/questioning ending). Used to ask oneself or others whether something should be done; can sound a bit emphatic or contemplative. In polite speech you'd use 해야 하나요? or 해야 합니까? Negative question: 해야 하나? can imply surprise or doubt. Context determines whether it's about obligation or simple wondering.
target_language_example: 오늘 그 일은 내가 해야 하나?
native_language_example: Should I do that task today?

meaning: 'Do I/we have to (do)...?' or 'Should (I/we) do...?' (polite question)
additional_notes: Polite interrogative form asking whether an action is necessary, obligatory, or appropriate. Formed from verb stem + -아/어야 (must/should) + 하나요 (polite question). Subject is usually inferred from context; you can add pronouns like 제가, 우리가, etc. Common in spoken and written Korean; tone is polite but not overly formal.
native_language_example: What should I do? / How should I handle this?

meaning: 'must / have to / should' (expressing obligation or necessity).
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to express that something is necessary or required. Conjugates with tense and politeness by changing 해야 하다 (dictionary) → 해야 해요 (polite) → 해야 합니다 (formal). Often contracted in speech to 해야 해 or 해야 돼 (when 하다 becomes 돼). Use with negative: ~하지 않아도 되다 (not have to) or ~하면 안 되다 (must not).
native_language_example: I have to do my homework today.

meaning: You/We should do (it); what should I/we do? (polite, asking for guidance or expressing obligation)
additional_notes: 해야 하죠 combines the verb stem + 해야 (must/should) with 하죠, a polite/softened ending used to ask a question or state expectation. Used when asking what should be done, expressing mild surprise or complaint about obligation, or seeking instructions. Can be used with 먼저 '뭘/어떻게' to form questions: 뭘 해야 하죠? / 어떻게 해야 하죠?
target_language_example: 이 문제를 지금 어떻게 해결해야 하죠?
native_language_example: How should I/We solve this problem now?

meaning: 'should do' or 'have to (do)'; expresses that something ought to be done (often as a question or mild suggestion).
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem + 해야 to suggest obligation or expectation. In questions it often softens or seeks advice (e.g., '뭘 해야 하지?' = 'What should I do?'). It can be combined with question words (뭐, 어떻게, 어디 등). Tone is neutral and common in spoken Korean.
target_language_example: 지금은 먼저 사과를 해야 하지 않을까?
native_language_example: Shouldn't I apologize first now?

meaning: 'to be something one must do' / 'to-do (that should be done)'.
additional_notes: Literally from 하다 (to do) + -어야 하다 (must/should) + modifier form. Used before nouns to describe an action or task that is necessary or expected (e.g., 해야 할 일 = 'work to be done' / 'things one must do'). Common in sentences about duties, obligations, or required actions.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things I need to do today.

meaning: whether/what one should do; expressing uncertainty about what action to take
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to talk about not knowing or asking what action to take, or whether to do something. Often appears in phrases like '뭘(무엇을) 해야 할지' (what to do) or '해야 할지 말지' (whether to do it or not). Common in questions and indirect statements. '해야' comes from 하다 (to do) in future/obligation sense + 할지 (part of the question/uncertainty marker '-지' with '-할' from 하다).
native_language_example: I don't know what to do next.

meaning: must / have to (need to do something).
additional_notes: Colloquial present-tense obligation using 하다 + 해야 하다 contracted to '해야 해' (soft obligation or instruction). Can express question (What should I do?/How should I do it?) or command (You must study). Tone depends on context; it's informal to neutral — not overly polite. For more polite form use '해야 해요' or '해야 합니다'.
target_language_example: 너 내일까지 숙제 꼭 해야 해.
native_language_example: You must finish the homework by tomorrow.

meaning: 'must' / 'have to' (polite)
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity in polite speech. Attached to a verb stem: verb stem + 해야 해요. Can be softened to 해야 돼요 (similar meaning). Context determines strength (urgent: '당장 해야 해요' = 'You must do it now').
native_language_example: I have to prepare for the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: 'can do (for someone)' or 'able to do (something) for someone'.
additional_notes: Derived from 하다 (to do) + 주다 (to give/do for someone) in the ability form 수 있다. Used when asking or stating whether someone can do a favor or provide something for another person. Often appears in questions (해줄 수 있죠?/해줄 수 있나?) and casual requests. Politeness level depends on sentence ending; add polite endings like 있나요/있어요 for softer requests.
native_language_example: Can you take care of this by today?

meaning: expresses that something was done (past) — often used to ask or emphasize that an action happened
additional_notes: Combination of the past verb form 했(다) + -던 (past habitual/retrospective modifier) + 거야 (colloquial ending for explanation or question). Used in spoken Korean to confirm, emphasize, or ask about a past action or state. In questions it adds surprise, accusation, or seeking clarification; in statements it can emphasize that the action was indeed done. Tone and context determine nuance.
target_language_example: 너 그 일을 이미 했던 거야?
native_language_example: So you already did that job?

meaning: 'good luck' (as an object in expressions like 'wish someone good luck')
additional_notes: 행운 means 'luck' or 'good fortune'. 행운을 빌다 (often shortened to 행운을) is a common phrase meaning 'to wish (someone) good luck.' You will hear variations in formality: 행운을 빌어(요)! (casual/polite), 행운을 빌어! (casual/encouraging), and simply 행운을 빌어/빌어요. Can be used when someone is about to take an exam, start a job, perform, etc.
target_language_example: 시험 잘 보길 바랄게. 행운을 빌어!
native_language_example: I hope you do well on the exam. Good luck!

meaning: at/on the scene; at the site (of an event, incident, work site)
additional_notes: 현장 (scene/site) + 에 (location particle). Used to say someone is or was physically at a location like a crime scene, incident site, construction site, or work location. Context determines the type of site (범죄 현장 = crime scene, 사건 현장 = incident scene, 시내 현장 = site in downtown). Often paired with verbs like 있다 (to be), 가다 (to go), or 오다 (to come).
